    "oldString":"## Output: `graph_t`\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    int           n_boxes;\n    box_t        *boxes;            // array of box descriptors\n    int           n_connections;\n    connection_t *connections;\n    int           n_size_classes;\n    int          *size_classes;     // distinct slot sizes the graph uses\n    int           n_entry_boxes;\n    int          *entry_box_ids;    // indices into boxes[]\n    int           n_languages;\n    const char  **languages;        // distinct language names used\n} graph_t;\n\ntypedef struct {\n    char         *id;               // user-defined box id (\"classifier\", \"stamp\", …)\n    char         *kind;             // \"call\" | \"data\"\n    char         *lang;             // \"lua\" | \"c\" | \"bash\" | ...; NULL for data and iterator/comparator\n    char         *ref;               // file path; NULL for data/iterator/comparator\n    char         *fn;                // function name; NULL for data/iterator/comparator\n    int           n_inputs;\n    input_decl_t *inputs;\n    int           output_capacity;  // bytes; 0 if variable-size (uses large-value heap)\n    int           is_comparator;\n    int           is_iterator;\n    int           n_iter_outputs;\n    char        **iter_output_names;\n    // …\n} box_t;\n\ntypedef struct {\n    int   from_box_id;\n    char *from_branch;              // NULL for plain call; \"lt\"/\"eq\"/\"gt\" for comparator;\n                                    // iterator output name otherwise\n    int   to_box_id;\n    char *to_input_name;\n    int   to_input_index;\n} connection_t;\n```\n\nStrings are owned by the graph (allocated from a single arena attached\nto the graph; freed when the graph is destroyed at the end of the run)."

          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"## Output: `graph_t`\n\n`graph_t` is opaque; the structs it holds (`box_t`, `connection_t`,\n`input_decl_t`, `routing_t`) are public so the dispatch layer can walk\nthem without going through accessors. Routing is a tagged union on `routing_kind_t`\n(plain / comparator / iterator / randomizer / weighted / distributor)\ncarrying the per-kind parameters in the same struct.\n\nEach connection holds both its original string endpoint refs (for\ndiagnostics) and the resolved integer indices (`to_box_idx`,\n`to_input_idx`). The topology pass fills the indices in; the dispatch\nlayer uses only the indices.\n\nThe graph also exposes:\n- `n_languages` / `languages[]` — distinct language names across call\n  boxes, filled in by `graph_attach_runtime`.\n- `entry_box_id` — single name from `meta.json` (the multi-entry set\n  described below is the work this iteration adds).\n- `map_dir` — the directory the graph was loaded from, kept so the\n  dispatch layer can resolve relative paths inside read / write boxes.\n\nStrings are owned by the graph (allocated from a single JSON arena\nattached to the graph; freed when the graph is destroyed at the end\nof the run). The box / connection / input arrays are plain malloc and\nfreed in `graph_destroy`.",

    "newString":"### 3. Schema validation\nBox kinds and what they mean at runtime:\n\n- **`call`** is a verb — a box that runs a function. Each call box\n  becomes a dispatch task in the pool when its inputs are ready. The\n  branching primitives that used to be separate box kinds\n  (comparator / iterator) are now expressed as a `routing` field on a\n  call box; the dispatch layer reads `routing.kind` to pick the\n  outgoing branch.\n- **`read`** is a value source. It can carry an inline `value`\n  literal or a `path` that the dispatch layer reads at run time.\n  When `value` is set the canvas hides the `path` input port. A\n  read box has no function to invoke — it just produces a value\n  downstream consumers can read like any other slot.\n- **`write`** is a file sink. It consumes one input and emits the\n  string `\"true\"` downstream after a successful write so it can be\n  chained.\n\nRequired fields per kind:\n- `id`, `kind` always required.\n- For `kind == \"call\"`: `ref` (source file) plus a `routing` object\n  (`{ \"kind\": \"plain\" | \"comparator\" | \"iterator\" | ... }` with the\n  per-kind parameters). `lang` and `fn` are optional — `lang` falls\n  back to the file-extension lookup in the spec registry, `fn`\n  defaults to the box id at dispatch time.\n- For `kind == \"read\"`: at least one of `value` (inline literal) or\n  `path` (file). Either can also arrive at run time on the implicit\n  `path` input port — the run-time check lives in dispatch.\n- For `kind == \"write\"`: no extra fields beyond `inputs` (the input\n  carries the bytes to write and the path).\n\nBox ids must be unique across the map. Connection endpoints must\nreference valid box ids and valid input port names.",

          "new_string":"### 6. Entry-box detection\nAn \"entry box\" is one the pool runner submits as an initial task.     "newString":" * Pipeline: directory walk, JSON parse, per-box schema validation,\n * topology resolution (string refs → integer indices), non-iterator\n * cycle rejection, per-edge same-language classification (issue 312),\n * entry-box detection. graph_attach_runtime then allocates input\n * slots sized per the feeders' declared output_capacity, resolves\n * each call box's language spec, and enumerates the distinct\n * languages and slot size classes the map uses.\n *\n * Errors out of any phase abort the load and return NULL with a\n * diagnostic via *err.\n */",
    "originalFile":"/* src/010-graph-loader.h — C graph loader (phase 3), public API.\n *\n * What it is, in a sentence: reads a map directory off disk, parses\n * every JSON file in it, and produces an in-memory graph_t that the\n * dispatch layer (issue 304) and the pool runner (issue 301) walk\n * to drive a run.\n *\n * Designed in issue 305. Aligned to the unified routing schema\n * from issue 233 — every call box carries a routing.kind, and the\n * legacy `comparand` / `iterator_outputs` fields are gone. The data\n * and file_write box kinds from issue 229 are dispatch-layer\n * primitives — they have no function to invoke.\n *\n * Memory model: every string the graph_t holds (box ids, refs,\n * function names, branch tags, paths, input port names) lives in a\n * single json_arena_t owned by the graph_t. graph_destroy frees the\n * arena, the box / connection / input arrays, and the graph_t in\n * one call.\n *\n * Errors: graph_load returns NULL on failure and sets *err to a\n * malloc'd diagnostic of the form \"<file>:<line>: <message>\". The\n * caller frees *err. The hard-crash policy of the rest of phase 3\n * (issue 303) applies upstream — graph_load's caller decides\n * whether to abort or surface the error.\n *\n * What's implemented now: phases 1 (directory walk), 2 (JSON\n * parse), and the first part of 3 (per-box schema validation —\n * kind valid, id unique, kind-specific required fields present,\n * routing schema validated).\n *\n * What's deferred to follow-ons within 305:\n *  - Phase 4: topology validation. Connections currently store\n *    string refs (to_box / to_input); resolving those to integer\n *    indices, verifying both endpoints exist, and detecting\n *    non-iterator cycles all land in the next iteration.\n *  - Phase 5: slot size class enumeration.\n *  - Phase 6: entry-box detection.\n *  - Phase 7: language enumeration.\n *\n * None of those block 301 / 303 / 306 from starting.\n */\n\n#ifndef SORAMECH_GRAPH_LOADER_H\n#define SORAMECH_GRAPH_LOADER_H\n\n#include <stddef.h>\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\nextern \"C\" {\n#endif\n\n/* {{{ Box kinds */\ntypedef enum {\n    BOX_CALL,    /* runs a function via a language spec                */\n    BOX_READ,    /* value source — inline literal or file at `path`    */\n    BOX_WRITE,   /* file sink — writes one input, emits \"true\" downstream */\n} box_kind_t;\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Routing kinds (issue 233 unified schema) */\ntypedef enum {\n    ROUTING_PLAIN,\n    ROUTING_COMPARATOR,\n    ROUTING_ITERATOR,\n    ROUTING_RANDOMIZER,    /* not yet parsed; reserved */\n    ROUTING_WEIGHTED,      /* not yet parsed; reserved */\n    ROUTING_DISTRIBUTOR,   /* not yet parsed; reserved */\n} routing_kind_t;\n\ntypedef struct {\n    routing_kind_t kind;\n    int            n_outputs;   /* iterator / randomizer / weighted / distributor */\n    double         comparand;   /* comparator */\n    /* Weighted routing: arena-owned double array of n_outputs\n     * entries. Normalised at runtime. NULL for other kinds. */\n    const double  *weights;\n} routing_t;\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Input port declaration */\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *name;       /* port name; arena-owned     */\n    const char *type;       /* \"string\" by convention     */\n    const char *literal;    /* NULL or arena-owned value  */\n    int         optional;   /* issue 230 optional flag    */\n} input_decl_t;\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Outgoing connection */\n/* String refs are preserved for diagnostics; resolved integer\n * indices are filled in by the topology pass and let the dispatch\n * layer (issue 304) avoid string lookups at runtime. */\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *to_box;       /* destination box id (arena-owned)        */\n    const char *to_input;     /* destination port name                   */\n    const char *from_branch;  /* NULL for plain output; else branch name */\n    int         to_box_idx;   /* resolved index into graph->boxes        */\n    int         to_input_idx; /* resolved index into target's inputs[]   */\n} connection_t;\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Box */\n/* Tagged so the forward declaration `typedef struct box box_t;` in\n * langs/lang-spec.h matches and the compile callback can accept a\n * `const box_t *` parameter. */\ntypedef struct box {\n    const char    *id;\n    box_kind_t     kind;\n\n    /* Call boxes */\n    const char    *lang;          /* \"lua\" / \"c\" / \"bash\" / NULL    */\n    const char    *ref;           /* source file (call only)        */\n    const char    *fn;            /* function name (call only)      */\n    const char    *returns;       /* declared output type: \"string\"/\"int\"/\n                                   * \"double\"/\"bool\"/\"bytes\"/\"json\"/\"void\"\n                                   * or NULL when the user hasn't said.\n                                   * Read by specs on the JSON-output\n                                   * path (issue 307 item 2). */\n    routing_t      routing;       /* call only                      */\n    int            output_capacity; /* 0 means variable-size        */\n\n    /* Per-box compile hints, optional, currently used by the C spec\n     * (issue 307). Lua / Bash boxes leave these at NULL / 0. All\n     * point into the graph's arena; no separate ownership. */\n    const char    *cflags;        /* extra flags appended to `cc`   */\n    int            n_link_libs;\n    const char   **link_libs;     /* each becomes `-l<name>`        */\n    int            n_headers;\n    const char   **headers;       /* `#include`d by generated wrappers */\n\n    /* Read boxes */\n    const char    *path;          /* file path (read only; ignored if value set) */\n    const char    *value;         /* inline literal; if set, read emits this directly */\n\n    /* Common */\n    int            n_inputs;\n    input_decl_t  *inputs;\n    int            n_connections;\n    connection_t  *connections;\n\n    /* Runtime state — populated by graph_attach_runtime, left at\n     * defaults (-1 / NULL / 0) by graph_load alone. */\n    int            spec_idx;       /* index into the spec registry; -1 if no spec  */\n    int           *input_slot_ids; /* n_inputs entries; -1 if not allocated yet    */\n    int           *input_slot_modes;/* 0 = PEEK (1-cell), 1 = POP (N-cell)         */\n    int            counter_slot_id;/* atomic-counter slot for iterator routing; -1 */\n    int            multi_spawn;    /* 1 if the box may fire many times in one run  */\n\n    /* 312 per-edge fast-path classification.\n     *\n     * One bit per input port: true iff the producer feeding that\n     * port shares this box's language. When set, the dispatch\n     * passes the slot's bytes to invoke_native as-is; when cleared\n     * the dispatch calls json_to_native first.\n     *\n     * One bit per outgoing connection (not per output port — a\n     * single output may fan to consumers of different languages):\n     * true iff the consumer on the other end of that connection\n     * shares this box's language. When set, push native bytes\n     * directly; when cleared, call native_to_json first and push\n     * JSON. */\n    int           *input_edge_native;   /* n_inputs entries, or NULL              */\n    int           *output_edge_native;  /* n_connections entries, or NULL         */\n} box_t;\n\n/* Slot mode constants used by box_t.input_slot_modes[]. */\n#define SLOT_MODE_PEEK 0\n#define SLOT_MODE_POP  1\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Graph */\ntypedef struct graph graph_t;\n\n/* Read a map directory and build the graph. Returns NULL on any\n * failure and sets *err to a malloc'd \"<file>:<line>: <message>\"\n * diagnostic. The caller frees *err. */\ngraph_t *graph_load(const char *map_dir, char **err);\n\n/* Free the graph and every byte it owns. Safe on NULL. */\nvoid     graph_destroy(graph_t *g);\n\n/* Accessors. */\nconst char  *graph_name        (const graph_t *g);\nconst char  *graph_description (const graph_t *g);\nconst char  *graph_entry_box_id(const graph_t *g);\nconst char  *graph_map_dir     (const graph_t *g);\nint          graph_n_boxes     (const graph_t *g);\nconst box_t *graph_box         (const graph_t *g, int i);\nconst box_t *graph_box_by_id   (const graph_t *g, const char *id);\n\n/* Find a box's index by id; -1 if missing. */\nint          graph_box_index   (const graph_t *g, const char *id);\n\n/* Distinct language names used by call boxes in the map (filled\n * in by graph_attach_runtime). The pool's spec init can use this\n * to skip workers for specs the map doesn't actually use. */\nint          graph_n_languages (const graph_t *g);\nconst char  *graph_language    (const graph_t *g, int i);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Runtime attach (phase 5 + 7)\n *\n * Allocates one slot per input port for every box and resolves each\n * call box's language spec from the registry. After this call, the\n * dispatch layer can read inputs via `box->input_slot_ids[i]` and\n * invoke the spec via `spec_registry_at(r, box->spec_idx)`.\n *\n * Slot defaults for this iteration:\n *   - cell_capacity = `default_cell_bytes` (or 4096 if 0)\n *   - n_cells = 1 (peek mode)\n *   - flags = 0\n *\n * Iterator-fed wires and the multi-cell pop mode land in a follow-on\n * — they need compile-time wire classification (issue 305 phase 5\n * proper) that this iteration ducks. Returns 0 on success, -1 with\n * *err set on the first resolution or allocation failure. */\nstruct slot_store;        /* opaque forward decl */\nstruct spec_registry;     /* opaque forward decl */\nint graph_attach_runtime(graph_t *g,\n                         struct slot_store    *slots,\n                         struct spec_registry *specs,\n                         int                   default_cell_bytes,\n                         char                **err);\n/* }}} */\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\n}\n#endif\n\n#endif /* SORAMECH_GRAPH_LOADER_H */\n",

/* resolved index into target's inputs[]   */\n} connection_t;\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Box */\n/* Tagged so the forward declaration `typedef struct box box_t;` in\n * langs/lang-spec.h matches and the compile callback can accept a\n * `const box_t *` parameter. */\ntypedef struct box {\n    const char    *id;\n    box_kind_t     kind;\n\n    /* Call boxes */\n    const char    *lang; They are now one helper. dst_lang may\n * be NULL when the caller doesn't care about the native count. */\ntypedef struct {\n    int n_feeders;     /* total connections ending at (dst_box, port)        */\n    int n_native;      /* feeders that are call boxes sharing dst_lang       */\n    int n_non_read;    /* feeders that aren't BOX_READ value sources         */\n    int has_variable;  /* any feeder declares output_capacity == 0           */\n    int max_capacity;  /* max declared output_capacity across feeders (>= 0) */\n} input_feeders_t;\n\nstatic input_feeders_t scan_input_feeders(const struct graph *g,\n                                          int dst_box, int port_idx,\n                                          const char *dst_lang)\n{\n    input_feeders_t f = {0};\n    for (int p = 0; p < g->n_boxes; p++) {\n        const box_t *prod = &g->boxes[p];\n        for (int k = 0; k < prod->n_connections; k++) {\n            const connection_t *c = &prod->connections[k];\n            if (c->to_box_idx   != dst_box)  continue;\n            if (c->to_input_idx != port_idx) continue;\n            f.n_feeders++;\n            if (prod->kind != BOX_READ) f.n_non_read++;\n            if (dst_lang && prod->kind == BOX_CALL && prod->lang &&\n                strcmp(prod->lang, dst_lang) == 0) {\n                f.n_native++;\n            }\n            if (prod->output_capacity == 0) {\n                f.has_variable = 1;\n            } else if (prod->output_capacity > f.max_capacity) {\n                f.max_capacity = prod->output_capacity;\n            }\n        }\n    }\n    return f;\n}\n/* }}} */",

          "new_string":"/* {{{ detect_entry_boxes() — phase 6\n *\n * Fills g->entry_box_ids with the indices of boxes the pool runner\n * should submit as initial tasks. A box qualifies when:\n *   - it is BOX_CALL or BOX_WRITE (the kinds that run as tasks —\n *     BOX_READ is a value source, never a task), AND\n *   - every non-optional input port has zero non-read feeders.\n *     Read boxes (literal-or-file value sources) don't count as\n *     upstream computation; a box fed only by reads can fire\n *     immediately on startup. Optional ports are ignored.\n *\n * A zero-input call box passes the loop vacuously and qualifies.\n *\n * The scan reuses scan_input_feeders so its definition of \"feeder\"\n * matches the native-edge and large-value passes — single source of\n * truth for \"what feeds (box, port)\". */\nstatic int detect_entry_boxes(graph_t *g, char **err)\n{\n    if (g->n_boxes <= 0) {\n        g->n_entry_boxes = 0;\n        g->entry_box_ids = NULL;\n        return 0;\n    }\n    int *ids = malloc((size_t)g->n_boxes * sizeof(int));\n    if (!ids) { *err = err_fmt(\"out of memory\"); return -1; }\n\n    int count = 0;\n    for (int i = 0; i < g->n_boxes; i++) {\n        const box_t *b = &g->boxes[i];\n        if (b->kind != BOX_CALL && b->kind != BOX_WRITE) continue;\n\n        int qualifies = 1;\n        for (int port = 0; port < b->n_inputs; port++) {\n            if (b->inputs[port].optional) continue;\n            input_feeders_t f = scan_input_feeders(g, i, port, NULL);\n            if (f.n_non_read > 0) { qualifies = 0; break; }\n        }\n        if (qualifies) ids[count++] = i;\n    }\n    g->n_entry_boxes = count;\n    g->entry_box_ids = (count > 0) ? ids : (free(ids), NULL);\n    return 0;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ resolve_topology() — phase 4 (partial: endpoints only) */",

Optional ports are ignored.\n *\n * A zero-input call box passes the loop vacuously and qualifies.\n *\n * The scan reuses scan_input_feeders so its definition of \"feeder\"\n * matches the native-edge and large-value passes — single source of\n * truth for \"what feeds (box, port)\". */\nstatic int detect_entry_boxes(graph_t *g, char **err)\n{\n    if (g->n_boxes <= 0) {\n        g->n_entry_boxes = 0;\n        g->entry_box_ids = NULL;\n        return 0;\n    }\n    int *ids = malloc((size_t)g->n_boxes * sizeof(int));\n    if (!ids) { *err = err_fmt(\"out of memory\"); return -1; }\n\n    int count = 0;\n    for (int i = 0; i < g->n_boxes; i++) {\n        const box_t *b = &g->boxes[i];\n        if (b->kind != BOX_CALL && b->kind != BOX_WRITE) continue;\n\n        int qualifies = 1;\n        for (int port = 0; port < b->n_inputs; port++) {\n            if (b->inputs[port].optional) continue;\n            input_feeders_t f = scan_input_feeders(g, i, port, NULL);\n            if (f.n_non_read > 0) { qualifies = 0; break; }\n        }\n        if (qualifies) ids[count++] = i;\n    }\n    g->n_entry_boxes = count;\n    g->entry_box_ids = (count > 0) ? ids : (free(ids), NULL);\n    return 0;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ resolve_topology() — phase 4 (partial: endpoints only) */",

          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"        for (int i = 0; i < g->n_boxes; i++) {\n            const box_t *b = &g->boxes[i];\n            if (b->kind != BOX_CALL || !b->lang) continue;\n            int seen = 0;\n            for (int k = 0; k < g->n_languages; k++) {\n                if (strcmp(g->languages[k], b->lang) == 0) { seen = 1; break; }\n            }\n            if (!seen) g->languages[g->n_languages++] = b->lang;\n        }\n    }\n\n    /* Distinct slot cell widths used across input ports. Each port's\n     * cell width was picked from max(feeder output_capacity,\n     * default_cell_bytes), so the same reverse-scan helper drives\n     * both the slot allocation above and this enumeration. The\n     * slot store's free-list pre-population (issue 302) can use\n     * this set to amortise allocations per class. */\n    free(g->size_classes);\n    g->size_classes   = NULL;\n    g->n_size_classes = 0;\n    int total_ports = 0;\n    for (int i = 0; i < g->n_boxes; i++) total_ports += g->boxes[i].n_inputs;\n    if (total_ports > 0) {\n        g->size_classes = calloc((size_t)total_ports, sizeof(int));\n        if (!g->size_classes) {\n            if (err) *err = err_fmt(\"out of memory\");\n            return -1;\n        }\n        for (int i = 0; i < g->n_boxes; i++) {\n            const box_t *b = &g->boxes[i];\n            for (int j = 0; j < b->n_inputs; j++) {\n                input_feeders_t fdr = scan_input_feeders(g, i, j, NULL);\n                int width = (fdr.max_capacity > default_cell_bytes)\n                                ? fdr.max_capacity : default_cell_bytes;\n                int seen = 0;\n                for (int k = 0; k < g->n_size_classes; k++) {\n                    if (g->size_classes[k] == width) { seen = 1; break; }\n                }\n                if (!seen) g->size_classes[g->n_size_classes++] = width;\n            }\n        }\n    }\n    return 0;\n}",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/src/010-graph-loader.c"
        }

ASSERT(s);\n    ASSERT(graph_attach_runtime(g, s, r, 64, &err) == 0);\n\n    /* Two distinct widths: 256 (for sink.a) and 1024 (for sink.b).\n     * The producer boxes themselves have no input ports,           "old_string":"## Current behavior\nThe C loader lives at `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` and replaces the\nphase 2 Lua loader. It opens a map directory, parses every JSON file\nunder it through the project's JSON parser, validates per-box schema,\nresolves connection endpoints to integer indices, rejects non-iterator\ncycles, and (via `graph_attach_runtime`) allocates input slots,\nresolves each call box's language spec, and enumerates the distinct\nlanguages a map uses. Per-edge same-language classification (issue\n312) also runs at load time.\n\nWhat is still missing from the design described below:\n- Distinct slot size class enumeration (phase 5). The attach pass\n  currently sizes every slot to a single `default_cell_bytes`, so the\n  per-box `output_capacity` declared in JSON only affects the\n  large-value flag, not the slot cell width.\n- A multi-entry-box array (phase 6). The graph remembers a single\n  `entry_box_id` from `meta.json` but does not derive the broader set\n  the spec describes.\n- `distributor` routing parsing (parser accepts `plain`,\n  `comparator`, `iterator`, `randomizer`, `weighted`).",
          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"## Current behavior\nThe C loader lives at `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` and replaces the\nphase 2 Lua loader. It opens a map directory, parses every JSON file\nunder it through the project's JSON parser, validates per-box schema,\nresolves connection endpoints to integer indices, rejects non-iterator\ncycles, derives the entry-box set, and (via `graph_attach_runtime`)\nallocates per-port input slots sized to fit declared producer output\ncapacities, resolves each call box's language spec, and enumerates\nthe distinct languages and slot size classes a map uses. Per-edge\nsame-language classification (issue 312) also runs at load time.\n\nThree small refactors landed in this iteration:\n- A single `scan_input_feeders` helper replaces three duplicated\n  reverse-scan loops that walked all producers feeding a given\n  `(box, port)`. Native-edge classification, large-value detection,\n  per-port slot sizing, size-class enumeration, and entry-box\n  detection all collect their facts from the same walk so any\n  future change to \"what counts as a feeder\" has one place to land.\n- All six routing kinds now parse uniformly (plain, comparator,\n  iterator, randomizer, weighted, distributor).\n- The `_routing_needs_counter_slot` set in `graph_attach_runtime`\n  now lists all four counter-using kinds (iterator, randomizer,\n  weighted, distributor) instead of three.\n\nFuture refactoring opportunities noted but not taken in this\niteration (each would route currently-duplicated logic through a\nsingle pathway, no behavior change):\n- The four `n_outputs`-from-JSON blocks in `parse_routing` are\n  near-identical and could share a tiny `parse_n_outputs` helper.\n- The two string-array parse blocks (`link_libs`, `headers`) are\n  near-identical and could share a `parse_string_array` helper.\n- `count_json_files_in_dir` + `load_boxes` both open the same dir;\n  a single-pass loader that grows the boxes array would remove the\n  double-walk.\n- `graph_box_index`, `graph_box_by_id`, and the inner lookup in\n  `resolve_topology` all do linear scans by id; a small hashmap or\n  sorted id list would collapse the O(n²) topology pass to O(n log\n  n) without changing observable behaviour.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/305-c-graph-loader.md"

        "type":"text",
        "text":"`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\nThe \"spaghetti\" you flagged shows up most when three places in the file each grow their own copy of the same reverse-scan loop, and then each one starts collecting one extra fact that the other two don't know about. Folding them into a single `scan_input_feeders` that returns a struct of facts means the next time you need a new fact about \"what feeds this port\" you add one line to the struct, not a fourth nested loop. Same shape works for any other \"scan-and-collect\" that's currently spread across passes.\n\nNotice that the helper sits one level *above* the slot store and the JSON parser — it doesn't reach into either. The loader stays the only thing that knows the topology, and downstream passes consume a small structured answer rather than re-walking the graph. That separation is what kept this refactor from cascading.\n\nA future move worth considering: a one-shot reverse index built right after `resolve_topology` so even `scan_input_feeders` becomes O(feeders) instead of O(n_boxes × avg_connections). Not worth doing yet — graphs are small — but the seam is in the right place for when it is.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\nIssue 305 is fully implemented. All seven phases now run in `graph_load` + `graph_attach_runtime`:\n- The phase-6 entry-box array is exposed via `graph_n_entry_boxes` / `graph_entry_box`.\n- Phase-5 slot widths are picked per-port from the max declared `output_capacity` across feeders, with the distinct set exposed via `graph_n_size_classes` / `graph_size_class`.\n- `distributor` routing parses cleanly and gets its counter slot.\n- The three duplicated reverse-scan loops are now one helper.\n- 18/18 loader tests pass and the full suite is green.\n\nThe issue file's \"current behavior\" section and stale header doc-block both match reality now, and a short list of further-refactor opportunities is recorded in the issue file so they're not lost. Want me to commit, or look at any of the remaining refactor seams next?"

Calling those \"deferred\" would mean the issue could never be closed, because any code can be tidier. Process\nspawn cost dominates; each call is its own fresh interpreter. There is\nno persistent Lua state between calls.\n\n## Concept\nThe Lua language spec implements `lang_spec_t` (issue 303) for Lua. It\nis the first reference implementation of the spec interface and the\nproof that the in-process FFI model works. It is also the simplest\ncase — no compile step, no out-of-process server.\n\nEach worker thread gets its own `lua_State`. States are not shared.\nPer-thread states need no locking on the call path; the state's\ninternals are only ever touched by the worker that owns it.\n\n`langs/lua/spec.c` is built into `langs/lua/spec.so` and loaded by\nthe pool runner via `dlopen` at startup, like any other spec.\n\n## Per-worker state\n\nInit creates a fresh `lua_State` and configures it:\n\n```c\nvoid *lua_init(int worker_idx) {\n    lua_State *L = luaL_newstate();\n    luaL_openlibs(L);\n    set_package_path(L);   // libs/, map src/, meta.json src_dirs\n    return L;\n}\n\nvoid lua_teardown(void *handle) {\n    lua_close((lua_State *)handle);\n}\n```",

        "content":"## Implementation log\n\n### Init + invoke + teardown — 2026-05-12\n\n`langs/lua/spec.c` now exports a real `lang_spec_t`:\n\n- `init(worker_idx)` creates a `lua_State` and opens the standard\n  libraries via `luaL_openlibs`. Returns the state as the per-\n  worker handle.\n- `teardown(handle)` calls `lua_close`.\n- `invoke(handle, file_path, fn_name, inputs, sizes, n, out_buf,\n  out_cap, out_size)` loads the file with `luaL_loadfile`,\n  executes the chunk (which is expected to return a module\n  table), pulls the named function out of that table, pushes each\n  input as a Lua string, calls via `lua_pcall`, and copies the\n  return as a string into the caller's buffer. The state's stack\n  is rewound to its baseline depth at every entry/exit so\n  cross-call leaks don't accumulate.         "text":"Looked at both. Status:\n\n**306 (Lua spec) — not blocked, and arguably already done.** Its implementation log records init/invoke/teardown, per-worker module cache, and (under issue 312's slice 4) full JSON input parsing + JSON output writing. The \"Open questions\" section is empty (\"(none currently)\"). The only thing the log explicitly deferred was \"rich return types (tables/closures), lands with 312\" — and that has since landed (the encoder in `langs/lua/spec.c` now turns Lua tables into JSON objects / arrays). I think 306 is ready to mark complete; the only work is a final verification pass + a body-update parallel to what we did for 305.\n\n**307 (C spec) — not blocked by another issue, but has one substantive piece of unfinished work inside its own scope.** The \"Remaining work\" section lists four items; three are done, item 2 is still open:\n\n> **JSON-output writing.** When `output_native == 0`, the C spec writes a JSON serialization of the return value rather than the user function's raw bytes. The wrapper knows the return type, so it can construct the JSON shape. Symmetric to (1); pending typed-wrapper generation so the spec knows what shape to serialize.\n\nThe dependency is internal — item 2 is gated on the typed-wrapper generation that the C spec hasn't built yet. The `headers` field on `box_t` is parsed but unused for the same reason (\"lights up with wrapper generation\"). That generator is the meat of what's left.\n\nSo my suggestion (most-valuable first):\n\n1. **Close out 306** — verify the spec body matches what shipped, drop the deferred-rich-returns line from the log since it's untrue now, and move it to `completed/` like we just did with 305.\n2. **Implement 307's typed-wrapper generation** — this is the substantive build: a small code generator that emits a per-box wrapper around the user's C function, converting native bytes ⇄ JSON per the declared input and return types. Once that's in, both item 2 (JSON output) and the dormant `headers` field light up together.\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\nThe pattern across 305/306/307 is the same: a phase-3 issue grows substantial scope, the implementation log accumulates a paragraph per slice, and by the time the work is \"done\" the issue body lags reality by a couple of months. The cure is the same maneuver we did on 305 — pull the \"Current behavior\" section forward to match what shipped, drop resolved open questions, and let the log keep its history. The issue file is a living spec, not a changelog.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\nWant me to start with 306 (close-out pass), then move to 307 (typed wrapper)? Or take them in a different order?"

If the serialized value exceeds that, abort\n(per the hard-crash policy in issue 303). For variable-size outputs\nthe box declares `output_capacity = 0` and uses the large-value heap\n(issue 302); the spec writes into that heap and stores the handle in\n`out_buf`.\n\ndkjson is the table serializer in both directions (input parsing\nabove and output serialization here). It is already vendored.\n\n## Error handling\n\nEvery `lua_pcall` is wrapped:\n```c\nint rc = lua_pcall(L, n_args, 1, 0);\nif (rc != LUA_OK) {\n    fprintf(stderr, \"[lua spec] %s:%s — %s\\n\",\n            file_path, fn_name, lua_tostring(L, -1));\n    lua_pop(L, 1);\n    return 1;  // dispatch layer aborts the program\n}\n```\n\nLua errors (`error(...)`, runtime errors, syntax errors during file\nload) all surface here as nonzero `pcall` returns. The spec prints\nthe box context and the Lua error message to stderr, then returns\nnonzero. The dispatch layer aborts.\n\nThere is no try-and-recover. Per issue 303, errors crash the program.\n\n## Build\n\n```\nlangs/lua/\n    spec.c          ← lang_spec_t implementation\n    Makefile        ← builds spec.so\n    spec.so         ← built artifact (gitignored)\n```\n\nThe Makefile target:\n```make\nspec.so: spec.c\n\t$(CC) -shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall \\\n\t    -I$(LUA_INCLUDE) \\\n\t    -o $@ $< \\\n\t    -L$(LUA_LIB) -lluajit-5.1\n```\n\nLuaJIT is the assumed runtime — it matches the phase 2 driver and the\nproject preference (LuaJIT-compatible Lua, no 5.4 syntax). The build\nlinks against the system LuaJIT shared library.\n\n## Open questions\n\n(none currently — earlier questions resolved as follows:)\n\n- nil return: valid. Zero-byte output, downstream consumers\n  interpret per their declared input type.\n- Multiple return values: wrapped into a table and JSON-encoded via\n  dkjson. No values dropped.\n- Table serializer: dkjson, already vendored. Used in both\n  directions (input parsing and output serialization).\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Set up `langs/lua/` directory with a Makefile that builds an empty\n   `spec.so` exporting a stub `soramech_lang_spec`.\n2. Implement `init` and `teardown`. Verify the pool runner can\n   `dlopen` the spec and call `init` per worker without errors.\n3. Implement file-and-function caching — load a file, store its\n   returned table in the registry, look it up later.\n4. Implement input marshalling: push bytes as strings, count args.\n5. Implement `lua_pcall` invocation with error wrapping.\n6. Implement string return marshalling. Smoke test: `maps/hello`\n   end-to-end through the pool.\n7. Implement number return marshalling.\n8. Implement table-via-JSON return marshalling.\n9. Add `package.path` resolution for libs/, src/, and `meta.src_dirs`.\n10. Test against `maps/classify-demo` and `maps/driver-test` (Lua\n    portions).\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `drivers/lua.sh` — phase 2 Lua driver, retired by this spec\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — interface header (issue 303)\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec contract this implements\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer that calls\n  `invoke`\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — large-value heap for\n  variable-size returns\n- `libs/dkjson` (vendored) — table-to-JSON serialization\n- `maps/hello`, `maps/classify-demo` — Lua-only smoke test maps\n\n## Implementation log\n\n### Init + invoke + teardown — 2026-05-12\n\n`langs/lua/spec.c` now exports a real `lang_spec_t`:\n\n- `init(worker_idx)` creates a `lua_State` and opens the standard\n  libraries via `luaL_openlibs`. Returns the state as the per-\n  worker handle.\n- `teardown(handle)` calls `lua_close`.\n- `invoke(handle, file_path, fn_name, inputs, sizes, n, out_buf,\n  out_cap, out_size)` loads the file with `luaL_loadfile`,\n  executes the chunk (which is expected to return a module\n  table), pulls the named function out of that table, pushes each\n  input as a Lua string, calls via `lua_pcall`, and copies the\n  return as a string into the caller's buffer. The state's stack\n  is rewound to its baseline depth at every entry/exit so\n  cross-call leaks don't accumulate. Errors at every step\n  surface as nonzero return and a stderr message.\n\nFive end-to-end tests in `tests/306-lua-spec-test.c` exercise the\ninit/teardown round-trip, a `greet(name, salutation)` call with\nboth args, the same call with one arg (the Lua side defaults\nsalutation to \"Hello\"), and the two failure modes (missing\nfunction, missing file). The test loads the spec through the\nreal spec registry via dlopen, so this is the actual artifact\nthe pool runner will consume.\n\nDeferred:\n- **Rich return types.** The current invoke serializes the return\n  with `lua_tolstring`, which handles strings/numbers/booleans/\n  nil via tostring semantics. Tables, closures, and other\n  structured values land with the fast-path work in issue 312.\n\n### Per-worker module cache — 2026-05-12\n\n`lua_init` now seeds an empty Lua table at\n`LUA_REGISTRYINDEX[LUA_CACHE_KEY]`. `lua_invoke` looks up the\nbox's `file_path` in that table; on a hit it skips the\n`luaL_loadfile + lua_pcall` round-trip and uses the cached\nmodule table directly; on a miss it loads, runs the chunk,\nverifies the module table shape, and stashes the result in the\ncache before proceeding.\n\nThe cache is per-worker (each worker has its own `lua_State`),\nwhich means no locking. It's also per-file-path string, so two\nboxes that share a source file share a module table on each\nworker — calling `M.greet` from one box doesn't reload the\nchunk when another box later calls `M.farewell` on the same\nfile.\n\nCache invalidation is intentionally absent for now: once a file\nis loaded, its module table sticks for the run. If the box\nsource changes mid-run, the worker won't notice. Fine for the\nread-once-then-execute usage; revisit when there's a use case\nfor hot-reload.\n",
      "totalLines":319,
      "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/306-lua-language-spec.md",

          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"# 306 — Lua language spec implementation (reference spec)\n\n## Status\ncomplete\n\n## Current behavior\n`langs/lua/spec.{c,Makefile}` builds `langs/lua/spec.so`, dlopened by\nthe pool runner via the spec registry (issue 303). The\n`is_native` bit per input is set by the graph loader's per-edge\nclassification (issue 312) — true when the producer feeding this port\nis a call box in the same language (Lua → Lua), false when bytes are\nJSON-encoded by an upstream of a different language (or by anyone\ndeliberately writing JSON).\n\n- `is_native == 1` → `lua_pushlstring(L, bytes, size)`. The user's\n  function sees the bytes as a Lua string and is free to call\n  `tonumber`, `tostring`, etc. on them — same convention as the\n  phase 2 driver.\n- `is_native == 0` → parse the bytes as JSON via the project parser\n  and push the resulting Lua value (table for arrays/objects,\n  number/string/boolean/nil for primitives).     "oldString":"## Input marshalling\n\nInputs arrive at `invoke` as `(void *bytes, int size)` pairs. The\nspec is responsible for converting each input's bytes into the Lua\nvalue type the user's function expects. The user's function sees\narguments as native Lua values — never a raw byte buffer that the\nfunction has to parse itself.\n\nEach input has a declared type in the box JSON\n(`{\"name\": \"count\", \"type\": \"number\"}`). The graph loader (issue 305)\nrecords this type on the `input_decl_t` and passes the type alongside\nthe bytes when calling `invoke`. The Lua spec dispatches on type:\n\n| Declared type | Lua spec action                                             |\n|---------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|\n| `string`      | `lua_pushlstring(L, bytes, size)`                           |\n| `number`      | parse with `strtod`, `lua_pushnumber`                       |\n| `integer`     | parse with `strtoll`, `lua_pushinteger`                     |\n| `boolean`     | strcmp against `\"true\"` / `\"false\"`, `lua_pushboolean`      |\n| `json`        | call `dkjson.decode` on the bytes, push the resulting table |\n| `bytes`       | `lua_pushlstring` (raw, may contain nulls)                  |\n| `any`         | treat as `string` for now                                   |\n\nThe Lua function then takes typed arguments:\n\n```lua\nfunction M.add(a, b)            -- both already numbers\n    return a + b\nend\n\nfunction M.classify(payload)    -- payload is already a table\n    return payload.kind\nend\n```\n\nThe user does not write `tonumber` or `dkjson.decode` calls inside\ntheir box function. The spec did that work before the function was\ncalled.\n\nIf a parse fails (`json` input that isn't valid JSON, `number` input\nthat isn't a number), the spec returns nonzero and the dispatch layer\naborts (per issue 303)."
  },

The spec converts the\nreturn into bytes for the output slot:\n\n| Return shape           | Spec action                                                   |\n|------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|\n| Single string          | `lua_tolstring` → copy into `out_buf`                         |\n| Single number          | `snprintf(\"%.17g\", ...)` into `out_buf`                       |\n| Single boolean         | write `\"true\"` or `\"false\"`                                   |\n| Single table           | `dkjson.encode` into `out_buf`                                |\n| Single nil             | `*out_size = 0` (zero-byte output)                            |\n| Multiple values        | wrap into a table `{v1, v2, ...}` and `dkjson.encode`         |\n\n`nil` is a valid return. The spec writes zero bytes and sets\n`*out_size = 0`. Downstream consumers receive a zero-byte slot value;\nhow they interpret it depends on their declared input type (typed\n`number` consumer fails to parse; typed `string` consumer gets an\nempty string; typed `json` consumer parses zero bytes as `null` via\ndkjson). We cannot demand that user functions never return nil, so we\nhandle it.\n\nMultiple return values are wrapped into a table and JSON-encoded.\nPhase 2 silently dropped extra returns; phase 3 keeps them — the\nserialized form is `[v1, v2, ...]`.\n\nOutput buffer is sized to the box's declared `output_capacity`\n(issue 305's `box_t`). If the serialized value exceeds that, abort\n(per the hard-crash policy in issue 303). For variable-size outputs\nthe box declares `output_capacity = 0` and uses the large-value heap\n(issue 302); the spec writes into that heap and stores the handle in\n`out_buf`.\n\ndkjson is the table serializer in both directions (input parsing\nabove and output serialization here). It is already vendored.",
          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"## Return marshalling\n\nThe Lua function returns one or more values. The spec converts the\nreturn into bytes for the output slot, with the format chosen by an\n`output_native` flag passed in from the dispatch layer (set by the\nloader's per-connection classification):\n\n- `output_native == 1` and a single string return → `lua_tolstring`,\n  raw bytes into `out_buf`.\n- Anything else (multi-return, non-string, or `output_native == 0`)\n  → JSON-encode via the project's `json_writer_t`. Lua tables become\n  JSON arrays or objects depending on shape; primitives become\n  their JSON spellings; `nil` becomes a zero-byte output.\n\n`nil` is a valid return — zero bytes, downstream consumers\ninterpret per their wire's classification (a native-input port sees\nan empty string; a JSON-input port parses zero bytes as `null`).\n\nMultiple return values are wrapped into a table `{v1, v2, ...}` and\nJSON-encoded. Phase 2 silently dropped extras; phase 3 keeps them.\n\nOutput buffer is sized from the producer's declared\n`output_capacity` (issue 305). If the serialized value exceeds that,\nabort per the hard-crash policy in issue 303. Variable-size outputs\ndeclare `output_capacity = 0` and use the large-value heap (issue\n302); the spec writes through the same `out_buf` pointer and the\nslot store handles the heap path transparently.\n\nThe JSON encoder is the project's own (`libs/json/json.c`, designed\nin issue 314) — dkjson was the original plan but the project parser\nshipped first and avoided a vendored Lua dependency on the encode\npath.",

Process spawn cost dominates; each call\nis its own freshly-launched executable. The phase 2 driver compiles\nto a standalone binary, not a `.so`.\n\n## Concept\nThe C language spec implements `lang_spec_t` (issue 303) for C. It is\nthe second reference implementation, and the first one that exercises\nthe `compile` callback. After compile, invocation is in-process via\n`dlopen` / `dlsym` — the user's compiled function is called directly\nthrough a function pointer, with no subprocess and no IPC.\n\nThis is the \"Option 1 — LuaJIT FFI\" model from\n`docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`, applied to C: same-process call,\nnanosecond-overhead invocation, native-typed access. The only thing\nthe C spec adds over the Lua spec is the compile step.\n\n## Per-worker state\n\n`init` returns a small struct holding the dlopen-handle cache:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    void  *so_handles[MAX_BOXES];   // per-file .so handle, indexed by file id\n    void  *fn_ptrs   [MAX_BOXES];   // per-(file, fn) cached function pointer\n    int    n_cached;\n    // (a hash table could replace these arrays if MAX_BOXES grows large)\n} c_handle_t;\n\nvoid *c_init(int worker_idx);\nvoid  c_teardown(void *handle);    // dlclose every cached handle\n```\n\nEach worker thread has its own cache. The same `.so` will end up\nloaded once per worker, since `dlopen` with the same path on the same\nprocess returns a refcounted handle (the underlying code segment is\nshared across all callers — the per-worker `dlopen` is just a\nrefcount bump after the first).\n\n## Compile callback\n\nThe C spec's `compile` callback receives the box's metadata in\naddition to the source and output paths, so it knows the function's\nsignature and can generate the wrapper:\n\n```c\nint c_compile(const char *src_path, const char *out_path, const box_t *box);\n```\n\n(This is a small extension to `lang_spec_t` in issue 303 — `compile`\ngains a `box_t` pointer. Lua's compile is NULL, so unaffected.)\n\nThe callback:\n1. Reads `box->inputs`, `box->returns`, `box->headers`, `box->link_libs`,\n   `box->cflags` from the box metadata.\n2. Generates a wrapper `.c` file (see \"Wrapper generation\" below) in\n   the map's `compiled/bin/` directory next to where the `.so` will\n   land.\n3. Forks and execs the system `cc` with:\n   - `-shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall` (defaults)\n   - The user's `cflags`, if any\n   - The wrapper `.c` and the user's `src_path` (if `ref` is set)\n   - `-o out_path`\n   - `-l<lib>` for each entry in `box->link_libs`\n4. Waits for the compiler, returns 0 on success, 1 on failure.\n\nIf the resulting `.so` is newer than the user's source and the\nwrapper, compile is skipped (mtime check, same as phase 2).\n\nThe compiler is `cc` — the system default. `gcc` on most Linux,\n`clang` on macOS. ## [361]

```json
{
  "sessionId":"a8fd7497-fc00-4f59-9644-b90753877f2a",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-22T18:40:01.096Z",
  "entrypoint":"cli",
  "version":"2.1.121",
  "gitBranch":"master",
  "message":{
    "content":[{
        "type":"tool_result",
        "is_error":false,
        "content":"reason for the spec interface in the first place.\n\nUsers do not write a SoraMech-specific C signature. They reference\nany C function — whether one they wrote themselves, or one from a\nlibrary (zlib, OpenCV, libcurl, anything they have headers for) —\nand the C spec generates a thin wrapper that bridges SoraMech's\nbytes-in / bytes-out ABI to the function's natural typed C\nsignature.\n\n### What the user provides\nEither:\n- A `.c` file containing the function, referenced by `ref` in the\n  box JSON; or\n- A library function from a header, no `.c` file of their own — the\n  `ref` field is omitted, the function name and headers are\n  declared in the box JSON, and the library is named in\n  `link_libs`.\n\n### Box JSON for a user-written function\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"classify\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"lang\": \"c\",\n  \"ref\": \"classify.c\",\n  \"fn\": \"classify\",\n  \"inputs\": [\n    {\"name\": \"text\",   \"type\": \"string\"},\n    {\"name\": \"weight\", \"type\": \"int\"}\n  ],\n  \"returns\": \"int\"\n}\n```\n\nThe user's `.c` file is naturally written:\n\n```c\n// maps/<name>/src/classify.c\nint classify(const char *text, int weight) {\n    if (text[0] >= '0' && text[0] <= '9') return weight * 1;\n    return weight * 2;\n}\n```\n\nNo header to include, no macro, no `int classify(SM_BOX_ARGS)`.\nJust a function with a typed signature.\n\n### Box JSON for a library function (no user source)\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"compress\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"lang\": \"c\",\n  \"fn\": \"compress2\",\n  \"headers\": [\"<zlib.h>\"],\n  \"link_libs\": [\"z\"],\n  \"inputs\": [\n    {\"name\": \"src\",   \"type\": \"bytes\"},\n    {\"name\": \"level\", \"type\": \"int\"}\n  ],\n  \"returns\": \"bytes\"\n}\n```\n\nThe wrapper includes `<zlib.h>`, calls `compress2`, and the linker\npulls in `libz` via `-lz`. No user-written `.c` file.\n\n### Wrapper generation\n\nThe compile callback emits a wrapper `.c` for each C box. The\nwrapper has a fixed entry-point name (`sm_box_entry`) that the spec\nalways `dlsym`s.           "new_string":"# 307 — C language spec implementation\n\n## Status\ncomplete\n\n## Current behavior\n`langs/c/spec.{c,Makefile}` builds `langs/c/spec.so`, dlopened by the\npool runner via the spec registry. C boxes compile lazily on first\nreference to a `.so` next to the user's source (mtime-checked), then\ninvoke through a fixed function signature looked up via dlsym, with\nno subprocess and no IPC. Per-worker dlopen handle and function-\npointer caches keep repeated calls to the same box at single-pointer\noverhead. Per-box `cflags`, `link_libs`, and `headers` fields on the\nbox JSON (parsed by the loader, issue 305) feed into the compile\ncommand line.\n\nCross-language JSON adaptation is symmetric on both sides:\n\n- **Input**: when the dispatch passes `input_native[i] == 0`,\n  `try_strip_json_primitive` parses the bytes as JSON. A JSON string\n  is unquoted into a per-invoke scratch buffer; JSON numbers, bools,\n  null, and parse failures pass through (their textual form is\n  already what `atol`/`strtod`/`strcmp` expect). ## [429]

```json
{
  "sessionId":"a8fd7497-fc00-4f59-9644-b90753877f2a",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-22T18:44:37.879Z",
  "entrypoint":"cli",
  "version":"2.1.121",
  "gitBranch":"master",
  "message":{
    "content":[{
        "type":"tool_result",
        "is_error":false,
        "content":"=== /mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/317-spec-json-bridge-for-data-boxes.md ===\n# 317 — Language spec JSON bridge for data boxes\n\n## Status\nin progress — Lua bridges fidelity-preserving (stage 2 landed\n2026-05-19); C and Bash still stubs\n\n## Current behavior\n\nA data box (`kind: data` in box JSON) emits a value the rest of\nthe graph routes downstream. Today the runner reads the box's\n`ref` file as raw bytes and emits them — there's no concept of\n\"authoring this datum in a particular language using that\nlanguage's natural structures.\" If you want to declare a Lua\ntable as a data box's value, you either:\n\n- Hand-translate the table to JSON, save it as a `.json` file,\n  and lose the Lua syntax niceties; or\n- Make it a call box that returns the table, paying for a full\n  spec invocation just to read a constant; or\n- Hard-code the bytes inline in the box's `data` field, with no\n  syntactic help from any host language.\n\nThis is the wrong shape. **A box author writes idiomatic code in\nthe language of their choice.** That's the rule 307 establishes\nfor call boxes: a C-box author writes a plain C function, no\nSoraMech-specific glue. The data-box equivalent should hold —\na Lua-data-box author should write a Lua file that returns\nwhatever they want returned (a table, a string, a number), and\nSoraMech should know how to lift that into the graph as a JSON\nwire value without the author writing a single SoraMech-specific\ncharacter.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nEvery language spec gains two callbacks, declared in\n`lang_spec_t` (issue 303):\n\n```c\n/* Serialize a native-language value into JSON text.\n *\n *   ctx       — per-worker handle from spec.init.\n *   src       — caller-meaningful pointer to the native value.\n *               Format is spec-specific (see \"Native handle\n *               representation\" below).\n *   src_size  — size hint, or 0 if the spec interprets `src`\n *               without a length.\n *   out_buf   — destination buffer for JSON text (caller-owned).\n *   out_cap   — capacity of out_buf.\n *   out_size  — set to the bytes written.\n *\n\n=== /mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/244-data-box-pull-on-demand.md ===\n# 244 — Data boxes as round-robin default providers, pulled on demand\n\n## Status\nopen · design\n\n## Current behavior\n\nIssue 229 renamed `kind: data` to `kind: read` and reshaped the box\nso its value can come from either a file path or an inline literal.\nThe current dispatch model (304) treats a read box as a producer:\nat pool startup the runner pushes the read box's value into every\nconsumer slot wired from it. After that single push, the read box\nis \"done\" — it never pushes again.\n\nThis breaks down in two cases:\n\n1. **Multiple read boxes feeding the same input slot.** The slot\n   ends up holding one value (whichever read box's startup-push\n   landed first) and silently ignores the others. The user's\n   intent — \"rotate among these values\" — is not honored.\n2. **A read box feeding a slot whose other producers fire many\n   times.** Once the read box's startup push is consumed, the slot\n   sits empty until a call-box producer fills it. If the consumer\n   fires N times and the call-box producer also fires N times,\n   the read box's value is consumed at most once. The user's\n   intent — \"this is a default that's always available\" — is not\n   honored.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nA read box is an **inexhaustible source**, not a one-shot producer.\nIts declared value is always available, on every consumer's\nrequest. Consumers pull from read boxes when they need a value and\nno value is currently waiting in the slot.\n\n### Pull, not push\n\nRead boxes do not push at startup, do not appear in the pool's task\nqueue, and do not have task structs of their own.     "stdout":"=== /mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/317-spec-json-bridge-for-data-boxes.md ===\n# 317 — Language spec JSON bridge for data boxes\n\n## Status\nin progress — Lua bridges fidelity-preserving (stage 2 landed\n2026-05-19); C and Bash still stubs\n\n## Current behavior\n\nA data box (`kind: data` in box JSON) emits a value the rest of\nthe graph routes downstream. Today the runner reads the box's\n`ref` file as raw bytes and emits them — there's no concept of\n\"authoring this datum in a particular language using that\nlanguage's natural structures.\" If you want to declare a Lua\ntable as a data box's value, you either:\n\n- Hand-translate the table to JSON, save it as a `.json` file,\n  and lose the Lua syntax niceties; or\n- Make it a call box that returns the table, paying for a full\n  spec invocation just to read a constant; or\n- Hard-code the bytes inline in the box's `data` field, with no\n  syntactic help from any host language.\n\nThis is the wrong shape. **A box author writes idiomatic code in\nthe language of their choice.** That's the rule 307 establishes\nfor call boxes: a C-box author writes a plain C function, no\nSoraMech-specific glue. The data-box equivalent should hold —\na Lua-data-box author should write a Lua file that returns\nwhatever they want returned (a table, a string, a number), and\nSoraMech should know how to lift that into the graph as a JSON\nwire value without the author writing a single SoraMech-specific\ncharacter.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nEvery language spec gains two callbacks, declared in\n`lang_spec_t` (issue 303):\n\n```c\n/* Serialize a native-language value into JSON text.\n *\n *   ctx       — per-worker handle from spec.init.\n *   src       — caller-meaningful pointer to the native value.\n *               Format is spec-specific (see \"Native handle\n *               representation\" below).\n *   src_size  — size hint, or 0 if the spec interprets `src`\n *               without a length.\n *   out_buf   — destination buffer for JSON text (caller-owned).\n *   out_cap   — capacity of out_buf.\n *   out_size  — set to the bytes written.\n *\n\n=== /mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/244-data-box-pull-on-demand.md ===\n# 244 — Data boxes as round-robin default providers, pulled on demand\n\n## Status\nopen · design\n\n## Current behavior\n\nIssue 229 renamed `kind: data` to `kind: read` and reshaped the box\nso its value can come from either a file path or an inline literal.\nThe current dispatch model (304) treats a read box as a producer:\nat pool startup the runner pushes the read box's value into every\nconsumer slot wired from it. After that single push, the read box\nis \"done\" — it never pushes again.\n\nThis breaks down in two cases:\n\n1. **Multiple read boxes feeding the same input slot.** The slot\n   ends up holding one value (whichever read box's startup-push\n   landed first) and silently ignores the others. The user's\n   intent — \"rotate among these values\" — is not honored.\n2. **A read box feeding a slot whose other producers fire many\n   times.** Once the read box's startup push is consumed, the slot\n   sits empty until a call-box producer fills it. If the consumer\n   fires N times and the call-box producer also fires N times,\n   the read box's value is consumed at most once. The user's\n   intent — \"this is a default that's always available\" — is not\n   honored.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nA read box is an **inexhaustible source**, not a one-shot producer.\nIts declared value is always available, on every consumer's\nrequest. Consumers pull from read boxes when they need a value and\nno value is currently waiting in the slot.\n\n### Pull, not push\n\nRead boxes do not push at startup, do not appear in the pool's task\nqueue, and do not have task structs of their own. They are\n**callable sources** whose state lives in the box's runtime record:\n\n- For an inline literal (`value` field set), the value sits in the\n  box's record as bytes ready to copy.\n- For a file path (`path` field set), the bytes are read once at\n  graph load and cached in the box's record. The user editing the\n  file mid-run is not supported; the cached bytes are the source of\n  truth for the run.\n\nThe attempt-task model from the architecture doc makes the pull\nhappen naturally. When an attempt task examines a consumer's input"
  },

Writes an error message\n * via the spec's existing error-reporting plumbing. */\nint (*native_to_json)(void *ctx,\n                      const void *src, uint32_t src_size,\n                      char *out_buf, uint32_t out_cap, uint32_t *out_size);\n\n/* Inverse: parse JSON text into a native-language value. The\n * native value is stored wherever the spec considers natural\n * (Lua: pushed to the worker's lua_State stack; C: written into\n * a typed struct supplied by `dst`; Bash: written as a textual\n * representation back into dst).\n *\n *   ctx       — per-worker handle.\n *   src       — JSON text.\n *   src_size  — JSON text length in bytes.\n *   dst       — caller-supplied target; semantics per spec.\n *   dst_cap   — capacity, where meaningful.\n *   dst_size  — set to the bytes / native units consumed.\n *\n * Returns 0 on success, -1 on error. */\nint (*json_to_native)(void *ctx,\n                      const char *src, uint32_t src_size,\n                      void *dst, uint32_t dst_cap, uint32_t *dst_size);\n```\n\nThese are the same fields 312's same-language fast path\nreserves; this issue is the one that requires every spec to\n**actually implement them**, driven by the data-box use case.\n(312 needs them too, but its driver is performance; 317 needs\nthem for correctness — a data box can't function without them.)\n\n### The rule, restated\n\nThe author of a data box writes a `.lua` / `.c` / `.sh` /\n`.<whatever>` file that returns or produces a value using\n*their language's native idioms*. No SoraMech macros. No\nSoraMech includes. No SoraMech-specific JSON shape constraints\nbeyond \"what your spec's native_to_json can convert.\"\n\nIf the author returns a Lua table, the Lua spec's\n`native_to_json` converts it. If they return a C struct, the C\nspec's `native_to_json` walks it according to the type declared\nin the box. If they print JSON-ish text from a bash script, the\nbash spec's `native_to_json` is a no-op identity (the script\nalready produced JSON).\n\nThe contract belongs to the spec author, not the box author.\nThat's the inversion: **SoraMech bends to the language, not the\nother way around.**\n\n## Native handle representation\n\nThe shape of `src` / `dst` in the callbacks is per-spec. Each\nspec documents what it accepts:\n\n- **Lua spec**: `src` is the index of a value already pushed\n  onto the worker's `lua_State`. `src_size` is unused. The\n  spec's `native_to_json` reads the value at that stack index\n  and writes JSON. `json_to_native` pushes the parsed JSON value\n  onto the stack, and `dst_size` reports the number of stack\n  slots used (always 1 for SoraMech's flat-value model).\n- **C spec**: `src` is a typed pointer + the box's declared\n  output type drives the walk. `src_size` is the type's\n  storage footprint. Mirror image for `json_to_native`. (This\n  ties into 307's typed-wrapper-generation work — the same\n  type system describes both the wrapper signature and the\n  JSON shape.)\n- **Bash spec**: `src` is text the script produced.\n  `native_to_json` validates and reshapes to JSON if needed (a\n  bash script that prints `42` becomes JSON `42`; a script that\n  prints `{\"a\":1}` passes through unchanged). `json_to_native`\n  is similarly a near-identity. The spec author is encouraged\n  to require scripts produce well-formed JSON in the first\n  place rather than write a bash-syntax parser.\n\nThe dispatch layer doesn't know or care which representation a\nspec uses. It only ever passes `src` and `src_size` to the\nspec's callback. The spec is opaque to the runtime; that's the\nwhole point.\n\n## Data box semantics\n\nA data box's `data` field becomes optional. The box gains\noptional `lang` and `ref` fields:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"config\",\n  \"kind\": \"data\",\n  \"lang\": \"lua\",\n  \"ref\": \"config.lua\"\n}\n```\n\nAt graph load, the runner:\n\n1. Resolves the spec for `lang`.\n2. Calls the spec's `init` (already done at worker startup).\n3. At box-fire time, asks the spec to execute the `ref` file\n   and produce a native value (this is essentially the same\n   \"load this file, run it, get its return value\" path the\n   spec already implements for call boxes — call boxes call a\n   named function; data boxes take the file's return value).\n4. Calls the spec's `native_to_json` to convert the native\n   value to JSON text.\n5. Pushes that JSON text down the wire as the box's output —\n   same as today's data path, just with the value sourced\n   from a language-native file.\n\nIf the box has no `lang` and a literal `data` field, the legacy\ninline-data path applies unchanged.\n\n## Why every spec must implement these\n\nThe same JSON the data box emits is consumed by some downstream\nbox (call, comparator, file_write, whatever). That downstream\nbox, if it's in a different language, will eventually need\n*its* spec's `json_to_native` to convert the JSON back. So the\ntwo callbacks are paired — every spec that participates in the\ngraph needs both. A spec that implements `native_to_json` but\nnot `json_to_native` can only be data-box sources; a spec with\nonly `json_to_native` can only be call-box sinks. We require\nboth so any language can play any role.\n\nSpecs that haven't been updated yet should set both callbacks\nto a stub that returns -1 with a clear error message (\"spec\n`<name>`: native_to_json not implemented; this box's value\ncan't be routed cross-language\"). The hard-fail makes the gap\nloud rather than producing wrong output.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. Extend the `lang_spec_t` declaration in\n   `langs/lang-spec.h` if not already done by 312's\n   infrastructure work. (Per the round summary, the slot is\n   reserved.)\n2. Implement `native_to_json` and `json_to_native` in each\n   spec:\n   - **Lua spec**: walk the value at the stack index. Use the\n     existing C JSON writer (`libs/json/json.c`). Handle Lua\n     tables both as arrays (1-indexed contiguous integer keys)\n     and as objects. Refuse functions, userdata, threads.\n   - **C spec**: depends on 307's typed-wrapper machinery. For\n     now, a stub that only supports scalar types (int, double,\n     string) is enough to get data boxes working in C.\n   - **Bash spec**: validate-and-pass-through. The script is\n     expected to produce JSON. `native_to_json` runs the JSON\n     parser to validate; `json_to_native` is identity.\n3. Extend the data box runtime path in `src/012-dispatch.c`\n   (or wherever data boxes dispatch from) to consult `lang` /\n   `ref` when set and route through the spec callback chain.\n4. Add a fixture: `tests/maps/cross-lang-data/` with a Lua\n   data box, a C consumer, and a Bash consumer all reading the\n   same value. The integration check asserts each consumer\n   sees the right data.\n5. Update each spec's `*.info.md` to document the native handle\n   shape its callbacks expect.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — extend the contract\n- `langs/lua/spec.c`, `langs/c/spec.c`, `langs/bash/spec.c` —\n  implement the callbacks\n- `langs/{lua,c,bash}/spec.info.md` — document native handle\n  semantics per spec\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — data-box dispatch path\n- `tests/maps/cross-lang-data/` — new fixture (see step 4)\n- `issues/307-c-language-spec.md` — same author-writes-natural-\n  code principle; this issue extends it from call boxes to data\n  boxes\n- `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — reuses the same\n  spec callbacks for a different (performance) reason\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Bash's `json_to_native` is a near-identity because the\n  scripts already deal in text. Is there value in having it\n  validate and reformat for consistency? Probably yes; cheap\n  insurance against malformed downstream input.\n- Should the Lua spec auto-detect array-vs-object tables, or\n  require the box author to annotate? Auto-detect (contiguous\n  1-indexed integer keys → array; otherwise object) is what\n  every other lua-to-json library does and is intuitive enough.\n- C spec's `native_to_json` for arbitrary structs is a real\n  rabbit hole. Tie scope to 307 — the same type declarations\n  drive both the wrapper and the JSON walk. Until 307 lands,\n  only scalar types are supported for C data boxes.\n\n## Implementation log\n\n### 2026-05-19 — Lua bridges landed\n\nImplemented the first concrete pair of bridges. Scope: only the\nLua spec; C and Bash still NULL their bridge slots and fall back\nto the uniform-byte default.\n\n**Design decisions made during this round (kept for later\nimplementers of the C / Bash bridges):**\n\n- **Bridge signature has the worker handle as the first arg.**\n  The previous declaration in `lang-spec.h` was missing it; without\n  it Lua can't reach its `lua_State`. C and Bash will need it for\n  the same reason once they grow real bridges.\n\n- **Stack-protocol convention for the native side.** The bridge\n  reads / writes the producer's working store directly, not the\n  `src` / `dst` buffers. For Lua: `native_to_json` consumes the\n  value at the top of the `lua_State` (pops on success); `json_to_native`\n  pushes the reconstructed value to the top. The `src` / `dst`\n  buffers carry only the JSON side of the conversion. This keeps\n  the wire format opaque to specs and avoids inventing a \"native\n  byte\" serialization just so it can fit through a buffer.\n\n- **Wire primitive vocabulary.** Three JSON-with-extensions\n  primitives are reserved for the harder types; this round did not\n  emit any of them, but every future bridge must agree on the\n  names: `$ref` (shared-memory pointer + length), `$function_pointer`\n  (decomposed callable: address + signature), `$lang_opaque`\n  (last-resort sealed envelope routed only between same-language\n  endpoints — escape hatch, not a default).\n\n- **No handles, no back-routing.** The wire must carry data the\n  destination spec can reconstruct on its own — never a token that\n  says \"operations on this value cross back to the source spec.\"\n  See `memory/feedback_cross_language_pitfalls.md` for the longer\n  argument; the principle constrains every bridge implementation.\n\n- **Type ambiguities are resolved by wiring, not by annotation.**\n  When a function signature has hidden pairings (a `char *` with a\n  separate length argument, a `union` with a discriminator, a\n  callback with a context pointer), the destination spec exposes\n  *each* parameter as its own input slot on the box. The user wires\n  them according to the function's English docs. The system never\n  prompts the user with vocabulary words it has no general way to\n  ask about.\n\n**Files touched:**\n\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — `lang_bridge_fn` now takes `void *handle`\n  as its first parameter; the doc comment documents the stack\n  protocol.\n- `langs/lua/spec.c` — added `encode_value`, `decode_node`,\n  `lua_native_to_json`, `lua_json_to_native`. Wired the last two\n  into `soramech_lang_spec`.\n- `langs/lua/Makefile` — folds `libs/json/json.c` straight into\n  `spec.so` so the spec stays self-contained.\n- `tests/317-lua-bridge-test.c` — new round-trip test (JSON →\n  lua_State → JSON, compare).\n- `Makefile` — added the test's dependency line.\n\n**Tests:** 5/5 in `317-lua-bridge-test`; full suite green.\n\n### 2026-05-19 — stage 2: Lua array fidelity\n\nStage 1 lost `null` inside arrays — `[true,false,null]` round-tripped\nas `[true,false]`. Stage 2 fixes it by applying the n-field\nconvention from the fidelity directive below.\n\nWhat changed in the code:\n\n- `decode_node` (JSON → Lua): the JSON_ARRAY case now creates a Lua\n  table with a string key `n` set to the array's length, then\n  fills integer keys 1..n. JSON `null` elements use `lua_rawseti`\n  with nil — which deletes the key, leaving an absent slot. The\n  table now carries enough information to reconstruct the array\n  losslessly.\n\n- `encode_value` (Lua → JSON): table emission reads `n` first. If\n  the field is a non-negative integer, the table is treated as a\n  declared-length array — the encoder walks 1..n and emits null\n  for any missing slot via the existing nil → null path. Tables\n  without `n` fall through to the existing array-vs-object\n  heuristic for idiomatic Lua values.\n\nWhat the tests prove now:\n\n- `[]`, `[null]`, `[null,null]`, `[null,1,2]`, `[1,null,3]`,\n  `[1,2,null]`, `[true,false,null]` all round-trip exactly.\n\nWhat this costs:\n\n- Lua tables that have crossed the bridge carry a `n` field\n  visible to `pairs()`. The fidelity directive accepts this:\n  \"We can intrude on idiomatic Lua because we're fundamentally\n  translating from Lua to JSON.\" Box authors who write Lua\n  tables by hand and want them treated as JSON arrays can also\n  set `n` themselves; otherwise the existing heuristic still\n  catches `{1, 2, 3}`-shaped tables.\n\n## Fidelity directive (added 2026-05-19, supersedes earlier \"lossy is OK\" thinking)\n\nThe wire format (JSON) is canonical. **A value leaving a box's\noutput slot and entering the wire must not lose fidelity.** The\nbridge intrudes on the language as needed to achieve that. The\nlanguage's idioms are upheld on the in-language side (inside the\nbox's source file); on the wire side the bridge is allowed —\nrequired — to use whatever encoding preserves the shape.\n\nThis reverses the earlier instinct that lossy round-trips were\n\"the box author's problem.\" They're the bridge's problem. The\nbox author writes idiomatic Lua / C / bash; the bridge converts\nwithout dropping anything.\n\n### Concrete rules per language\n\n- **Lua → JSON** (and JSON → Lua → JSON round-trip): preserve\n  array shape including embedded nulls. The decoder pushes\n  arrays as `{n = N, [1] = ..., [2] = ..., ...}` where `n` is the\n  intended length and missing integer keys are real nil slots.\n  The encoder reads `n` if present and emits a full-length JSON\n  array with `null` at every missing slot. Idiomatic Lua tables\n  without `n` continue to encode via the existing\n  array-vs-object heuristic — `n` is only required when the\n  caller cares about distinguishing \"trailing nil\" from \"shorter\n  array.\" Same scheme handles intermixed nil-in-middle too.\n\n- **Lua → JSON** (type annotations): the bridge may emit a\n  type-tagged JSON shape when the destination language needs\n  more than JSON's native types convey (e.g. int vs float when\n  the Lua value is whole-numbered but the destination expects a\n  float, or vice versa). The tag lives in the JSON itself, not\n  in a sidecar protocol. Suggested shape: a `$type` key inside a\n  small wrapper object, only emitted when the encoder can tell\n  the unwrapped value would be ambiguous downstream.\n\n- **C → JSON**: C functions have declared types — emit those\n  types as part of the JSON, so any downstream language can\n  honour them without guessing. Lua receivers may use the type\n  to coerce (e.g. force `2` instead of `2.0`); receivers that\n  don't care can ignore the type tag.\n\n- **JSON → C**: when the wire value doesn't fit the destination\n  C type (a float arriving at an int slot, a string at a number\n  slot), the C bridge **truncates / coerces and records a\n  warning** at map-compile time. The warning surfaces in the\n  compile output, not at run time. Silent dropping is forbidden;\n  hard-failing the compile is too aggressive — the user may\n  know the truncation is fine.\n\n- **JSON → Lua / JSON → bash**: same coercion rule, with\n  language-appropriate fallbacks. The receiver records the\n  warning.\n\n### Why this lives in the bridge, not the box author\n\nA box author writes a function in their language. They don't\nwrite a SoraMech-aware serializer. The bridge — which is the\nspec author's responsibility, not the box author's — owns every\ndetail of how their language's values reach JSON and how JSON\nreaches their language's values. The box author writes\nidiomatic code; the bridge does whatever is necessary on the\nJSON side, including unwrapping `n`-fielded tables back into\nidiomatic Lua at decode time so subsequent in-language calls\nsee clean tables.\n\nThis is the same principle the rest of 317 already states: the\nspec bends to the language at the box surface, and bends the\nwire shape to the language at the bridge. The language never\nbends to the wire.\n\n**Next implementation slices:**\n\n1. ~~**Lua bridges, stage 2 — fidelity preservation.**~~ Done\n   2026-05-19. The n-field convention is implemented; every JSON\n   array shape round-trips faithfully. See the stage-2 entry in\n   the implementation log above.\n2. Bash bridges — near-identity (scripts are already producing\n   text). `native_to_json` validates the text is well-formed JSON;\n   `json_to_native` is identity. No `lua_State`-style scratch\n   needed, so the bridge can ignore `handle`. Type fidelity is\n   trivial because bash already deals only in text.\n3. C bridges — depends on 307's typed wrapper work. Until 307\n   lands, scalar types (int / double / string) is enough to\n   unblock data-box semantics. The coerce-and-warn rule from\n   the fidelity directive governs how mismatched types behave.\n4. Wire the bridges into the dispatch layer (issue 312's\n   wire-classification path) so cross-language edges actually\n   round-trip through them.\n5. Add a map-compile warning channel that the C / Lua / bash\n   bridges feed into when they truncate or coerce. Surface\n   the warnings in the compile output — silent loss is\n   forbidden by the fidelity directive.\n",
