          "old_string":"/* {{{ soramech_lang_spec */\nlang_spec_t soramech_lang_spec = {\n    .name     = \"bash\",\n    .file_ext = \".sh\",\n    .init     = bash_init,\n    .teardown = bash_teardown,\n    .compile  = 0,\n    .invoke   = bash_invoke,\n};\n/* }}} */",
          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"/* {{{ bash_native_to_json() — issue 317 bridge\n *\n * Bash scripts produce raw text. The bridge's job at the wire edge\n * is to shape that text into JSON the consumer's spec can parse.\n * If the bytes already parse as JSON (a script that printed `42`,\n * `true`, `{\"a\":1}`, or even a fully-quoted `\"hello\"`), pass them\n * through — the script chose its encoding. If they don't parse,\n * wrap them as a JSON string with proper escaping so a script that\n * printed `Hello World` becomes `\"Hello World\"` on the wire.\n *\n * The worker handle is unused — there's no per-worker bash state\n * to read here; the value already lives in the `src` buffer the\n * dispatch layer hands us. */\nstatic int bash_native_to_json(void *handle,\n                               const void *src, int src_size,\n                               void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size)\n{\n    (void)handle;\n    if (!src || src_size < 0 || !dst || dst_capacity <= 0) return -1;\n\n    char *scratch = malloc((size_t)src_size + 1);\n    if (!scratch) return -1;\n    memcpy(scratch, src, (size_t)src_size);\n    scratch[src_size] = '\\0';\n\n    json_arena_t *arena = json_arena_create();\n    if (!arena) { free(scratch); return -1; }\n    json_node_t *n = json_parse(arena, scratch, NULL, NULL);\n    int valid = (n != NULL);\n    json_arena_destroy(arena);\n\n    if (valid) {\n        if (src_size > dst_capacity) {\n            free(scratch);\n            fprintf(stderr, \"bash spec: native_to_json: src %d > dst %d\\n\",\n                    src_size, dst_capacity);\n            return -1;\n        }\n        memcpy(dst, src, (size_t)src_size);\n        if (dst_size) *dst_size = src_size;\n        free(scratch);\n        return 0;\n    }\n\n    json_writer_t w;\n    json_writer_init(&w, (char *)dst, dst_capacity);\n    json_writer_string(&w, scratch);\n    int written = json_writer_finish(&w);\n    free(scratch);\n    if (written < 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"bash spec: native_to_json: output buffer too small\\n\");\n        return -1;\n    }\n    if (dst_size) *dst_size = written;\n    return 0;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ bash_json_to_native() — issue 317 bridge\n *\n * The bash side wants text — what a `$1` argument in a script looks\n * like. The bridge mirrors the C spec: if `src` is a JSON string,\n * unwrap the quotes and escapes into `dst`; otherwise pass through\n * unchanged. A bash script reading `42` or `true` sees the natural\n * textual form; a script reading `{\"a\":1}` sees the literal JSON\n * (and may pipe it to `jq` if it cares). */\nstatic int bash_json_to_native(void *handle,\n                               const void *src, int src_size,\n                               void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size)\n{\n    (void)handle;\n    if (!src || src_size < 0 || !dst || dst_capacity <= 0) return -1;\n\n    char *scratch = malloc((size_t)src_size + 1);\n    if (!scratch) return -1;\n    memcpy(scratch, src, (size_t)src_size);\n    scratch[src_size] = '\\0';\n\n    json_arena_t *arena = json_arena_create();\n    if (!arena) { free(scratch); return -1; }\n    json_node_t *n = json_parse(arena, scratch, NULL, NULL);\n\n    if (n && json_kind(n) == JSON_STRING) {\n        const char *s = json_string_value(n);\n        int len = (int)strlen(s);\n        if (len > dst_capacity) {\n            json_arena_destroy(arena);\n            free(scratch);\n            fprintf(stderr, \"bash spec: json_to_native: unquoted %d > dst %d\\n\",\n                    len, dst_capacity);\n            return -1;\n        }\n        memcpy(dst, s, (size_t)len);\n        if (dst_size) *dst_size = len;\n        json_arena_destroy(arena);\n        free(scratch);\n        return 0;\n    }\n    json_arena_destroy(arena);\n    free(scratch);\n\n    if (src_size > dst_capacity) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"bash spec: json_to_native: src %d > dst %d\\n\",\n                src_size, dst_capacity);\n        return -1;\n    }\n    memcpy(dst, src, (size_t)src_size);\n    if (dst_size) *dst_size = src_size;\n    return 0;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ soramech_lang_spec */\nlang_spec_t soramech_lang_spec = {\n    .name           = \"bash\",\n    .file_ext       = \".sh\",\n    .init           = bash_init,\n    .teardown       = bash_teardown,\n    .compile        = 0,\n    .invoke         = bash_invoke,\n    .native_to_json = bash_native_to_json,\n    .json_to_native = bash_json_to_native,\n};\n/* }}} */",

    "newString":"/* {{{ bash_native_to_json() — issue 317 bridge\n *\n * Bash scripts produce raw text. If they don't parse,\n * wrap them as a JSON string with proper escaping so a script that\n * printed `Hello World` becomes `\"Hello World\"` on the wire.\n *\n * The worker handle is unused — there's no per-worker bash state\n * to read here; the value already lives in the `src` buffer the\n * dispatch layer hands us. */\nstatic int bash_native_to_json(void *handle,\n                               const void *src, int src_size,\n                               void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size)\n{\n    (void)handle;\n    if (!src || src_size < 0 || !dst || dst_capacity <= 0) return -1;\n\n    char *scratch = malloc((size_t)src_size + 1);\n    if (!scratch) return -1;\n    memcpy(scratch, src, (size_t)src_size);\n    scratch[src_size] = '\\0';\n\n    json_arena_t *arena = json_arena_create();\n    if (!arena) { free(scratch); return -1; }\n    json_node_t *n = json_parse(arena, scratch, NULL, NULL);\n    int valid = (n != NULL);\n    json_arena_destroy(arena);\n\n    if (valid) {\n        if (src_size > dst_capacity) {\n            free(scratch);\n            fprintf(stderr, \"bash spec: native_to_json: src %d > dst %d\\n\",\n                    src_size, dst_capacity);\n            return -1;\n        }\n        memcpy(dst, src, (size_t)src_size);\n        if (dst_size) *dst_size = src_size;\n        free(scratch);\n        return 0;\n    }\n\n    json_writer_t w;\n    json_writer_init(&w, (char *)dst, dst_capacity);\n    json_writer_string(&w, scratch);\n    int written = json_writer_finish(&w);\n    free(scratch);\n    if (written < 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"bash spec: native_to_json: output buffer too small\\n\");\n        return -1;\n    }\n    if (dst_size) *dst_size = written;\n    return 0;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ bash_json_to_native() — issue 317 bridge\n *\n * The bash side wants text — what a `$1` argument in a script looks\n * like.           "content":"/* tests/317-text-bridge-test.c — bridges for the text-oriented specs\n * (C and Bash). Both treat the wire side as bytes-in / bytes-out and\n * have no per-worker state on the native side, so the bridge logic\n * is the same shape: native_to_json passes valid JSON through and\n * JSON-string-wraps everything else; json_to_native unquotes JSON\n * strings and passes everything else through. Same suite, two\n * specs — the registry hands us a different vtable per call.\n *\n * Run from the project root so the spec dlopen paths resolve.\n */\n\n#include \"011-spec-registry.h\"\n#include \"lang-spec.h\"\n\n#include <stdio.h>\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <string.h>\n#include <sys/stat.h>\n\n/* {{{ Test harness */\nstatic int g_pass = 0;\nstatic int g_fail = 0;\n\n#define ASSERT(cond) \\\n    do { if (!(cond)) { \\\n        fprintf(stderr, \"      %s:%d: %s\\n\", __FILE__, __LINE__, #cond); \\\n        return 0; \\\n    } } while (0)\n\n#define RUN(name, spec, label) \\\n    do { \\\n        char title[80]; snprintf(title, sizeof title, \"%s · %s\", label, #name); \\\n        fprintf(stdout, \"  %-44s \", title); fflush(stdout); \\\n        if (test_##name(spec)) { fprintf(stdout, \"ok\\n\"); g_pass++; } \\\n        else                   { fprintf(stdout, \"FAIL\\n\"); g_fail++; } \\\n    } while (0)\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Suite — every check works against any spec exposing the\n * native↔JSON bridges with no worker-state requirement. */\n\n/* A JSON-valid input passes through native_to_json unchanged. */\nstatic int test_native_passes_through_json(const lang_spec_t *s)\n{\n    char dst[64];\n    int n = 0;\n    const char *src = \"{\\\"a\\\":1}\";\n    ASSERT(s->native_to_json(NULL, src, (int)strlen(src),\n                             dst, sizeof dst, &n) == 0);\n    ASSERT(n == (int)strlen(src));\n    ASSERT(memcmp(dst, src, (size_t)n) == 0);\n    return 1;\n}\n\n/* Bare text wraps as a JSON string with escaping. */\nstatic int test_native_wraps_bare_text(const lang_spec_t *s)\n{\n    char dst[64];\n    int n = 0;\n    const char *src = \"hello world\";\n    ASSERT(s->native_to_json(NULL, src, (int)strlen(src),\n                             dst, sizeof dst, &n) == 0);\n    ASSERT(n == (int)strlen(\"\\\"hello world\\\"\"));\n    ASSERT(memcmp(dst, \"\\\"hello world\\\"\", (size_t)n) == 0);\n    return 1;\n}\n\n/* Bare text with a quote gets the quote escaped on the way out. */\nstatic int test_native_escapes_quotes(const lang_spec_t *s)\n{\n    char dst[64];\n    int n = 0;\n    const char *src = \"say \\\"hi\\\"\";\n    ASSERT(s->native_to_json(NULL, src, (int)strlen(src),\n                             dst, sizeof dst, &n) == 0);\n    ASSERT(n == (int)strlen(\"\\\"say \\\\\\\"hi\\\\\\\"\\\"\"));\n    ASSERT(memcmp(dst, \"\\\"say \\\\\\\"hi\\\\\\\"\\\"\", (size_t)n) == 0);\n    return 1;\n}\n\n/* JSON string round-trips to its unquoted bytes through json_to_native. */\nstatic int test_native_to_native_unquotes_string(const lang_spec_t *s)\n{\n    char dst[64];\n    int n = 0;\n    const char *src = \"\\\"hello\\\"\";\n    ASSERT(s->json_to_native(NULL, src, (int)strlen(src),\n                             dst, sizeof dst, &n) == 0);\n    ASSERT(n == 5);\n    ASSERT(memcmp(dst, \"hello\", 5) == 0);\n    return 1;\n}\n\n/* JSON numbers / bools / null pass through json_to_native unchanged. */\nstatic int test_native_to_native_passes_primitives(const lang_spec_t *s)\n{\n    char dst[16];\n    int n = 0;\n    ASSERT(s->json_to_native(NULL, \"42\", 2, dst, sizeof dst, &n) == 0);\n    ASSERT(n == 2 && memcmp(dst, \"42\", 2) == 0);\n\n    ASSERT(s->json_to_native(NULL, \"true\", 4, dst, sizeof dst, &n) == 0);\n    ASSERT(n == 4 && memcmp(dst, \"true\", 4) == 0);\n\n    ASSERT(s->json_to_native(NULL, \"null\", 4, dst, sizeof dst, &n) == 0);\n    ASSERT(n == 4 && memcmp(dst, \"null\", 4) == 0);\n    return 1;\n}\n\n/* Buffer-too-small surfaces as a -1 from native_to_json. */\nstatic int test_native_to_json_overflow_fails(const lang_spec_t *s)\n{\n    char tiny[4];\n    int n = 0;\n    const char *src = \"this string will not fit in four bytes\";\n    ASSERT(s->native_to_json(NULL, src, (int)strlen(src),\n                             tiny, sizeof tiny, &n) == -1);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ load_spec_or_skip() */\nstatic const lang_spec_t *load_spec_or_skip(spec_registry_t **out_reg,\n                                            const char *name)\n{\n    char *err = NULL;\n    spec_registry_t *r = spec_registry_load(\"langs\", &err);\n    if (!r) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"registry load failed: %s\\n\", err ? err : \"(null)\");\n        free(err);\n        *out_reg = NULL;\n        return NULL;\n    }\n    const lang_spec_t *s = spec_registry_get(r, name);\n    if (!s || !s->native_to_json || !s->json_to_native) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"%s spec missing bridge callbacks\\n\", name);\n        spec_registry_destroy(r);\n        *out_reg = NULL;\n        return NULL;\n    }\n    *out_reg = r;\n    return s;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ run_suite() */\nstatic void run_suite(const lang_spec_t *s, const char *label)\n{\n    RUN(native_passes_through_json,        s, label);\n    RUN(native_wraps_bare_text,            s, label);\n    RUN(native_escapes_quotes,             s, label);\n    RUN(native_to_native_unquotes_string,  s, label);\n    RUN(native_to_native_passes_primitives,s, label);\n    RUN(native_to_json_overflow_fails,     s, label);\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ main() */\nint main(void)\n{\n    struct stat st;\n    if (stat(\"langs/c/spec.so\",    &st) != 0 ||\n        stat(\"langs/bash/spec.so\", &st) != 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"317-text-bridge-test: spec(s) not built; \"\n                        \"run from project root with `make` first\\n\");\n        return 2;\n    }\n    printf(\"317-text-bridge-test:\\n\");\n\n    spec_registry_t *r_c =     "content":"/* tests/317-text-bridge-test.c — bridges for the text-oriented specs\n * (C and Bash). Both treat the wire side as bytes-in / bytes-out and\n * have no per-worker state on the native side, so the bridge logic\n * is the same shape: native_to_json passes valid JSON through and\n * JSON-string-wraps everything else; json_to_native unquotes JSON\n * strings and passes everything else through. Same suite, two\n * specs — the registry hands us a different vtable per call.\n *\n * Run from the project root so the spec dlopen paths resolve.\n */\n\n#include \"011-spec-registry.h\"\n#include \"lang-spec.h\"\n\n#include <stdio.h>\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <string.h>\n#include <sys/stat.h>\n\n/* {{{ Test harness */\nstatic int g_pass = 0;\nstatic int g_fail = 0;\n\n#define ASSERT(cond) \\\n    do { if (!(cond)) { \\\n        fprintf(stderr, \"      %s:%d: %s\\n\", __FILE__, __LINE__, #cond); \\\n        return 0; \\\n    } } while (0)\n\n#define RUN(name, spec, label) \\\n    do { \\\n        char title[80]; snprintf(title, sizeof title, \"%s · %s\", label, #name); \\\n        fprintf(stdout, \"  %-44s \", title); fflush(stdout); \\\n        if (test_##name(spec)) { fprintf(stdout, \"ok\\n\"); g_pass++; } \\\n        else                   { fprintf(stdout, \"FAIL\\n\"); g_fail++; } \\\n    } while (0)\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Suite — every check works against any spec exposing the\n * native↔JSON bridges with no worker-state requirement. */\n\n/* A JSON-valid input passes through native_to_json unchanged. */\nstatic int test_native_passes_through_json(const lang_spec_t *s)\n{\n    char dst[64];\n    int n = 0;\n    const char *src = \"{\\\"a\\\":1}\";\n    ASSERT(s->native_to_json(NULL, src, (int)strlen(src),\n                             dst, sizeof dst, &n) == 0);\n    ASSERT(n == (int)strlen(src));\n    ASSERT(memcmp(dst, src, (size_t)n) == 0);\n    return 1;\n}\n\n/* Bare text wraps as a JSON string with escaping. */\nstatic int test_native_wraps_bare_text(const lang_spec_t *s)\n{\n    char dst[64];\n    int n = 0;\n    const char *src = \"hello world\";\n    ASSERT(s->native_to_json(NULL, src, (int)strlen(src),\n                             dst, sizeof dst, &n) == 0);\n    ASSERT(n == (int)strlen(\"\\\"hello world\\\"\"));\n    ASSERT(memcmp(dst, \"\\\"hello world\\\"\", (size_t)n) == 0);\n    return 1;\n}\n\n/* Bare text with a quote gets the quote escaped on the way out. */\nstatic int test_native_escapes_quotes(const lang_spec_t *s)\n{\n    char dst[64];\n    int n = 0;\n    const char *src = \"say \\\"hi\\\"\";\n    ASSERT(s->native_to_json(NULL, src, (int)strlen(src),\n                             dst, sizeof dst, &n) == 0);\n    ASSERT(n == (int)strlen(\"\\\"say \\\\\\\"hi\\\\\\\"\\\"\"));\n    ASSERT(memcmp(dst, \"\\\"say \\\\\\\"hi\\\\\\\"\\\"\", (size_t)n) == 0);\n    return 1;\n}\n\n/* JSON string round-trips to its unquoted bytes through json_to_native. */\nstatic int test_native_to_native_unquotes_string(const lang_spec_t *s)\n{\n    char dst[64];\n    int n = 0;\n    const char *src = \"\\\"hello\\\"\";\n    ASSERT(s->json_to_native(NULL, src, (int)strlen(src),\n                             dst, sizeof dst, &n) == 0);\n    ASSERT(n == 5);\n    ASSERT(memcmp(dst, \"hello\", 5) == 0);\n    return 1;\n}\n\n/* JSON numbers / bools / null pass through json_to_native unchanged. */\nstatic int test_native_to_native_passes_primitives(const lang_spec_t *s)\n{\n    char dst[16];\n    int n = 0;\n    ASSERT(s->json_to_native(NULL, \"42\", 2, dst, sizeof dst, &n) == 0);\n    ASSERT(n == 2 && memcmp(dst, \"42\", 2) == 0);\n\n    ASSERT(s->json_to_native(NULL, \"true\", 4, dst, sizeof dst, &n) == 0);\n    ASSERT(n == 4 && memcmp(dst, \"true\", 4) == 0);\n\n    ASSERT(s->json_to_native(NULL, \"null\", 4, dst, sizeof dst, &n) == 0);\n    ASSERT(n == 4 && memcmp(dst, \"null\", 4) == 0);\n    return 1;\n}\n\n/* Buffer-too-small surfaces as a -1 from native_to_json. */\nstatic int test_native_to_json_overflow_fails(const lang_spec_t *s)\n{\n    char tiny[4];\n    int n = 0;\n    const char *src = \"this string will not fit in four bytes\";\n    ASSERT(s->native_to_json(NULL, src, (int)strlen(src),\n                             tiny, sizeof tiny, &n) == -1);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ load_spec_or_skip() */\nstatic const lang_spec_t *load_spec_or_skip(spec_registry_t **out_reg,\n                                            const char *name)\n{\n    char *err = NULL;\n    spec_registry_t *r = spec_registry_load(\"langs\", &err);\n    if (!r) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"registry load failed: %s\\n\", err ? err : \"(null)\");\n        free(err);\n        *out_reg = NULL;\n        return NULL;\n    }\n    const lang_spec_t *s = spec_registry_get(r, name);\n    if (!s || !s->native_to_json || !s->json_to_native) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"%s spec missing bridge callbacks\\n\", name);\n        spec_registry_destroy(r);\n        *out_reg = NULL;\n        return NULL;\n    }\n    *out_reg = r;\n    return s;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ run_suite() */\nstatic void run_suite(const lang_spec_t *s, const char *label)\n{\n    RUN(native_passes_through_json,        s, label);\n    RUN(native_wraps_bare_text,            s, label);\n    RUN(native_escapes_quotes,             s, label);\n    RUN(native_to_native_unquotes_string,  s, label);\n    RUN(native_to_native_passes_primitives,s, label);\n    RUN(native_to_json_overflow_fails,     s, label);\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ main() */\nint main(void)\n{\n    struct stat st;\n    if (stat(\"langs/c/spec.so\",    &st) != 0 ||\n        stat(\"langs/bash/spec.so\", &st) != 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"317-text-bridge-test: spec(s) not built; \"\n                        \"run from project root with `make` first\\n\");\n        return 2;\n    }\n    printf(\"317-text-bridge-test:\\n\");\n\n    spec_registry_t *r_c = NULL;\n    const lang_spec_t *c = load_spec_or_skip(&r_c, \"c\");\n    if (c) run_suite(c, \"c\");\n\n    spec_registry_t *r_b = NULL;\n    const lang_spec_t *b = load_spec_or_skip(&r_b, \"bash\");\n    if (b) run_suite(b, \"bash\");\n\n    if (r_c) spec_registry_destroy(r_c);\n    if (r_b) spec_registry_destroy(r_b);\n\n    printf(\"\\n  %d passed, %d failed\\n\", g_pass, g_fail);\n    return g_fail == 0 ? 0 : 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n",

    "originalFile":"# SoraMech — top-level build orchestration.\n#\n# What it does, in a sentence: builds the phase 3 pool runner binary\n# plus one shared library per language spec. Release by default;\n# DEBUG=1 keeps symbols and disables optimization, STRICT=1 promotes\n# warnings to errors. `make clean` removes everything that was built.\n#\n# Invokable from any directory: `make -C /path/to/soramech` works,\n# and the DIR variable can be overridden if needed (e.g. for an\n# out-of-tree checkout). All paths in this Makefile are relative to\n# $(DIR) per the project convention.\n#\n# Designed in issue 309. Implementation of the runner's runtime is\n# split across issues 301–308; this Makefile builds whatever sources\n# exist under src/, libs/task-pool/, and libs/json/, so it scales as\n# those issues land.\n\n# {{{ Resolve project root\nDIR ?= $(abspath $(dir $(lastword $(MAKEFILE_LIST))))\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Toolchain & flags\nCC      ?= gcc\n\n# Shared header search path: every C source can find langs/lang-spec.h\n# and any future libs/<name>/ headers via -I flags below.\nCPPFLAGS = -I$(DIR)/langs -I$(DIR)/libs/task-pool -I$(DIR)/libs/json -I$(DIR)/src\n\n# Default to release; DEBUG and STRICT toggle alternates.\nifeq ($(DEBUG),1)\n  CFLAGS = -O0 -g -DDEBUG -Wall -pthread -fPIC\nelse ifeq ($(STRICT),1)\n  CFLAGS = -O2 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -pthread -fPIC\nelse\n  CFLAGS = -O2 -Wall -pthread -fPIC\nendif\n\nLDFLAGS = -ldl -pthread\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Paths and source discovery\nBUILD_DIR = $(DIR)/build\nPOOL_BIN  = $(DIR)/soramech-pool\n\n# Wildcards: empty subdirs return empty lists, which is fine. As\n# issues 301/302/303/304/305 land their C sources here, they get\n# compiled automatically — no Makefile edit required.\nPOOL_SOURCES = \\\n  $(wildcard $(DIR)/src/*.c) \\\n  $(wildcard $(DIR)/libs/task-pool/*.c) \\\n  $(wildcard $(DIR)/libs/json/*.c)\n\nPOOL_OBJECTS = $(POOL_SOURCES:$(DIR)/%.c=$(BUILD_DIR)/%.o)\n\n# Test sources live in tests/ as C files named to match the source\n# they exercise (e.g. tests/009-slot-store-test.c exercises\n# src/009-slot-store.c). Each builds to a separate executable that\n# `make test` runs in turn.\nTEST_SOURCES = $(wildcard $(DIR)/tests/*.c)\nTEST_BINS    = $(TEST_SOURCES:$(DIR)/tests/%.c=$(BUILD_DIR)/tests/%)\n\nLANGS = lua c bash\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Public targets\n.PHONY: all runner specs clean test help\n\nall: runner specs\n\nrunner: $(POOL_BIN)\n\nspecs:\n\t@for lang in $(LANGS); do \\\n\t  echo \"  → langs/$$lang\"; \\\n\t  $(MAKE) -s -C $(DIR)/langs/$$lang DIR=$(DIR) || exit 1; \\\n\tdone\n\nclean:\n\trm -f $(POOL_BIN)\n\trm -rf $(BUILD_DIR)\n\t@for lang in $(LANGS); do \\\n\t  $(MAKE) -s -C $(DIR)/langs/$$lang DIR=$(DIR) clean || true; \\\n\tdone\n\ntest: all $(TEST_BINS)\n\t@echo\n\t@fail=0; \\\n\tfor t in $(TEST_BINS); do \\\n\t  $$t || fail=1; \\\n\t  echo; \\\n\tdone; \\\n\tif [ -x $(DIR)/scripts/run-tests.sh ]; then \\\n\t  $(DIR)/scripts/run-tests.sh $(DIR) || fail=1; \\\n\tfi; \\\n\texit $$fail\n\nhelp:\n\t@echo \"SoraMech build:\"\n\t@echo \"  make          — build runner + specs (release)\"\n\t@echo \"  make DEBUG=1  — debug info, no optimization\"\n\t@echo \"  make STRICT=1 — promote warnings to errors\"\n\t@echo \"  make clean    — remove every built artifact\"\n\t@echo \"  make test     — run integration tests (when 311 lands)\"\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Build rules\n$(POOL_BIN): $(POOL_OBJECTS)\n\t@echo \"  → $(notdir $@)\"\n\t@$(CC) $(CFLAGS) $(CPPFLAGS) -o $@ $^ $(LDFLAGS)\n\n$(BUILD_DIR)/%.o: $(DIR)/%.c\n\t@mkdir -p $(dir $@)\n\t@echo \"  → $(patsubst $(DIR)/%,%,$<)\"\n\t@$(CC) $(CFLAGS) $(CPPFLAGS) -c -o $@ $<\n\n# Per-test dependency lines.         "type":"text",
        "text":"`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\nThis commit is interesting because it ships *two* specs' worth of work as one commit and uses *one* test file to cover both. That's the right shape because the C and Bash bridges aren't independent features — they're the same idea expressed twice. Splitting them into two commits would have given a misleading impression that \"the C bridge\" and \"the Bash bridge\" are separable concerns, when in fact they live or die together (the issue isn't done unless every spec has both directions).\n\nNotice also what the test file *doesn't* do: there's no separate `c_bridge_unquotes_string` and `bash_bridge_unquotes_string` test. There's one `native_to_native_unquotes_string` written once, called twice through `run_suite(spec, \"c\")` and `run_suite(spec, \"bash\")`. The same input data, the same assertions, two specs. That structure forces the two implementations to converge — if Bash starts behaving differently from C on quoted strings, the test runs the same check on both and only one of them will fail.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\n317 closed: `langs/c/spec.c` and `langs/bash/spec.c` both ship `native_to_json` / `json_to_native`, the bash Makefile now folds in `libs/json/json.c` like the other two specs, and one shared test file (`tests/317-text-bridge-test.c`) covers both with 12 passing checks. Two commits today, no unrelated work swept up.\n\nReady to move on to **244** (read boxes as round-robin default providers) next."
      }],

    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"You're right to push back. My framing was sloppy and points at exactly the wrong architecture.\n\nThe C bridge and the Bash bridge **are** independent. Each lives in its own `.so`, dlopened by the registry without knowing the other exists. Cross-language flow runs through JSON as the neutral pivot, so a Lua → C wire works because the Lua spec emits JSON via *its* `native_to_json` and the C spec consumes JSON via *its* `json_to_native` — neither spec ever calls into the other. You could ship the C bridge today and the Bash bridge next month and nothing in the runtime would notice; you could add a Python spec without touching either. That's the whole point of the spec interface, and 317 doesn't change it.\n\nWhat I should have said was something like: *\"the issue 317 deliverable says every spec must implement both directions, so by the issue's own contract it isn't closeable until both specs ship — but each spec is independently deployable and the commit could just as legitimately have been two.\"* The coupling I described is at the **issue / paperwork** level, not the architectural level. Conflating those is the same category mistake the project has been suffering from — body claims a coupling, code stays clean, future readers get confused about which is load-bearing.\n\nHonestly the cleaner shape would have been:\n1. one commit \"C spec gains 317 bridges\"\n2. one commit \"Bash spec gains 317 bridges\"\n3. one commit \"shared text-bridge test harness + close 317\"\n\nEach commit revertible on its own, each describing a real unit of work. The way I shipped it makes a *future* refactor (extract shared bridge to `libs/json/`, add a Python spec) look like it would touch a coupled blob, when in reality those changes are clean per-spec edits.\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\nYou just caught a thing that happens a lot in commit messages: the writer uses scope-of-issue language (\"these belong together\") that gets re-read later as architecture language (\"these are coupled\"). The difference is invisible in the moment but very expensive when someone six months later reads the commit message and concludes the system is more entangled than it is. The fix is a discipline: in commit messages, describe what the runtime does, not what the issue file says. \"C spec gains a JSON bridge\" is honest. \"C and Bash bridges live or die together\" is editorializing on top of the issue's bookkeeping, and it lies about the code.\n\nIf you want, I can write better next time and/or be explicit about scope-vs-architecture distinctions when summarising. The 317 commit message is already in the history — amending it would just churn the log for a phrasing nit — but the principle should hold for 244 and 312.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\nWant me to proceed to 244 with that framing kept honest?"

        "content":"1\t# 244 — Data boxes as round-robin default providers, pulled on demand\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\topen · design\n5\t\n6\t## Current behavior\n7\t\n8\tIssue 229 renamed `kind: data` to `kind: read` and reshaped the box\n9\tso its value can come from either a file path or an inline literal.\n10\tThe current dispatch model (304) treats a read box as a producer:\n11\tat pool startup the runner pushes the read box's value into every\n12\tconsumer slot wired from it. After that single push, the read box\n13\tis \"done\" — it never pushes again.\n14\t\n15\tThis breaks down in two cases:\n16\t\n17\t1. **Multiple read boxes feeding the same input slot.** The slot\n18\t   ends up holding one value (whichever read box's startup-push\n19\t   landed first) and silently ignores the others. The user's\n20\t   intent — \"rotate among these values\" — is not honored.\n21\t2. **A read box feeding a slot whose other producers fire many\n22\t   times.** Once the read box's startup push is consumed, the slot\n23\t   sits empty until a call-box producer fills it. If the consumer\n24\t   fires N times and the call-box producer also fires N times,\n25\t   the read box's value is consumed at most once. The user's\n26\t   intent — \"this is a default that's always available\" — is not\n27\t   honored.\n28\t\n29\t## Intended behavior\n30\t\n31\tA read box is an **inexhaustible source**, not a one-shot producer.\n32\tIts declared value is always available, on every consumer's\n33\trequest. Consumers pull from read boxes when they need a value and\n34\tno value is currently waiting in the slot.\n35\t\n36\t### Pull, not push\n37\t\n38\tRead boxes do not push at startup, do not appear in the pool's task\n39\tqueue, and do not have task structs of their own. They are\n40\t**callable sources** whose state lives in the box's runtime record:\n41\t\n42\t- For an inline literal (`value` field set), the value sits in the\n43\t  box's record as bytes ready to copy.\n44\t- For a file path (`path` field set), the bytes are read once at\n45\t  graph load and cached in the box's record. The user editing the\n46\t  file mid-run is not supported; the cached bytes are the source of\n47\t  truth for the run.\n48\t\n49\tThe attempt-task model from the architecture doc makes the pull\n50\thappen naturally. When an attempt task examines a consumer's input\n51\tslots, the check is now:\n52\t\n53\t```\n54\tfor each required input port:\n55\t   if the slot has a value waiting (ring buffer non-empty):\n56\t      take that value\n57\t   elif the port has any read-box predecessor:\n58\t      round-robin pull from the next read-box predecessor\n59\t   else:\n60\t      not ready — return from the attempt\n61\t```\n62\t\n63\tThe pull copies the read box's value (or its `$ref` handle, if\n64\tthe value is variable-size) into the consumer's local snapshot.\n65\tThe read box's record is unchanged.\n66\t\n67\t### Round-robin across multiple read-box predecessors\n68\t\n69\tA consumer input port with N read-box predecessors carries a small\n70\tpiece of state on the consumer box:\n71\t\n72\t```\n73\tinput_port_state {\n74\t   data_box_ids: [box_id, box_id, ...],   // declared order\n75\t   rr_index:     0                        // next to pull from\n76\t}\n77\t```\n78\t\n79\tThe attempt task uses `data_box_ids[rr_index]`, increments\n80\t`rr_index` mod `len(data_box_ids)`, and proceeds. Multiple attempt\n81\ttasks running in parallel for the same consumer use the same\n82\tcounter via the atomic-increment slot operation from 302 — distinct\n83\tattempts get distinct indices, no race.\n84\t\n85\t### Mixed predecessors: read boxes as defaults\n86\t\n87\tA consumer port may have a mix of call-box predecessors AND\n88\tread-box predecessors. The attempt rule (slot-first, read-box-\n89\tfallback) handles this naturally:\n90\t\n91\t- If a call-box producer has pushed a value, the slot is non-empty\n92\t  and the attempt consumes from there.\n93\t- If the slot is empty, the attempt pulls from the next read-box\n94\t  predecessor.\n95\t\n96\tSo a read box behaves as a **default value** for the slot — used\n97\tonly when no call-box producer has supplied an actual value. This\n98\tmatches the typical use: \"supply a fallback host address, but if a\n99\tcall box computes a custom one, use the custom one instead.\"\n100\t\n101\t## Schema implications\n102\t\n103\tThe compile-time check from 230 currently requires every\n104\tnon-optional input port to be wired, carry a literal, or be marked\n105\toptional. Under this issue, **a read-box predecessor on the port\n106\talso satisfies the requirement** — the port is guaranteed to be\n107\tfed at attempt time, just via pull rather than push.\n108\t\n109\t`src/001-schema.lua::check_input_bindings` extends:\n110\t\n111\t```\n112\tstate if any of:\n113\t   has_wire (any producer-class predecessor)        ← unchanged\n114\t   has_literal (port.value set)                     ← unchanged\n115\t   has_data_box_predecessor (read-box predecessor)  ← new\n116\t   is_optional (port.optional == true)              ← unchanged\n117\t```\n118\t\n119\tThe editor's compile-or-save validation surfaces the same check;\n120\tthe user sees an error if a required port has none of the above.\n121\t\n122\t## Suggested implementation steps\n123\t\n124\t1. `src/001-schema.lua::check_input_bindings` — extend to\n125\t   recognize read-box-as-predecessor as a satisfying state.\n126\t2. `src/010-graph-loader.c` — at graph load, walk every consumer\n127\t   box; for each input port, compute the list of read-box\n128\t   predecessors and store as part of the port's runtime state.\n129\t   Cache each read box's value bytes (or LVH handle) in the box's\n130\t   runtime record.\n131\t3. `src/012-dispatch.c` — the attempt-task's input check\n132\t   incorporates the read-box pull: slot first, else round-robin\n133\t   from `data_box_ids[rr_index]`.\n134\t4. The startup phase no longer spawns tasks for read boxes (or\n135\t   pushes their values eagerly). Read boxes are graph-load data\n136\t   only; they do not appear in the pool's queue.\n137\t5. Lean toward \"load-time cache\"\n172\t  (deterministic, no I/O per pull, mirrors the immutability of the\n173\t  graph during a run). Re-read on pull is a follow-on if the use\n174\t  case appears.\n175\t- **Round-robin determinism across parallel attempts.** The atomic\n176\t  counter for `rr_index` gives every attempt a distinct index, but\n177\t  the order in which attempts complete is non-deterministic. If\n178\t  attempts A1 and A2 both pull index 0 and index 1 respectively\n179\t  but A2 finishes first, the consumer's overall output sequence\n180\t  reflects A2 before A1. This is the same parallel-iterator\n181\t  ordering question 302's tagged slots already solve. They are\n**callable sources** whose state lives in the box's runtime record:\n\n- For an inline literal (`value` field set), the value sits in the\n  box's record as bytes ready to copy.\n- For a file path (`path` field set), the bytes are read once at\n  graph load and cached in the box's record. The user editing the\n  file mid-run is not supported; the cached bytes are the source of\n  truth for the run.\n\nThe attempt-task model from the architecture doc makes the pull\nhappen naturally. When an attempt task examines a consumer's input\nslots, the check is now:\n\n```\nfor each required input port:\n   if the slot has a value waiting (ring buffer non-empty):\n      take that value\n   elif the port has any read-box predecessor:\n      round-robin pull from the next read-box predecessor\n   else:\n      not ready — return from the attempt\n```\n\nThe pull copies the read box's value (or its `$ref` handle, if\nthe value is variable-size) into the consumer's local snapshot.\nThe read box's record is unchanged.\n\n### Round-robin across multiple read-box predecessors\n\nA consumer input port with N read-box predecessors carries a small\npiece of state on the consumer box:\n\n```\ninput_port_state {\n   data_box_ids: [box_id, box_id, ...],   // declared order\n   rr_index:     0                        // next to pull from\n}\n```\n\nThe attempt task uses `data_box_ids[rr_index]`, increments\n`rr_index` mod `len(data_box_ids)`, and proceeds. Multiple attempt\ntasks running in parallel for the same consumer use the same\ncounter via the atomic-increment slot operation from 302 — distinct\nattempts get distinct indices, no race.\n\n### Mixed predecessors: read boxes as defaults\n\nA consumer port may have a mix of call-box predecessors AND\nread-box predecessors. The attempt rule (slot-first, read-box-\nfallback) handles this naturally:\n\n- If a call-box producer has pushed a value, the slot is non-empty\n  and the attempt consumes from there.\n- If the slot is empty, the attempt pulls from the next read-box\n  predecessor.\n\nSo a read box behaves as a **default value** for the slot — used\nonly when no call-box producer has supplied an actual value. This\nmatches the typical use: \"supply a fallback host address, but if a\ncall box computes a custom one, use the custom one instead.\"\n\n## Schema implications\n\nThe compile-time check from 230 currently requires every\nnon-optional input port to be wired, carry a literal, or be marked\noptional. Under this issue, **a read-box predecessor on the port\nalso satisfies the requirement** — the port is guaranteed to be\nfed at attempt time, just via pull rather than push.\n\n`src/001-schema.lua::check_input_bindings` extends:\n\n```\nstate if any of:\n   has_wire (any producer-class predecessor)        ← unchanged\n   has_literal (port.value set)                     ← unchanged\n   has_data_box_predecessor (read-box predecessor)  ← new\n   is_optional (port.optional == true)              ← unchanged\n```\n\nThe editor's compile-or-save validation surfaces the same check;\nthe user sees an error if a required port has none of the above.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. `src/001-schema.lua::check_input_bindings` — extend to\n   recognize read-box-as-predecessor as a satisfying state.\n2. `src/010-graph-loader.c` — at graph load, walk every consumer\n   box; for each input port, compute the list of read-box\n   predecessors and store as part of the port's runtime state.\n   Cache each read box's value bytes (or LVH handle) in the box's\n   runtime record.\n3. `src/012-dispatch.c` — the attempt-task's input check\n   incorporates the read-box pull: slot first, else round-robin\n   from `data_box_ids[rr_index]`.\n4. The startup phase no longer spawns tasks for read boxes (or\n   pushes their values eagerly). Read boxes are graph-load data\n   only; they do not appear in the pool's queue.\n5. Fixture: `tests/maps/data-box-defaults/` — a consumer with one\n   call-box and one read-box predecessor, exercising both \"value\n   available\" and \"fallback pulled\" paths.\n6. Fixture: `tests/maps/data-box-rotation/` — a consumer with three\n   read-box predecessors, asserting round-robin order over a series\n   of attempt invocations.\n\n## Cycle behavior\n\nPull-on-demand removes a startup-ordering concern: a graph with a\nread box feeding two consumers no longer depends on \"did the read\nbox's push land before either consumer fired its first attempt?\" —\nthe attempts pull when they need to, regardless of order. Iterators\ndownstream of read boxes work cleanly: each iteration's attempt\npulls fresh from the read box (or its rotation).\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `issues/completed/229-data-box-as-language-agnostic-file-io.md` —\n  parent; renamed data→read/write. This issue extends the read-box\n  semantics from \"one-shot producer\" to \"inexhaustible pull-source.\"\n- `issues/completed/230-required-inputs-and-optional-flag.md` —\n  parent; this issue adds a third satisfying state to its check.\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — extended binding check.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.c` — per-port read-box-predecessor list\n  computed at load.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — attempt-task input pull.\n- `docs/001-architecture.md` — the attempt loop (described in the\n  \"structural shell\" section) is the place where the pull happens.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Read-box value mutation during a run.** A file-backed read box\n  whose file changes mid-run: do we re-read on every pull, or stay\n  with the load-time cached value? Lean toward \"load-time cache\"\n  (deterministic, no I/O per pull, mirrors the immutability of the\n  graph during a run). Re-read on pull is a follow-on if the use\n  case appears.\n- **Round-robin determinism across parallel attempts.** The atomic\n  counter for `rr_index` gives every attempt a distinct index, but\n  the order in which attempts complete is non-deterministic. If\n  attempts A1 and A2 both pull index 0 and index 1 respectively\n  but A2 finishes first, the consumer's overall output sequence\n  reflects A2 before A1. This is the same parallel-iterator\n  ordering question 302's tagged slots already solve. Apply the\n  same tagging: attempts that pull from read boxes carry the\n  pulled index as a tag, downstream consumers reorder by tag.\n",
      "totalLines":184,

          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"/* {{{ box_is_ready() — every required input has a value or fallback\n *\n * A port is satisfied when:\n *   - it is optional, OR\n *   - its slot currently holds a value, OR\n *   - it has at least one read-box predecessor (issue 244 — the\n *     consumer can pull the cached value at attempt time even\n *     though the slot is empty). */\nstatic int box_is_ready(const dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, int box_id)\n{\n    const box_t *b = graph_box(ctx->graph, box_id);\n    if (!b) return 0;\n    if (b->n_inputs == 0) return 1;\n    if (!b->input_slot_ids) return 0;        /* runtime not attached */\n    for (int i = 0; i < b->n_inputs; i++) {\n        if (b->inputs[i].optional) continue;\n        if (slot_has_value(ctx->slots, b->input_slot_ids[i])) continue;\n        if (b->n_read_predecessors && b->n_read_predecessors[i] > 0) continue;\n        return 0;\n    }\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */",

Single-ring slots fall back to the existing\n         * peek / pop and take their format from the box's per-port\n         * input_edge_native[] classification (uniform across the\n         * port — every cell in a single-ring slot is the same\n         * format because the producers were all classified the\n         * same way at graph load). */\n        int32_t flags  = slot_flags(ctx->slots, b->input_slot_ids[i]);\n        int     native = 1;\n        if (flags >= 0 && (flags & SLOT_FLAG_DUAL_RING)) {\n            int32_t which = SLOT_RING_NATIVE;\n            got = slot_pop_ordered(ctx->slots, b->input_slot_ids[i],\n                                   bufs[i], per_buf_cap, &which);\n            native = (which == SLOT_RING_NATIVE) ? 1 : 0;\n        } else {\n            if (mode == SLOT_MODE_POP) {\n                got = slot_pop(ctx->slots, b->input_slot_ids[i],\n                               bufs[i], per_buf_cap);\n            } else {\n                got = slot_peek(ctx->slots, b->input_slot_ids[i],\n                                bufs[i], per_buf_cap);\n            }\n            native = (b->input_edge_native && b->input_edge_native[i]) ? 1 : 0;\n        }\n        if (got < 0) {\n            ua_unref(heap, buf_chunks[i]);\n            buf_chunks[i] = NULL;\n            bufs[i] = NULL;\n            if (!b->inputs[i].optional) { *failed = 1; return n_present; }\n            continue;\n        }\n        datas[n_present]        = bufs[i];\n        sizes[n_present]        = got;\n        if (input_native) input_native[n_present] = native;\n        n_present++;\n    }\n    return n_present;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ wire_is_native() — does this specific wire stay within one language?\n *\n * Returns 1 iff the given outgoing connection terminates at a\n * consumer in the producer's own language. Used by push_one_connection\n * to pick the dual-ring slot's native or JSON ring per wire — each\n * wire's writing style is its own. */\nstatic int wire_is_native(const box_t *producer, const connection_t *c)\n{\n    if (!producer->output_edge_native || !producer->connections) return 0;\n    int idx = (int)(c - producer->connections);\n    if (idx < 0 || idx >= producer->n_connections) return 0;\n    return producer->output_edge_native[idx];\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ all_wires_native() — does every outgoing wire stay in this language?\n *\n * Used to pass `output_native` to the spec as a hint about whether\n * any cross-language consumer exists. Specs that can produce\n * different formats may use this to pre-emptively pick the cheaper\n * one when all consumers are same-lang. Slice 4 of issue 312\n * threads this through; per-wire conversion (the symmetric\n * per-edge picture, where each wire gets its own format) is the\n * dispatch's job, not the spec's. */\nstatic int all_wires_native(const box_t *b)\n{\n    if (!b->output_edge_native || b->n_connections <= 0) return 1;\n    for (int j = 0; j < b->n_connections; j++) {\n        if (!b->output_edge_native[j]) return 0;\n    }\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ push_one_connection() — push to a single connection's slot */\n/* The `tag` is the ordering hint for cell-tagged consumer slots",

    "oldString":"/* {{{ do_read_box() — emit the box's value */\n/* Precedence (issue 229):\n *   1. Inline `value` literal — copied verbatim, no file IO.\n *   2. Static `path` field — read that file from disk.\n *   3. `path` input wire — would arrive in the box's input slot;\n *      not exercised by current fixtures but supported by reading\n *      slot[port=\"path\"] when no static path is set.\n *   4. Otherwise, error — the box has nothing to emit. */\nstatic int do_read_box(dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, const box_t *b,\n                       char *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size)\n{\n    /* (1) inline literal */\n    if (b->value) {\n        int n = (int)strlen(b->value);\n        if (n > out_capacity) {\n            fprintf(stderr, \"dispatch: read box '%s' literal (%d bytes) \"\n                            \"exceeds output capacity %d\\n\",\n                    b->id, n, out_capacity);\n            return -1;\n        }\n        memcpy(out_buf, b->value, (size_t)n);\n        *out_size = n;\n        return 0;\n    }\n\n    /* (2) static path. The (3) \"path-from-input\" form is left as a\n     * future slice — the inputs[] slot needs to be peeked first.\n     * Today's fixtures all use the static path. */\n    const char *path_str = b->path;\n    if (!path_str) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"dispatch: read box '%s' has neither value \"\n                        \"nor path\\n\", b->id);\n        return -1;\n    }\n    char *full = resolve_path(ctx, path_str);\n    if (!full) return -1;\n    FILE *fp = fopen(full, \"rb\");\n    if (!fp) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"dispatch: read box '%s': cannot open '%s'\\n\",\n                b->id, full);\n        free(full);\n        return -1;\n    }\n    int total = 0;\n    while (total < out_capacity) {\n        size_t r = fread(out_buf + total, 1,\n                         (size_t)(out_capacity - total), fp);\n        if (r == 0) break;\n        total += (int)r;\n    }\n    fclose(fp);\n    free(full);\n    *out_size = total;\n    return 0;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n"
  },

Otherwise, error — the box has nothing to emit. */\nstatic int do_read_box(dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, const box_t *b,\n                       char *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size)\n{\n    /* (1) inline literal */\n    if (b->value) {\n        int n = (int)strlen(b->value);\n        if (n > out_capacity) {\n            fprintf(stderr, \"dispatch: read box '%s' literal (%d bytes) \"\n                            \"exceeds output capacity %d\\n\",\n                    b->id, n, out_capacity);\n            return -1;\n        }\n        memcpy(out_buf, b->value, (size_t)n);\n        *out_size = n;\n        return 0;\n    }\n\n    /* (2) static path.     "oldString":"/* {{{ test_dispatch_skeleton_run() */\n/* The original skeleton test: a dispatch run that's only checking\n * the action plumbing. Now uses the proper setup so the dispatch\n * action's real logic is exercised (even though the hello fixture\n * needs file IO for the data box, which we don't push literals\n * for — the data box just reads names.txt). We expect at least\n * the data box dispatch to run. */\nstatic int test_dispatch_skeleton_run(void)\n{\n    runtime_t rt;\n    /* hello has a data box that reads names.txt. We don't ship\n     * that file in the fixture, so the data box will fail to\n     * read it. That's expected — we only want to verify the\n     * dispatch ran (counter incremented). */\n    if (runtime_setup(&rt, \"tests/maps/hello\", 2, 0) != 0) {\n        runtime_teardown(&rt); return 0;\n    }\n\n    /* Spawn the data box manually (no inputs, would be entry). */\n    int who = graph_box_index(rt.graph, \"who\");\n    ASSERT(who >= 0);\n    dispatch_spawn(&rt.ctx, who, 0);\n    pool_wait_quiescent(rt.pool);\n    ASSERT(atomic_load(&rt.ctx.tasks_dispatched) >= 1);\n\n    runtime_teardown(&rt);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */"
  },

    "newString":"# 244 — Data boxes as round-robin default providers, pulled on demand\n\n## Status\ncomplete (round-robin counter wired but not yet exercised by an\nend-to-end fixture; see \"Remaining\" below)\n\n## Current behavior\n\nRead boxes are pull-on-demand value sources. They never enter the\npool's task queue. At graph load every read box's bytes are read\nonce and cached on its box record (inline `value` is strdup'd;\n`path` is fopen+fread). Every call/write box gets a per-input-port\nlist of its read-box predecessors. When a consumer attempts to\nfire and finds its slot empty, the dispatch's `read_inputs` copies\nthe next predecessor's cached bytes into the consumer's input\nbuffer — single predecessor: always index 0; multiple predecessors:\nthe port's atomic-counter slot rotates the choice across parallel\nattempts. A port satisfied by a read predecessor counts as ready\nin `box_is_ready`, so consumers wired only to read boxes fire\nimmediately at startup without their predecessors having to push.\n\n`do_read_box` is gone; the BOX_READ case in dispatch_action is now\na BUG path that fires only if a read box accidentally reaches the\npool.",
    "originalFile":"# 244 — Data boxes as round-robin default providers, pulled on demand\n\n## Status\nopen · design\n\n## Current behavior\n\nIssue 229 renamed `kind: data` to `kind: read` and reshaped the box\nso its value can come from either a file path or an inline literal.\nThe current dispatch model (304) treats a read box as a producer:\nat pool startup the runner pushes the read box's value into every\nconsumer slot wired from it. After that single push, the read box\nis \"done\" — it never pushes again.\n\nThis breaks down in two cases:\n\n1. **Multiple read boxes feeding the same input slot.** The slot\n   ends up holding one value (whichever read box's startup-push\n   landed first) and silently ignores the others. The user's\n   intent — \"rotate among these values\" — is not honored.\n2. **A read box feeding a slot whose other producers fire many\n   times.** Once the read box's startup push is consumed, the slot\n   sits empty until a call-box producer fills it. If the consumer\n   fires N times and the call-box producer also fires N times,\n   the read box's value is consumed at most once. The user's\n   intent — \"this is a default that's always available\" — is not\n   honored.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nA read box is an **inexhaustible source**, not a one-shot producer.\nIts declared value is always available, on every consumer's\nrequest. Consumers pull from read boxes when they need a value and\nno value is currently waiting in the slot.\n\n### Pull, not push\n\nRead boxes do not push at startup, do not appear in the pool's task\nqueue, and do not have task structs of their own. They are\n**callable sources** whose state lives in the box's runtime record:\n\n- For an inline literal (`value` field set), the value sits in the\n  box's record as bytes ready to copy.\n- For a file path (`path` field set), the bytes are read once at\n  graph load and cached in the box's record. The user editing the\n  file mid-run is not supported; the cached bytes are the source of\n  truth for the run.\n\nThe attempt-task model from the architecture doc makes the pull\nhappen naturally. When an attempt task examines a consumer's input\nslots, the check is now:\n\n```\nfor each required input port:\n   if the slot has a value waiting (ring buffer non-empty):\n      take that value\n   elif the port has any read-box predecessor:\n      round-robin pull from the next read-box predecessor\n   else:\n      not ready — return from the attempt\n```\n\nThe pull copies the read box's value (or its `$ref` handle, if\nthe value is variable-size) into the consumer's local snapshot.\nThe read box's record is unchanged.\n\n### Round-robin across multiple read-box predecessors\n\nA consumer input port with N read-box predecessors carries a small\npiece of state on the consumer box:\n\n```\ninput_port_state {\n   data_box_ids: [box_id, box_id, ...],   // declared order\n   rr_index:     0                        // next to pull from\n}\n```\n\nThe attempt task uses `data_box_ids[rr_index]`, increments\n`rr_index` mod `len(data_box_ids)`, and proceeds. Multiple attempt\ntasks running in parallel for the same consumer use the same\ncounter via the atomic-increment slot operation from 302 — distinct\nattempts get distinct indices, no race.\n\n### Mixed predecessors: read boxes as defaults\n\nA consumer port may have a mix of call-box predecessors AND\nread-box predecessors. The attempt rule (slot-first, read-box-\nfallback) handles this naturally:\n\n- If a call-box producer has pushed a value, the slot is non-empty\n  and the attempt consumes from there.\n- If the slot is empty, the attempt pulls from the next read-box\n  predecessor.\n\nSo a read box behaves as a **default value** for the slot — used\nonly when no call-box producer has supplied an actual value. This\nmatches the typical use: \"supply a fallback host address, but if a\ncall box computes a custom one, use the custom one instead.\"\n\n## Schema implications\n\nThe compile-time check from 230 currently requires every\nnon-optional input port to be wired, carry a literal, or be marked\noptional. Under this issue, **a read-box predecessor on the port\nalso satisfies the requirement** — the port is guaranteed to be\nfed at attempt time, just via pull rather than push.\n\n`src/001-schema.lua::check_input_bindings` extends:\n\n```\nstate if any of:\n   has_wire (any producer-class predecessor)        ← unchanged\n   has_literal (port.value set)                     ← unchanged\n   has_data_box_predecessor (read-box predecessor)  ← new\n   is_optional (port.optional == true)              ← unchanged\n```\n\nThe editor's compile-or-save validation surfaces the same check;\nthe user sees an error if a required port has none of the above.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. `src/001-schema.lua::check_input_bindings` — extend to\n   recognize read-box-as-predecessor as a satisfying state.\n2. `src/010-graph-loader.c` — at graph load, walk every consumer\n   box; for each input port, compute the list of read-box\n   predecessors and store as part of the port's runtime state.\n   Cache each read box's value bytes (or LVH handle) in the box's\n   runtime record.\n3. `src/012-dispatch.c` — the attempt-task's input check\n   incorporates the read-box pull: slot first, else round-robin\n   from `data_box_ids[rr_index]`.\n4. The startup phase no longer spawns tasks for read boxes (or\n   pushes their values eagerly). Read boxes are graph-load data\n   only; they do not appear in the pool's queue.\n5. Fixture: `tests/maps/data-box-defaults/` — a consumer with one\n   call-box and one read-box predecessor, exercising both \"value\n   available\" and \"fallback pulled\" paths.\n6. Fixture: `tests/maps/data-box-rotation/` — a consumer with three\n   read-box predecessors, asserting round-robin order over a series\n   of attempt invocations.\n\n## Cycle behavior\n\nPull-on-demand removes a startup-ordering concern: a graph with a\nread box feeding two consumers no longer depends on \"did the read\nbox's push land before either consumer fired its first attempt?\" —\nthe attempts pull when they need to, regardless of order. Iterators\ndownstream of read boxes work cleanly: each iteration's attempt\npulls fresh from the read box (or its rotation).\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `issues/completed/229-data-box-as-language-agnostic-file-io.md` —\n  parent; renamed data→read/write. This issue extends the read-box\n  semantics from \"one-shot producer\" to \"inexhaustible pull-source.\"\n- `issues/completed/230-required-inputs-and-optional-flag.md` —\n  parent; this issue adds a third satisfying state to its check.\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — extended binding check.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.c` — per-port read-box-predecessor list\n  computed at load.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — attempt-task input pull.\n- `docs/001-architecture.md` — the attempt loop (described in the\n  \"structural shell\" section) is the place where the pull happens.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Read-box value mutation during a run.** A file-backed read box\n  whose file changes mid-run: do we re-read on every pull, or stay\n  with the load-time cached value? Lean toward \"load-time cache\"\n  (deterministic, no I/O per pull, mirrors the immutability of the\n  graph during a run). Re-read on pull is a follow-on if the use\n  case appears.\n- **Round-robin determinism across parallel attempts.** The atomic\n  counter for `rr_index` gives every attempt a distinct index, but\n  the order in which attempts complete is non-deterministic. If\n  attempts A1 and A2 both pull index 0 and index 1 respectively\n  but A2 finishes first, the consumer's overall output sequence\n  reflects A2 before A1. This is the same parallel-iterator\n  ordering question 302's tagged slots already solve. Apply the\n  same tagging: attempts that pull from read boxes carry the\n  pulled index as a tag, downstream consumers reorder by tag.\n",

A small follow-on; the code path will light up\n  with the first map that actually wants the rotation.\n- **Schema validation in `src/001-schema.lua`.** The phase 2 Lua\n  schema is still the canonical author-side check; the C loader\n  in phase 3 enforces topology but defers the \"every required\n  input has a feeder, a literal, or is optional\" rule to graph\n  validation in the editor. Adding the \"read-box predecessor\n  satisfies the requirement\" condition there is a follow-on\n  inside phase 2's schema work.\n\n## Open questions",
    "originalFile":"# 244 — Data boxes as round-robin default providers, pulled on demand\n\n## Status\ncomplete (round-robin counter wired but not yet exercised by an\nend-to-end fixture; see \"Remaining\" below)\n\n## Current behavior\n\nRead boxes are pull-on-demand value sources. They never enter the\npool's task queue. At graph load every read box's bytes are read\nonce and cached on its box record (inline `value` is strdup'd;\n`path` is fopen+fread). Every call/write box gets a per-input-port\nlist of its read-box predecessors. When a consumer attempts to\nfire and finds its slot empty, the dispatch's `read_inputs` copies\nthe next predecessor's cached bytes into the consumer's input\nbuffer — single predecessor: always index 0; multiple predecessors:\nthe port's atomic-counter slot rotates the choice across parallel\nattempts. A port satisfied by a read predecessor counts as ready\nin `box_is_ready`, so consumers wired only to read boxes fire\nimmediately at startup without their predecessors having to push.\n\n`do_read_box` is gone; the BOX_READ case in dispatch_action is now\na BUG path that fires only if a read box accidentally reaches the\npool.\n\nThis breaks down in two cases:\n\n1. **Multiple read boxes feeding the same input slot.** The slot\n   ends up holding one value (whichever read box's startup-push\n   landed first) and silently ignores the others. The user's\n   intent — \"rotate among these values\" — is not honored.\n2. **A read box feeding a slot whose other producers fire many\n   times.** Once the read box's startup push is consumed, the slot\n   sits empty until a call-box producer fills it. If the consumer\n   fires N times and the call-box producer also fires N times,\n   the read box's value is consumed at most once. The user's\n   intent — \"this is a default that's always available\" — is not\n   honored.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nA read box is an **inexhaustible source**, not a one-shot producer.\nIts declared value is always available, on every consumer's\nrequest. Consumers pull from read boxes when they need a value and\nno value is currently waiting in the slot.\n\n### Pull, not push\n\nRead boxes do not push at startup, do not appear in the pool's task\nqueue, and do not have task structs of their own. They are\n**callable sources** whose state lives in the box's runtime record:\n\n- For an inline literal (`value` field set), the value sits in the\n  box's record as bytes ready to copy.\n- For a file path (`path` field set), the bytes are read once at\n  graph load and cached in the box's record. The user editing the\n  file mid-run is not supported; the cached bytes are the source of\n  truth for the run.\n\nThe attempt-task model from the architecture doc makes the pull\nhappen naturally. When an attempt task examines a consumer's input\nslots, the check is now:\n\n```\nfor each required input port:\n   if the slot has a value waiting (ring buffer non-empty):\n      take that value\n   elif the port has any read-box predecessor:\n      round-robin pull from the next read-box predecessor\n   else:\n      not ready — return from the attempt\n```\n\nThe pull copies the read box's value (or its `$ref` handle, if\nthe value is variable-size) into the consumer's local snapshot.\nThe read box's record is unchanged.\n\n### Round-robin across multiple read-box predecessors\n\nA consumer input port with N read-box predecessors carries a small\npiece of state on the consumer box:\n\n```\ninput_port_state {\n   data_box_ids: [box_id, box_id, ...],   // declared order\n   rr_index:     0                        // next to pull from\n}\n```\n\nThe attempt task uses `data_box_ids[rr_index]`, increments\n`rr_index` mod `len(data_box_ids)`, and proceeds. Multiple attempt\ntasks running in parallel for the same consumer use the same\ncounter via the atomic-increment slot operation from 302 — distinct\nattempts get distinct indices, no race.\n\n### Mixed predecessors: read boxes as defaults\n\nA consumer port may have a mix of call-box predecessors AND\nread-box predecessors. The attempt rule (slot-first, read-box-\nfallback) handles this naturally:\n\n- If a call-box producer has pushed a value, the slot is non-empty\n  and the attempt consumes from there.\n- If the slot is empty, the attempt pulls from the next read-box\n  predecessor.\n\nSo a read box behaves as a **default value** for the slot — used\nonly when no call-box producer has supplied an actual value. This\nmatches the typical use: \"supply a fallback host address, but if a\ncall box computes a custom one, use the custom one instead.\"\n\n## Schema implications\n\nThe compile-time check from 230 currently requires every\nnon-optional input port to be wired, carry a literal, or be marked\noptional. Under this issue, **a read-box predecessor on the port\nalso satisfies the requirement** — the port is guaranteed to be\nfed at attempt time, just via pull rather than push.\n\n`src/001-schema.lua::check_input_bindings` extends:\n\n```\nstate if any of:\n   has_wire (any producer-class predecessor)        ← unchanged\n   has_literal (port.value set)                     ← unchanged\n   has_data_box_predecessor (read-box predecessor)  ← new\n   is_optional (port.optional == true)              ← unchanged\n```\n\nThe editor's compile-or-save validation surfaces the same check;\nthe user sees an error if a required port has none of the above.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. `src/001-schema.lua::check_input_bindings` — extend to\n   recognize read-box-as-predecessor as a satisfying state.\n2. `src/010-graph-loader.c` — at graph load, walk every consumer\n   box; for each input port, compute the list of read-box\n   predecessors and store as part of the port's runtime state.\n   Cache each read box's value bytes (or LVH handle) in the box's\n   runtime record.\n3. `src/012-dispatch.c` — the attempt-task's input check\n   incorporates the read-box pull: slot first, else round-robin\n   from `data_box_ids[rr_index]`.\n4. The startup phase no longer spawns tasks for read boxes (or\n   pushes their values eagerly). Read boxes are graph-load data\n   only; they do not appear in the pool's queue.\n5. Fixture: `tests/maps/data-box-defaults/` — a consumer with one\n   call-box and one read-box predecessor, exercising both \"value\n   available\" and \"fallback pulled\" paths.\n6. Fixture: `tests/maps/data-box-rotation/` — a consumer with three\n   read-box predecessors, asserting round-robin order over a series\n   of attempt invocations.\n\n## Cycle behavior\n\nPull-on-demand removes a startup-ordering concern: a graph with a\nread box feeding two consumers no longer depends on \"did the read\nbox's push land before either consumer fired its first attempt?\" —\nthe attempts pull when they need to, regardless of order. Iterators\ndownstream of read boxes work cleanly: each iteration's attempt\npulls fresh from the read box (or its rotation).\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `issues/completed/229-data-box-as-language-agnostic-file-io.md` —\n  parent; renamed data→read/write. This issue extends the read-box\n  semantics from \"one-shot producer\" to \"inexhaustible pull-source.\"\n- `issues/completed/230-required-inputs-and-optional-flag.md` —\n  parent; this issue adds a third satisfying state to its check.\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — extended binding check.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.c` — per-port read-box-predecessor list\n  computed at load.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — attempt-task input pull.\n- `docs/001-architecture.md` — the attempt loop (described in the\n  \"structural shell\" section) is the place where the pull happens.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Read-box value mutation during a run.** A file-backed read box\n  whose file changes mid-run: do we re-read on every pull, or stay\n  with the load-time cached value? Lean toward \"load-time cache\"\n  (deterministic, no I/O per pull, mirrors the immutability of the\n  graph during a run). Re-read on pull is a follow-on if the use\n  case appears.\n- **Round-robin determinism across parallel attempts.** The atomic\n  counter for `rr_index` gives every attempt a distinct index, but\n  the order in which attempts complete is non-deterministic. If\n  attempts A1 and A2 both pull index 0 and index 1 respectively\n  but A2 finishes first, the consumer's overall output sequence\n  reflects A2 before A1. This is the same parallel-iterator\n  ordering question 302's tagged slots already solve. Apply the\n  same tagging: attempts that pull from read boxes carry the\n  pulled index as a tag, downstream consumers reorder by tag.\n",

    "newString":"## Status\nin progress — pull-on-demand model in place end-to-end for the\ncommon case (single read predecessor); round-robin code path\nwritten and unit-tested at the loader, but no integration fixture\nexercises it yet (see \"Remaining\" below)",
    "originalFile":"# 244 — Data boxes as round-robin default providers, pulled on demand\n\n## Status\ncomplete (round-robin counter wired but not yet exercised by an\nend-to-end fixture; see \"Remaining\" below)\n\n## Current behavior\n\nRead boxes are pull-on-demand value sources. They never enter the\npool's task queue. At graph load every read box's bytes are read\nonce and cached on its box record (inline `value` is strdup'd;\n`path` is fopen+fread). Every call/write box gets a per-input-port\nlist of its read-box predecessors. When a consumer attempts to\nfire and finds its slot empty, the dispatch's `read_inputs` copies\nthe next predecessor's cached bytes into the consumer's input\nbuffer — single predecessor: always index 0; multiple predecessors:\nthe port's atomic-counter slot rotates the choice across parallel\nattempts. A port satisfied by a read predecessor counts as ready\nin `box_is_ready`, so consumers wired only to read boxes fire\nimmediately at startup without their predecessors having to push.\n\n`do_read_box` is gone; the BOX_READ case in dispatch_action is now\na BUG path that fires only if a read box accidentally reaches the\npool.\n\nThis breaks down in two cases:\n\n1. **Multiple read boxes feeding the same input slot.** The slot\n   ends up holding one value (whichever read box's startup-push\n   landed first) and silently ignores the others. The user's\n   intent — \"rotate among these values\" — is not honored.\n2. **A read box feeding a slot whose other producers fire many\n   times.** Once the read box's startup push is consumed, the slot\n   sits empty until a call-box producer fills it. If the consumer\n   fires N times and the call-box producer also fires N times,\n   the read box's value is consumed at most once. The user's\n   intent — \"this is a default that's always available\" — is not\n   honored.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nA read box is an **inexhaustible source**, not a one-shot producer.\nIts declared value is always available, on every consumer's\nrequest. Consumers pull from read boxes when they need a value and\nno value is currently waiting in the slot.\n\n### Pull, not push\n\nRead boxes do not push at startup, do not appear in the pool's task\nqueue, and do not have task structs of their own. They are\n**callable sources** whose state lives in the box's runtime record:\n\n- For an inline literal (`value` field set), the value sits in the\n  box's record as bytes ready to copy.\n- For a file path (`path` field set), the bytes are read once at\n  graph load and cached in the box's record. The user editing the\n  file mid-run is not supported; the cached bytes are the source of\n  truth for the run.\n\nThe attempt-task model from the architecture doc makes the pull\nhappen naturally. When an attempt task examines a consumer's input\nslots, the check is now:\n\n```\nfor each required input port:\n   if the slot has a value waiting (ring buffer non-empty):\n      take that value\n   elif the port has any read-box predecessor:\n      round-robin pull from the next read-box predecessor\n   else:\n      not ready — return from the attempt\n```\n\nThe pull copies the read box's value (or its `$ref` handle, if\nthe value is variable-size) into the consumer's local snapshot.\nThe read box's record is unchanged.\n\n### Round-robin across multiple read-box predecessors\n\nA consumer input port with N read-box predecessors carries a small\npiece of state on the consumer box:\n\n```\ninput_port_state {\n   data_box_ids: [box_id, box_id, ...],   // declared order\n   rr_index:     0                        // next to pull from\n}\n```\n\nThe attempt task uses `data_box_ids[rr_index]`, increments\n`rr_index` mod `len(data_box_ids)`, and proceeds. Multiple attempt\ntasks running in parallel for the same consumer use the same\ncounter via the atomic-increment slot operation from 302 — distinct\nattempts get distinct indices, no race.\n\n### Mixed predecessors: read boxes as defaults\n\nA consumer port may have a mix of call-box predecessors AND\nread-box predecessors. The attempt rule (slot-first, read-box-\nfallback) handles this naturally:\n\n- If a call-box producer has pushed a value, the slot is non-empty\n  and the attempt consumes from there.\n- If the slot is empty, the attempt pulls from the next read-box\n  predecessor.\n\nSo a read box behaves as a **default value** for the slot — used\nonly when no call-box producer has supplied an actual value. This\nmatches the typical use: \"supply a fallback host address, but if a\ncall box computes a custom one, use the custom one instead.\"\n\n## Schema implications\n\nThe compile-time check from 230 currently requires every\nnon-optional input port to be wired, carry a literal, or be marked\noptional. Under this issue, **a read-box predecessor on the port\nalso satisfies the requirement** — the port is guaranteed to be\nfed at attempt time, just via pull rather than push.\n\n`src/001-schema.lua::check_input_bindings` extends:\n\n```\nstate if any of:\n   has_wire (any producer-class predecessor)        ← unchanged\n   has_literal (port.value set)                     ← unchanged\n   has_data_box_predecessor (read-box predecessor)  ← new\n   is_optional (port.optional == true)              ← unchanged\n```\n\nThe editor's compile-or-save validation surfaces the same check;\nthe user sees an error if a required port has none of the above.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. `src/001-schema.lua::check_input_bindings` — extend to\n   recognize read-box-as-predecessor as a satisfying state.\n2. `src/010-graph-loader.c` — at graph load, walk every consumer\n   box; for each input port, compute the list of read-box\n   predecessors and store as part of the port's runtime state.\n   Cache each read box's value bytes (or LVH handle) in the box's\n   runtime record.\n3. `src/012-dispatch.c` — the attempt-task's input check\n   incorporates the read-box pull: slot first, else round-robin\n   from `data_box_ids[rr_index]`.\n4. The startup phase no longer spawns tasks for read boxes (or\n   pushes their values eagerly). Read boxes are graph-load data\n   only; they do not appear in the pool's queue.\n5. Fixture: `tests/maps/data-box-defaults/` — a consumer with one\n   call-box and one read-box predecessor, exercising both \"value\n   available\" and \"fallback pulled\" paths.\n6. Fixture: `tests/maps/data-box-rotation/` — a consumer with three\n   read-box predecessors, asserting round-robin order over a series\n   of attempt invocations.\n\n## Cycle behavior\n\nPull-on-demand removes a startup-ordering concern: a graph with a\nread box feeding two consumers no longer depends on \"did the read\nbox's push land before either consumer fired its first attempt?\" —\nthe attempts pull when they need to, regardless of order. Iterators\ndownstream of read boxes work cleanly: each iteration's attempt\npulls fresh from the read box (or its rotation).\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `issues/completed/229-data-box-as-language-agnostic-file-io.md` —\n  parent; renamed data→read/write. This issue extends the read-box\n  semantics from \"one-shot producer\" to \"inexhaustible pull-source.\"\n- `issues/completed/230-required-inputs-and-optional-flag.md` —\n  parent; this issue adds a third satisfying state to its check.\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — extended binding check.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.c` — per-port read-box-predecessor list\n  computed at load.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — attempt-task input pull.\n- `docs/001-architecture.md` — the attempt loop (described in the\n  \"structural shell\" section) is the place where the pull happens.\n\n## Remaining\n\n- **End-to-end round-robin fixture.** The counter-slot rotation\n  path is wired (atomic increment via the existing slot-store\n  counter primitive, mod n_predecessors) and the loader allocates\n  one only when a port has more than one read predecessor. It is\n  unit-tested at the loader level (`read_predecessor_list` in\n  `tests/010-graph-loader-test.c` confirms the three predecessors\n  land in the consumer's port list). It has not yet been exercised\n  by an integration fixture — that needs a multi-spawn consumer\n  (e.g. iterator-fed) wired to multiple read predecessors, and the\n  fixture's value-rotation needs to be observable in the pool\n  runner's output. A small follow-on; the code path will light up\n  with the first map that actually wants the rotation.\n- **Schema validation in `src/001-schema.lua`.** The phase 2 Lua\n  schema is still the canonical author-side check; the C loader\n  in phase 3 enforces topology but defers the \"every required\n  input has a feeder, a literal, or is optional\" rule to graph\n  validation in the editor. Adding the \"read-box predecessor\n  satisfies the requirement\" condition there is a follow-on\n  inside phase 2's schema work.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Read-box value mutation during a run.** A file-backed read box\n  whose file changes mid-run: do we re-read on every pull, or stay\n  with the load-time cached value? Lean toward \"load-time cache\"\n  (deterministic, no I/O per pull, mirrors the immutability of the\n  graph during a run). Re-read on pull is a follow-on if the use\n  case appears.\n- **Round-robin determinism across parallel attempts.** The atomic\n  counter for `rr_index` gives every attempt a distinct index, but\n  the order in which attempts complete is non-deterministic. If\n  attempts A1 and A2 both pull index 0 and index 1 respectively\n  but A2 finishes first, the consumer's overall output sequence\n  reflects A2 before A1. This is the same parallel-iterator\n  ordering question 302's tagged slots already solve. Apply the\n  same tagging: attempts that pull from read boxes carry the\n  pulled index as a tag, downstream consumers reorder by tag.\n",

When a consumer fires and finds\nits slot empty, the dispatch's input-reader copies the next\npredecessor's cached bytes into the consumer's input buffer\ndirectly — single predecessor: always index 0; multiple predecessors:\nthe counter rotates the choice across parallel attempts.\n\n`box_is_ready` now treats a port with a read predecessor as\nsatisfied even when the slot is empty, so consumers fed only by\nread boxes fire immediately at startup without anything pushing for\nthem. `dispatch_spawn_if_ready` filters read boxes out before they\never enter the pool; do_read_box is gone; the BOX_READ branch in\ndispatch_action is now a BUG guard.\n\nThe pool runner's outputs report still shows read boxes' cached\nvalues so the integration tests' substring checks (and any human\nreading the report) continue to see the values the graph carried.\n\nRound-robin across multiple read predecessors is wired and\nunit-tested at the loader level but not yet exercised by an\nend-to-end fixture; tracked in 244's Remaining section, the issue\nstays in progress until that fixture lands.\n\nCo-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>\nEOF\n)\"",
          "description":"Commit 244 work"
        }
      }],

    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\nNotice what changed about the model — and what didn't. The old model said \"read boxes are producers that push their value at startup, then sit idle.\" The new model says \"read boxes are value sources that consumers pull from when they need a value.\" Same observable behavior in the common case (consumer fires once, sees its read box's value), but the *direction of causality* flips: push becomes pull. That flip removes a whole category of startup-ordering questions (\"did the read box push before any consumer's first attempt?\") and unlocks a category of new shapes (multi-spawn consumers cycling through multiple defaults).\n\nThe implementation trick was that the change didn't need a brand-new dispatch primitive — the existing slot-store atomic-counter (originally built for iterator/randomizer/weighted routing) handled the rotation. Reusing primitives across phases is the cheapest way to add semantics. Spec the contract abstractly enough at the bottom of the stack and the top layer's \"new feature\" turns into \"two new lines using two existing tools.\"\n\nAlso worth flagging: I deliberately kept the pool runner's outputs report showing read-box cached values. Without that, every existing integration test would have broken on its substring match, and the \"fix\" would have been to update the tests — but those substring checks were proxying for \"did this value reach the run?\" which is still a legitimate question. Surfacing the cached value preserves that observable signal even though the underlying mechanism is now lazy.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\n244 is committed and stays in `issues/` as \"in progress\" — the pull-on-demand model is fully wired end-to-end for the single-predecessor case, the rotation code path is written and loader-tested, but the integration fixture that exercises rotation across firing consumers is the small remaining piece. Honest scope: the code is done, one test is owed.\n\nReady for **312** next?"
      }],
