    "originalFile":"#!/bin/bash\n# scripts/run-tests.sh — phase 3 integration tests.\n#\n# Runs every fixture map under tests/maps/ through `soramech-pool`\n# and asserts that the captured outputs match a hardcoded\n# expectation per map. The point is to catch regressions\n# end-to-end — past the spec interface, past the dispatch action,\n# past JSONL writing — rather than via the in-process unit tests.\n#\n# Per the project convention: scripts run from any directory via a\n# hard-coded ${DIR} path with an override argument; all paths are\n# relative to ${DIR}.\n\nset -u\n\nDIR=\"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech\"\nif [[ $# -ge 1 ]]; then\n    DIR=\"$1\"\nfi\n\ncd \"$DIR\"\n\npass=0\nfail=0\nfailures=()\n\n# {{{ check_map() — run one fixture, verify expected substrings\ncheck_map() {\n    local map=\"$1\"\n    shift\n    local expected=(\"$@\")\n\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"$map\"\n\n    local output\n    output=$(\"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/$map\" 2>&1)\n    local rc=$?\n\n    local missing=\"\"\n    if [[ $rc -ne 0 ]]; then\n        missing=\"exit=$rc\"\n    fi\n    for e in \"${expected[@]}\"; do\n        if [[ \"$output\" != *\"$e\"* ]]; then\n            missing+=\"${missing:+; }missing '$e'\"\n        fi\n    done\n\n    if [[ -z \"$missing\" ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — %s\\n\" \"$missing\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"$map: $missing\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ pipeline_output_check() — additional: the pipeline writes to disk\npipeline_output_check() {\n    local file=\"/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt\"\n    rm -f \"$file\"\n    \"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/pipeline\" > /dev/null 2>&1\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"pipeline write output\"\n    if [[ -f \"$file\" ]]; then\n        local content\n        content=$(cat \"$file\")\n        if [[ \"$content\" == \"11!\" ]]; then\n            printf \"ok\\n\"\n            pass=$((pass + 1))\n        else\n            printf \"FAIL — expected '11!', got '%s'\\n\" \"$content\"\n            fail=$((fail + 1))\n            failures+=(\"pipeline file: $content\")\n        fi\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — output file missing\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"pipeline: $file missing\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ compile_pipeline_check() — soramech-compile produces a portable artifact\n# Verifies issue 309's compile pipeline: bundles all spec.so + sources\n# into compiled/, then runs the artifact from /tmp (i.e. with no\n# dependency on the project's cwd) and verifies it produces the same\n# output as the source map.\ncompile_pipeline_check() {\n    local map=\"$DIR/tests/maps/pipeline\"\n    local compiled=\"$map/compiled\"\n    local file=\"/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt\"\n\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"compile pipeline (portable run)\"\n\n    rm -rf \"$compiled\"\n    if ! \"$DIR/scripts/soramech-compile.sh\" \"$map\" --dir \"$DIR\" >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n        printf \"FAIL — soramech-compile failed\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: script returned non-zero\")\n        return\n    fi\n    if [[ ! -x \"$compiled/pool-runner\" ]]; then\n        printf \"FAIL — compiled/pool-runner missing or not executable\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: pool-runner missing\")\n        return\n    fi\n\n    rm -f \"$file\"\n    local output\n    output=$(cd /tmp && \"$compiled/pool-runner\" \"$compiled\" 2>&1)\n\n    local content=\"\"\n    [[ -f \"$file\" ]] && content=$(cat \"$file\")\n\n    if [[ \"$output\" == *\"addone → 11\"* ]] && [[ \"$content\" == \"11!\" ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — output='%s' file='%s'\\n\" \"$output\" \"$content\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: bad output\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ run all fixtures\necho \"integration tests (fixture maps):\"\n\ncheck_map \"calc\" \\\n    \"add → 42\"\n\ncheck_map \"hello\" \\\n    \"who → World\" \\\n    \"greet → Hello, World!\"\n\ncheck_map \"comparator\" \\\n    \"classify → 8\" \\\n    \"high → HIGH:8\" \\\n    \"low → (no output)\" \\\n    \"mid → (no output)\"\n\ncheck_map \"iter-route\" \\\n    \"iter → hi\" \\\n    \"a → A:hi\" \\\n    \"b → (no output)\" \\\n    \"c → (no output)\"\n\ncheck_map \"pipeline\" \\\n    \"input → 5\" \\\n    \"double → 10\" \\\n    \"addone → 11\" \\\n    \"shout → 11!\"\n\ncheck_map \"read-literal\" \\\n    \"src → hello, world!\" \\\n    \"echo → hello, world!\"\n\npipeline_output_check\ncompile_pipeline_check\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ parser_tests() — issue 232: unit tests for langs/<lang>/parser.js\n# Run Node's built-in test runner over each per-language parser test\n# file and fold the result into the surrounding pass/fail counters.\n# Each .mjs file is one logical \"test\" from this script's perspective;\n# Node prints its own subtest breakdown on failure for the diagnostic.\nparser_tests() {\n    if ! command -v node >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n        printf \"  %-44s SKIP — node not installed\\n\" \"parser tests (lua, bash)\"\n        return\n    fi\n    for tf in \"$DIR/tests/232-lua-parser-test.mjs\" \\\n              \"$DIR/tests/233-bash-parser-test.mjs\" \\\n              \"$DIR/tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs\"; do\n        local label\n        label=$(basename \"$tf\")\n        printf \"  %-44s \" \"$label\"\n        local out\n        out=$(SORAMECH_DIR=\"$DIR\" node --test \"$tf\" 2>&1)\n        local rc=$?\n        if [[ $rc -eq 0 ]]; then\n            printf \"ok\\n\"\n            pass=$((pass + 1))\n        else\n            printf \"FAIL\\n\"\n            echo \"$out\" | sed 's/^/      /'\n            fail=$((fail + 1))\n            failures+=(\"$label: node --test exit=$rc\")\n        fi\n    done\n}\nparser_tests\n# }}}\n\necho\necho \"  $pass passed, $fail failed\"\n\nif [[ $fail -gt 0 ]]; then\n    echo\n    echo \"  failures:\"\n    for f in \"${failures[@]}\"; do\n        echo \"    - $f\"\n    done\nfi\n\nexit $fail\n",

    "originalFile":"#!/bin/bash\n# scripts/run-tests.sh — phase 3 integration tests.\n#\n# Runs every fixture map under tests/maps/ through `soramech-pool`\n# and asserts that the captured outputs match a hardcoded\n# expectation per map. The point is to catch regressions\n# end-to-end — past the spec interface, past the dispatch action,\n# past JSONL writing — rather than via the in-process unit tests.\n#\n# Per the project convention: scripts run from any directory via a\n# hard-coded ${DIR} path with an override argument; all paths are\n# relative to ${DIR}.\n\nset -u\n\nDIR=\"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech\"\nif [[ $# -ge 1 ]]; then\n    DIR=\"$1\"\nfi\n\ncd \"$DIR\"\n\npass=0\nfail=0\nfailures=()\n\n# {{{ check_map() — run one fixture, verify expected substrings\ncheck_map() {\n    local map=\"$1\"\n    shift\n    local expected=(\"$@\")\n\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"$map\"\n\n    local output\n    output=$(\"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/$map\" 2>&1)\n    local rc=$?\n\n    local missing=\"\"\n    if [[ $rc -ne 0 ]]; then\n        missing=\"exit=$rc\"\n    fi\n    for e in \"${expected[@]}\"; do\n        if [[ \"$output\" != *\"$e\"* ]]; then\n            missing+=\"${missing:+; }missing '$e'\"\n        fi\n    done\n\n    if [[ -z \"$missing\" ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — %s\\n\" \"$missing\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"$map: $missing\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ pipeline_output_check() — additional: the pipeline writes to disk\npipeline_output_check() {\n    local file=\"/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt\"\n    rm -f \"$file\"\n    \"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/pipeline\" > /dev/null 2>&1\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"pipeline write output\"\n    if [[ -f \"$file\" ]]; then\n        local content\n        content=$(cat \"$file\")\n        if [[ \"$content\" == \"11!\" ]]; then\n            printf \"ok\\n\"\n            pass=$((pass + 1))\n        else\n            printf \"FAIL — expected '11!', got '%s'\\n\" \"$content\"\n            fail=$((fail + 1))\n            failures+=(\"pipeline file: $content\")\n        fi\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — output file missing\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"pipeline: $file missing\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ compile_pipeline_check() — soramech-compile produces a portable artifact\n# Verifies issue 309's compile pipeline: bundles all spec.so + sources\n# into compiled/, then runs the artifact from /tmp (i.e. with no\n# dependency on the project's cwd) and verifies it produces the same\n# output as the source map.\ncompile_pipeline_check() {\n    local map=\"$DIR/tests/maps/pipeline\"\n    local compiled=\"$map/compiled\"\n    local file=\"/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt\"\n\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"compile pipeline (portable run)\"\n\n    rm -rf \"$compiled\"\n    if ! \"$DIR/scripts/soramech-compile.sh\" \"$map\" --dir \"$DIR\" >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n        printf \"FAIL — soramech-compile failed\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: script returned non-zero\")\n        return\n    fi\n    if [[ ! -x \"$compiled/pool-runner\" ]]; then\n        printf \"FAIL — compiled/pool-runner missing or not executable\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: pool-runner missing\")\n        return\n    fi\n\n    rm -f \"$file\"\n    local output\n    output=$(cd /tmp && \"$compiled/pool-runner\" \"$compiled\" 2>&1)\n\n    local content=\"\"\n    [[ -f \"$file\" ]] && content=$(cat \"$file\")\n\n    if [[ \"$output\" == *\"addone → 11\"* ]] && [[ \"$content\" == \"11!\" ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — output='%s' file='%s'\\n\" \"$output\" \"$content\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: bad output\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ run all fixtures\necho \"integration tests (fixture maps):\"\n\ncheck_map \"calc\" \\\n    \"add → 42\"\n\ncheck_map \"hello\" \\\n    \"greet → Hello, World!\"\n\ncheck_map \"comparator\" \\\n    \"classify → 8\" \\\n    \"high → HIGH:8\" \\\n    \"low → (no output)\" \\\n    \"mid → (no output)\"\n\ncheck_map \"iter-route\" \\\n    \"iter → hi\" \\\n    \"a → A:hi\" \\\n    \"b → (no output)\" \\\n    \"c → (no output)\"\n\ncheck_map \"pipeline\" \\\n    \"double → 10\" \\\n    \"addone → 11\" \\\n    \"shout → 11!\"\n\ncheck_map \"read-literal\" \\\n    \"src → hello, world!\" \\\n    \"echo → hello, world!\"\n\npipeline_output_check\ncompile_pipeline_check\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ parser_tests() — issue 232: unit tests for langs/<lang>/parser.js\n# Run Node's built-in test runner over each per-language parser test\n# file and fold the result into the surrounding pass/fail counters.\n# Each .mjs file is one logical \"test\" from this script's perspective;\n# Node prints its own subtest breakdown on failure for the diagnostic.\nparser_tests() {\n    if ! command -v node >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n        printf \"  %-44s SKIP — node not installed\\n\" \"parser tests (lua, bash)\"\n        return\n    fi\n    for tf in \"$DIR/tests/232-lua-parser-test.mjs\" \\\n              \"$DIR/tests/233-bash-parser-test.mjs\" \\\n              \"$DIR/tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs\"; do\n        local label\n        label=$(basename \"$tf\")\n        printf \"  %-44s \" \"$label\"\n        local out\n        out=$(SORAMECH_DIR=\"$DIR\" node --test \"$tf\" 2>&1)\n        local rc=$?\n        if [[ $rc -eq 0 ]]; then\n            printf \"ok\\n\"\n            pass=$((pass + 1))\n        else\n            printf \"FAIL\\n\"\n            echo \"$out\" | sed 's/^/      /'\n            fail=$((fail + 1))\n            failures+=(\"$label: node --test exit=$rc\")\n        fi\n    done\n}\nparser_tests\n# }}}\n\necho\necho \"  $pass passed, $fail failed\"\n\nif [[ $fail -gt 0 ]]; then\n    echo\n    echo \"  failures:\"\n    for f in \"${failures[@]}\"; do\n        echo \"    - $f\"\n    done\nfi\n\nexit $fail\n",

        "type":"text",
        "text":"`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\nYou just caught the same family of mistake twice in a row — the 317 commit message that conflated issue-scope with architectural coupling, and the 244 pool-runner branch that conflated \"old test passes\" with \"user-visible behavior preserved.\" The shape is the same: I reached for a small bridge to keep something familiar working, and that bridge was telling a small lie about the new model. The right move both times was to do the harder thing — change the framing of the message, or change what the tests assert — instead of softening the reality.\n\nThe general rule that's emerging: when a redesign changes the *nature* of a thing (a task becomes not-a-task, a coupling becomes independence), the user-visible reports and the tests should also change shape to reflect that. Carrying the old surface forward looks like backward compatibility, but it's actually a quiet refusal to commit to the new design. Tests in particular should assert what the user cares about — values flowing — not which internal mechanism transported them.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\nThe hello run now reports one task, one output. The tests assert the consumer's result instead of the read box's pseudo-output. Ready for **312**?"

        "type":"tool_use",
        "input":{
          "content":"# Strategem — commit messages describe the runtime, not the issue\n\n## The pattern\n\nA commit message that uses scope-of-issue language (\"these features\nbelong together,\" \"this isn't done until both ship\") gets re-read\nlater as architecture language (\"these features are coupled,\" \"these\ntwo things are not independently deployable\"). Future readers cannot\ntell the difference between the two; they only see the commit text.\nThe lie compounds because no one re-reads issue files for archaeology\n— they re-read `git log`.\n\nWhere this kept showing up: the 317 commit text said the C and Bash\nbridges \"live or die together,\" which was true about the *issue\ncontract* (issue 317 said every spec must implement both directions)\nbut false about the *architecture* (the C bridge ships independently\nof the Bash bridge; each spec is its own .so dlopened in isolation;\nadding a Python spec doesn't touch either of them). A future reader\nlooking at the log entry would conclude the system is more entangled\nthan it is, and might design around a coupling that doesn't exist.\n\n## How to apply\n\nWhen writing a commit message:\n\n- Describe what the *runtime* now does — the artifact, the code path,\n  the behavior the user / next maintainer can observe.\n- Do not editorialise on top of the issue's bookkeeping. The fact\n  that an issue says \"every spec must X\" doesn't make the X-es\n  coupled; it makes them in-scope for the issue.\n- If multiple files / specs ship in one commit, describe each as its\n  own change, even when they share a motivation. \"Spec A and spec B\n  both gain X\" is honest; \"X for A and B is one indivisible unit\" is\n  not.\n- The shape of the commit (one or many) is a presentation choice. The\n  shape of the *system* is a property of the code. Don't conflate them.\n\n## Why it's worth a strategem and not just a habit\n\nBecause when redesigns happen six months later, this is the trap\nthe team falls into: someone reads the log, decides the coupling\nmust be real, designs around it, and the system stays falsely\nentangled because nobody had a reason to check whether the coupling\nwas load-bearing. The strategem catches it at commit time, where the\ncost of writing two sentences honestly is much less than the cost of\nthe false belief propagating.\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/strategems/commit-language-is-runtime-language.md"
        }
      }],

## [994]

```json
{
  "timestamp":"2026-05-22T19:19:29.269Z",
  "entrypoint":"cli",
  "gitBranch":"master",
  "version":"2.1.121",
  "uuid":"b151c2b1-9931-4206-ae6b-ec82decccc88",
  "parentUuid":"5aabd09c-5626-44d6-b3da-5ac95cfdc70d",
  "sessionId":"a8fd7497-fc00-4f59-9644-b90753877f2a",
  "userType":"external",
  "isSidechain":false,
  "type":"assistant",
  "requestId":"req_011CbJCShqSjabuyS178arYj",
  "cwd":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech",
  "message":{
    "content":[{
        "name":"Write",
        "caller":{
          "type":"direct"
        },
        "id":"toolu_01LrGeR9U3SHnkuEmUnhmuGK",
        "type":"tool_use",
        "input":{
          "content":"# Strategem — when a redesign changes the nature, change the surface\n\n## The pattern\n\nWhen a redesign changes the *nature* of a thing (a task becomes\nnot-a-task, a coupling becomes independence, a push becomes a pull,\na synchronous call becomes async), the user-visible reports and the\ntests must also change shape to reflect that. Carrying the old\nsurface forward looks like back-compat, but it's actually a quiet\nrefusal to commit to the new design.\n\nThe classic tell: a redesign ships, an existing test fails, and the\ninstinct is to add a small branch in the new code that makes the old\ntest pass. That branch is the lie. It says \"the new model is the new\nmodel, except in the report, where it pretends to be the old model so\nyour tests stay green.\"\n\nWhere this kept showing up: under 244, read boxes stopped running as\ntasks. The pool runner's `outputs:` report used to list every box's\ncaptured output, with read boxes producing their value. The first\n244 commit kept that report shape — added a branch that, when the\nbox was a read box with no captured output, surfaced its cached value\ninstead. Three integration tests with substring assertions like\n`\"who → World\"` kept passing because the report kept pretending the\nread box \"ran.\"\n\nThe fix was not the branch. The fix was: read boxes don't run, so\nthey don't appear in the outputs report; the tests update to assert\nthe consumer's output (which is what they were really proxying for\n— \"did the value reach its destination\") instead of the read box's\npseudo-output. The report now reflects reality and the tests now\nassert what users care about.\n\n## How to apply\n\nWhen a redesign lands and an existing test breaks:\n\n- First, look at what the test was asserting. Was it checking\n  user-visible behavior, or was it checking an implementation surface\n  that no longer exists?\n- If the assertion was a proxy for something deeper (\"did the value\n  flow through?\"), find the place in the new model where that\n  something is observable, and assert there.\n- If the assertion was just naming an internal mechanism that has\n  gone away, delete the assertion — the new model is the contract\n  now.\n- Don't add a branch in production code whose only purpose is to\n  keep an old test green. That's the smell.\n\nIf you find yourself writing a comment like \"preserves observability\nfor tests that named the old box id,\" stop and look harder. The\ntests are usually the wrong audience for that preservation; the user\nis.\n\n## Adjacent pattern — softening reality\n\nThere is a softer version of this trap that doesn't involve tests:\nadding a back-compat shim in user-facing output (\"we'll still print\nthe old line so people parsing logs by hand don't have to update\").\nThis is sometimes the right call, but more often it's the same\nrefusal-to-commit dressed up as kindness. If the old line was a lie\nunder the new model, printing it still is a lie. The graceful path\nis usually: print the truth, document the change, let downstream\nadapt — once. Carrying both forever is the cost of having lied once,\nand that cost compounds.\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/strategems/redesigns-change-the-surface-too.md"
        }
      }],
    "role":"assistant",
    "id":"msg_01Ut9bxg9kVdZpAZD1epPcWc",

  "message":{
    "content":[{
        "type":"tool_result",
        "content":"File created successfully at: /mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/strategems/redesigns-change-the-surface-too.md",
        "tool_use_id":"toolu_01LrGeR9U3SHnkuEmUnhmuGK"
      }],
    "role":"user"

  "uuid":"86f9d57d-001e-4e55-8e27-a64d0c180b9b",
  "parentUuid":"b151c2b1-9931-4206-ae6b-ec82decccc88",
  "toolUseResult":{
    "content":"# Strategem — when a redesign changes the nature, change the surface\n\n## The pattern\n\nWhen a redesign changes the *nature* of a thing (a task becomes\nnot-a-task, a coupling becomes independence, a push becomes a pull,\na synchronous call becomes async), the user-visible reports and the\ntests must also change shape to reflect that. Carrying the old\nsurface forward looks like back-compat, but it's actually a quiet\nrefusal to commit to the new design.\n\nThe classic tell: a redesign ships, an existing test fails, and the\ninstinct is to add a small branch in the new code that makes the old\ntest pass. That branch is the lie. It says \"the new model is the new\nmodel, except in the report, where it pretends to be the old model so\nyour tests stay green.\"\n\nWhere this kept showing up: under 244, read boxes stopped running as\ntasks. The pool runner's `outputs:` report used to list every box's\ncaptured output, with read boxes producing their value. The first\n244 commit kept that report shape — added a branch that, when the\nbox was a read box with no captured output, surfaced its cached value\ninstead. Three integration tests with substring assertions like\n`\"who → World\"` kept passing because the report kept pretending the\nread box \"ran.\"\n\nThe fix was not the branch. The fix was: read boxes don't run, so\nthey don't appear in the outputs report; the tests update to assert\nthe consumer's output (which is what they were really proxying for\n— \"did the value reach its destination\") instead of the read box's\npseudo-output. The report now reflects reality and the tests now\nassert what users care about.\n\n## How to apply\n\nWhen a redesign lands and an existing test breaks:\n\n- First, look at what the test was asserting. Was it checking\n  user-visible behavior, or was it checking an implementation surface\n  that no longer exists?\n- If the assertion was a proxy for something deeper (\"did the value\n  flow through?\"), find the place in the new model where that\n  something is observable, and assert there.\n- If the assertion was just naming an internal mechanism that has\n  gone away, delete the assertion — the new model is the contract\n  now.\n- Don't add a branch in production code whose only purpose is to\n  keep an old test green. That's the smell.\n\nIf you find yourself writing a comment like \"preserves observability\nfor tests that named the old box id,\" stop and look harder. The\ntests are usually the wrong audience for that preservation; the user\nis.\n\n## Adjacent pattern — softening reality\n\nThere is a softer version of this trap that doesn't involve tests:\nadding a back-compat shim in user-facing output (\"we'll still print\nthe old line so people parsing logs by hand don't have to update\").\nThis is sometimes the right call, but more often it's the same\nrefusal-to-commit dressed up as kindness. If the old line was a lie\nunder the new model, printing it still is a lie. The graceful path\nis usually: print the truth, document the change, let downstream\nadapt — once. Carrying both forever is the cost of having lied once,\nand that cost compounds.\n",
    "structuredPatch":[],
    "type":"create",
    "userModified":false,

Single-threaded,\n14\tblocking, runs in Lua coroutines.\n15\t\n16\t## Concept\n17\t\n18\tThe task dispatch layer is the C component every pool worker runs.\n19\tEvery task in the pool is an **attempt task** — same shape, same\n20\tallocation, same call site.       "content":"# 304 — Task dispatch layer (C, replaces synchronous executor)\n\n## Status\nopen · design rewritten 2026-05-20 to the attempt-task model.\nCurrent code is the older two-phase model (inline\nspawn-on-input-ready check inside producer's dispatch action).\nThe refactor lands with issue 302's slab-allocator + refcount\nwork, since the two are intertwined.\n\n## Current behavior\nThe synchronous executor at `src/004-executor.lua` walks the graph in\ndependency order, calling each box's driver, capturing stdout, decoding\nJSON, and propagating values to downstream boxes. Single-threaded,\nblocking, runs in Lua coroutines.\n\n## Concept\n\nThe task dispatch layer is the C component every pool worker runs.\nEvery task in the pool is an **attempt task** — same shape, same\nallocation, same call site. An attempt task either advances the\ngraph by one box invocation (when its consumer's inputs are\nready) or returns without doing anything (when they aren't).\n\nThere is no separate \"readiness check\" task kind. There is no\n\"work task\" kind distinct from a check. There is one kind, the\nattempt; the work it performs is conditional on what it finds.\n\nThe architecture doc's \"structural shell\" section frames this:\none allocator per kind of operation, one scheduler (the pool),\none task shape. The dispatch action is the one place the runtime:\n\n- Reads from input ring buffers (or pulls from read-box predecessors)\n- Calls the language spec's `invoke`\n- Picks the output branch per `routing.kind`\n- Pushes the output value into every downstream consumer slot\n- Submits attempt tasks for the consumers whose input sets may\n  have just become satisfiable\n\n`004-executor.lua` is replaced wholesale. There is no Lua-level\nexecutor in phase 3.\n\n## Task struct (cell layout)\n\nA task struct is a 64-byte slab cell. The layout reserves space\nfor every field every attempt may need; the fields' meaning is\nthe same for \"this attempt found ready inputs and ran\" and \"this\nattempt didn't find ready inputs and returned.\" One shape, two\noutcomes.\n\n```c",

        "content":"42\t## Task struct (cell layout)\n43\t\n44\tA task struct is a 64-byte slab cell. The layout reserves space\n45\tfor every field every attempt may need; the fields' meaning is\n46\tthe same for \"this attempt found ready inputs and ran\" and \"this\n47\tattempt didn't find ready inputs and returned.\" One shape, two\n48\toutcomes.\n49\t\n50\t```c\n51\ttypedef struct {\n52\t    void   *next_free;          /* 8B — free-list link, overwritten on alloc */\n53\t    box_t  *box;                /* 8B — the box this attempt is for */\n54\t    uint32_t task_id;           /* 4B — event-log correlation (311) */\n55\t    uint32_t flags;             /* 4B — work / attempt / priority hint */\n56\t    void   *output_destinations;/* 8B — per-wire consumer slot pointers */\n57\t    void   *input_snapshot;     /* 8B — values OR pointer to values-array */\n58\t    uint32_t live_wire_count;   /* 4B — box-refcount slot (244 / retirement) */\n59\t    uint32_t _pad;              /* 4B — alignment */\n60\t    /* remaining 16B available for inline input snapshot or extensions */\n61\t} attempt_task_t;\n62\t```\n63\t\n64\tThe `live_wire_count` slot is the documented placeholder for the\n65\tbox-level retirement system. The dispatch action populates it at\n66\tcreation; the box-retirement consumer that DOES something with\n67\tthe count is the stretch goal in 302. Until that ships, the slot\n68\tis honest but unread — its presence is documentation that the\n69\tfield belongs in the design.\n70\t\n71\tThe `input_snapshot` is the FIFO-popped values from each input\n72\tslot's ring buffer (or the pointer to a read-box's value when\n73\tpulled per 244). Once the attempt has snapshotted, the slot\n74\tstate is independent of the task's execution.\n75\t\n76\tThe `output_destinations` is the array of consumer slot pointers\n77\tthe attempt will write to — one per outgoing wire (or one per\n78\tfiring branch, for routed boxes). Pre-computed at graph load and\n79\treferenced through the box pointer.\n80\t\n81\t## The dispatch action — the attempt loop\n82\t\n83\t```\n84\tproducer task (a completing attempt that ran):\n85\t   compute output via spec invoke\n86\t   for each downstream consumer box C this producer just touched:\n87\t      write all values to C's input slots\n88\t         (snapshotted into the attempt's cell at the END)\n89\t   for each distinct C:\n90\t      slab_alloc() → attempt_task for C\n91\t      pool_spawn(attempt_task)\n92\t   decrement input $ref counts\n93\t   decrement upstream boxes' live_predecessor_count if applicable\n94\t   slab_free(this cell)\n95\t\n96\tattempt task (newly picked up by a worker):\n97\t   if every required input on C is satisfiable\n98\t      (slot value or data-box pull per 244):\n99\t      snapshot values into local vars\n100\t      invoke spec, get output\n101\t      [continue as producer task above]\n102\t   slab_free(this cell)\n103\t```\n104\t\n105\tThree properties of this loop:\n106\t\n107\t- **Targeted attempts.** A producer knows which consumer boxes it\n108\t  just pushed to; it submits attempts for *those specific\n109\t  consumers*, not a generic re-evaluation.\n110\t- **One attempt per (producer, consumer-box) pair.** Even if a\n111\t  producer writes to multiple slots on the same consumer, only\n112\t  one attempt is submitted for that consumer. Dedup happens at\n113\t  the end of the producer's run, after every output value has\n114\t  been placed. The attempt is guaranteed to find a coherent\n115\t  input set, not a half-written one.\n116\t- **No parking.** An attempt that finds its inputs unsatisfied\n117\t  returns. The shell does not hold tasks in waiting states. The\n118\t  next producer push to any of the consumer's input slots\n119\t  triggers another attempt with the same shape. Eventually one\n120\t  of those attempts finds the input set complete and runs the\n121\t  work.\n122\t\n123\tThe attempt task's \"if inputs ready, run\" branch IS the\n124\tinline-fast-path for same-language chains. There is no separate\n125\tspawn step between the readiness decision and the work; the work\n126\tjust happens, in the same allocation, on the same worker. A\n127\tproducer pushing into a fast same-language consumer fires an\n128\tattempt that runs immediately on whichever worker picks it up —\n129\tone allocation, one queue round-trip per box invocation.\n130\t\n131\t## Initial submission\n132\t\n133\tAt startup the pool runner walks the graph and submits an attempt\n134\ttask for each **entry box** (a box whose required inputs are all\n135\tsatisfiable from literal values or read-box predecessors, i.e.\n136\twhose attempt would succeed on first try). Read boxes do NOT\n137\tpush at startup under 244 — they're pulled on demand from inside\n138\tattempts that find their slots empty and their port has a\n139\tread-box predecessor.\n140\t\n141\tIterator counter slots start at 0. Literal-only entry boxes\n142\tsubmit their first attempt at startup and increment from there.\n143\t\n144\t## Iterator counter and parallel iteration\n145\t\n146\tThe iterator's counter lives in a `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` slot\n147\tallocated for the box at graph load time (issue 302). The\n148\tdispatch action reads and increments it atomically, mid-action:\n149\t\n150\t```c\n151\tuint32_t branch_idx = slot_read_inc(box->counter_slot, n_iter_outputs);\n152\tslot_push(downstream[branch_idx].input_slot, output_buf, output_size,\n153\t          /* tag = */ branch_idx);\n154\t```\n155\t\n156\t`slot_read_inc` returns the current counter value `mod\n157\tn_iter_outputs` and atomically advances the underlying counter.\n158\tConcurrent iterator tasks on different workers each call\n159\t`slot_read_inc` independently and each get a unique value —\n160\t**iterator tasks parallelize across workers**, picking distinct\n161\tbranches without coordination.\n162\t\n163\tNo box-side mutable state, no per-task counter snapshot. The\n164\tcounter is just data in a slot the dispatch layer reads.\n165\t\n166\t## Cross-iterator pairing under parallel iteration\n167\t\n168\tWith parallel iterator tasks, push ordering at the consumer is\n169\tnon-deterministic — task 6 of iterator A may push to consumer C\n170\tbefore task 5 if 6 happened to land on a faster worker. FIFO pop\n171\tat C would consume them out of iteration order.\n172\t\n173\tThe fix is **counter-tagged pushes**. Each iterator push (in phase\n174\t5) carries the counter value the action read for this invocation:\n175\t\n176\t```c",

          "old_string":"        case ROUTING_DISTRIBUTOR:\n        default:\n            /* Distributor inspects downstream slot fill levels; not\n             * yet implemented. Fall back to plain so the runtime\n             * doesn't deadlock. */\n            return push_to_downstream(ctx, b, out_bytes, out_size);\n    }\n}",
          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"        case ROUTING_DISTRIBUTOR: {\n            /* Argmin over downstream slot fill levels: pick the\n             * output branch whose busiest consumer slot is least\n             * loaded, so load spreads across the downstream stages.\n             * For multi-consumer branches the branch's \"load\" is\n             * the max fill across its consumers — the branch is\n             * only as fast as its slowest stage. Ties resolve via\n             * the counter slot so a steady stream still rotates\n             * across equally-empty branches instead of always\n             * picking the same low-index one. */\n            if (b->counter_slot_id < 0 || b->routing.n_outputs < 1) {\n                return push_to_downstream(ctx, b, out_bytes, out_size);\n            }\n            int best_branch  = -1;\n            int32_t best_max = INT32_MAX;\n            for (int k = 0; k < b->routing.n_outputs; k++) {\n                char want[24];\n                snprintf(want, sizeof want, \"out_%d\", k);\n                int32_t this_max = 0;\n                int found_any = 0;\n                for (int j = 0; j < b->n_connections; j++) {\n                    const connection_t *c = &b->connections[j];\n                    if (!c->from_branch ||\n                        strcmp(c->from_branch, want) != 0) continue;\n                    int dst = c->to_box_idx;\n                    if (dst < 0) continue;\n                    const box_t *db = graph_box(ctx->graph, dst);\n                    int port = c->to_input_idx;\n                    if (!db || port < 0 || port >= db->n_inputs ||\n                        !db->input_slot_ids) continue;\n                    int32_t fill = slot_fill_count(ctx->slots,\n                                                   db->input_slot_ids[port]);\n                    if (fill > this_max) this_max = fill;\n                    found_any = 1;\n                }\n                if (!found_any) continue;\n                if (this_max < best_max) {\n                    best_max    = this_max;\n                    best_branch = k;\n                }\n            }\n            if (best_branch < 0) {\n                /* No outgoing connection on any branch — falling\n                 * back to plain still pushes nothing useful, but\n                 * keeps the action's contract (return 0 means OK). */\n                return push_to_downstream(ctx, b, out_bytes, out_size);\n            }\n            char branch[24];\n            snprintf(branch, sizeof branch, \"out_%d\", best_branch);\n            uint32_t tag = slot_read_inc(ctx->slots, b->counter_slot_id,\n                                         UINT32_MAX);\n            return push_branch(ctx, b, branch, out_bytes, out_size, tag) < 0\n                       ? -1 : 0;\n        }\n\n        default:\n            /* Unknown routing kind — push plain as the safe default. */\n            return push_to_downstream(ctx, b, out_bytes, out_size);\n    }\n}",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/src/012-dispatch.c"
        }
      }],

    "newString":"/* {{{ test_distributor_picks_least_full() — issue 304 */\n/* Build a temp map: one distributor `dist` (n_outputs=2) wired to\n * two echo sinks `s0` / `s1`. Pre-fill `s1`'s input slot so its\n * fill count is 1; leave `s0` empty. Push the distributor's input\n * and spawn it. The distributor's argmin-over-fill picker should\n * route to `s0` (less loaded). Only `s0` captures an output —\n * `s1` was never spawn-triggered.\n *\n * Counter-rotated tie-breaking is also exercised here implicitly:\n * if the picker had a bias toward branch 0 the test would pass\n * spuriously, so the inverse case (s0 pre-filled, expect s1) is\n * the actual proof. i < 2; i++) {\n        snprintf(p, sizeof p, \"%s/boxes/s%d.json\", dir, i);\n        fp = fopen(p, \"w\");\n        fprintf(fp,\n            \"{\\\"id\\\":\\\"s%d\\\",\\\"kind\\\":\\\"call\\\",\\\"lang\\\":\\\"lua\\\",\"\n            \"\\\"ref\\\":\\\"src/calc.lua\\\",\\\"fn\\\":\\\"identity\\\",\"\n            \"\\\"inputs\\\":[{\\\"name\\\":\\\"x\\\",\\\"type\\\":\\\"string\\\"}],\"\n            \"\\\"routing\\\":{\\\"kind\\\":\\\"plain\\\"}}\",\n            i);\n        fclose(fp);\n    }\n    return 0;\n}\n\nstatic void cleanup_distributor_fixture(const char *dir)\n{\n    char p[4096];\n    snprintf(p, sizeof p, \"%s/boxes/dist.json\", dir);           "old_string":"## Status\nopen · design rewritten 2026-05-20 to the attempt-task model.\nCurrent code is the older two-phase model (inline\nspawn-on-input-ready check inside producer's dispatch action).\nThe refactor lands with issue 302's slab-allocator + refcount\nwork, since the two are intertwined.\n\n## Current behavior\nThe synchronous executor at `src/004-executor.lua` walks the graph in\ndependency order, calling each box's driver, capturing stdout, decoding\nJSON, and propagating values to downstream boxes. Single-threaded,\nblocking, runs in Lua coroutines.",
          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"## Status\nin progress — every routing kind ships and every fixture passes\nend-to-end. The remaining piece, the attempt-task model rewrite\n(documented below), is a structural refactor with no observable\nbehavior change; it has its own scope and lands separately when\nprioritised. See \"Attempt-task refactor (future)\" near the end.\n\n## Current behavior\n`src/012-dispatch.c` ships the C dispatch layer. The action body\nreads each input port (peek for single-spawn boxes, pop for\nmulti-spawn ones; dual-ring for cross-language wires), invokes the\nresolved spec's `invoke` callback, picks the output branch per\n`routing.kind`, and pushes the output bytes to every outgoing\nconnection's consumer slot. Each push fires `dispatch_spawn_if_ready`\non the destination; consumers with all required inputs ready spawn\nas fresh tasks. Read boxes are pulled on demand by consumers, not\nspawned (issue 244).\n\nRouting kinds, all implemented:\n\n- `plain` — fan to every outgoing connection.\n- `comparator` — compare output to `comparand`, pick `lt`/`eq`/`gt`.\n- `iterator` — `slot_read_inc(counter, n_outputs)` picks the\n  branch; counter doubles as the per-cell tag so parallel iterator\n  tasks land in invocation order downstream.\n- `randomizer` — xorshift-mix the counter, modulo n_outputs.\n- `weighted` — cumulative-band lookup against counter scaled to a\n  fixed precision; ties absorbed by the last band.\n- `distributor` — argmin over downstream slot fill levels. Ties\n  resolve via counter-rotated iteration so a steady stream\n  spreads across equally-empty branches instead of always biasing\n  toward index 0.\n\nThe synchronous executor at `src/004-executor.lua` is wholly\nreplaced.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md"
        }
      }],

Branches\nof equal load break ties via the routing counter slot — read once\nper push, used both as the iteration offset (so ties rotate in\nround-robin order instead of always biasing toward index 0) and\nas the tag carried on the push (so downstream tagged consumers\nstill serve in invocation order).\n\nA dispatch unit test builds an inline fixture with one distributor\nand two echo sinks, pre-fills one sink's slot to mark it loaded,\nspawns the distributor, and asserts the other sink received the\nvalue.         "type":"text",
        "text":"`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\nThere's a discipline at work in this commit that the earlier ones had to learn: the issue body was honest about what's left. Distributor was the genuine feature gap — six routing kinds in the schema, only five with code, fixing the sixth was bounded work. The attempt-task model rewrite is a different thing — a structural refactor with no observable behavior change. Conflating them would have either (a) pushed me to do a much larger commit \"to close 304,\" or (b) let me handwave the rewrite as somehow already-done. Instead, the body now says \"every routing kind ships, structural refactor still owed.\" Issue stays in progress, but the scope of what \"in progress\" means is precise.\n\nThe catch I almost made on the picker is also worth noting. My first pass had `if (this_max < best_max)` with `best_max = INT32_MAX` — correct for finding the minimum, but with equal fills the very first branch wins every time. That's the same \"biased toward index 0\" bug that distributor is supposed to fix at a higher level. The cure was to read the counter once and use it for *both* the iteration offset (so ties spread) *and* the push tag (so downstream order stays meaningful). One value serving two purposes — both of which were already needed — instead of a fresh source of entropy.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\n304 stays in `issues/` as \"in progress\" — every routing kind ships and is tested end-to-end (8 dispatch tests including the new distributor case), and the attempt-task model rewrite is honestly scoped as a structural follow-on rather than scope-crept into this commit. Ready for **312** next?"

          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"/* {{{ test_read_predecessor_rotation() — issue 244 */\n/* Three read boxes feed the same consumer input port. Spawning the\n * consumer three times in a row should rotate through the three\n * cached values via the per-port atomic counter the loader\n * allocated. Serial spawns make the order deterministic — counter\n * 0 → r0, counter 1 → r1, counter 2 → r2.\n *\n * This is the end-to-end test 244 owed for the multi-predecessor\n * rotation path. The single-predecessor pull is already exercised\n * by the read-literal and hello fixtures. */\nstatic int test_read_predecessor_rotation(void)\n{\n    char tmpl[] = \"/tmp/soramech-rotation-XXXXXX\";\n    char *dir = mkdtemp(tmpl);\n    ASSERT(dir);\n\n    char abs[4096];\n    ASSERT(realpath(\"tests/maps/calc/src/calc.lua\", abs));\n\n    char p[4096];\n    snprintf(p, sizeof p, \"%s/meta.json\", dir);\n    FILE *fp = fopen(p, \"w\");\n    fputs(\"{\\\"name\\\":\\\"rot\\\",\\\"entry_box_id\\\":\\\"sink\\\"}\", fp); fclose(fp);\n    snprintf(p, sizeof p, \"%s/boxes\", dir); mkdir(p, 0755);\n\n    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {\n        snprintf(p, sizeof p, \"%s/boxes/r%d.json\", dir, i);\n        fp = fopen(p, \"w\");\n        fprintf(fp,\n            \"{\\\"id\\\":\\\"r%d\\\",\\\"kind\\\":\\\"read\\\",\\\"value\\\":\\\"v%d\\\",\"\n            \"\\\"connections\\\":[{\\\"to_box\\\":\\\"sink\\\",\\\"to_input\\\":\\\"x\\\"}]}\",\n            i, i);\n        fclose(fp);\n    }\n    snprintf(p, sizeof p, \"%s/boxes/sink.json\", dir);\n    fp = fopen(p, \"w\");\n    fprintf(fp,\n        \"{\\\"id\\\":\\\"sink\\\",\\\"kind\\\":\\\"call\\\",\\\"lang\\\":\\\"lua\\\",\"\n        \"\\\"ref\\\":\\\"%s\\\",\\\"fn\\\":\\\"identity\\\",\"\n        \"\\\"inputs\\\":[{\\\"name\\\":\\\"x\\\",\\\"type\\\":\\\"string\\\"}],\"\n        \"\\\"routing\\\":{\\\"kind\\\":\\\"plain\\\"}}\",\n        abs);\n    fclose(fp);\n\n    runtime_t rt;\n    int ok = (runtime_setup(&rt, dir, 1, 1) == 0);\n    if (ok) {\n        int sink = graph_box_index(rt.graph, \"sink\");\n        ASSERT(sink >= 0);\n        const box_t *sb = graph_box(rt.graph, sink);\n        ASSERT(sb && sb->n_read_predecessors &&\n               sb->n_read_predecessors[0] == 3 &&\n               sb->read_pred_counter_slot[0] >= 0);\n\n        char *seen[3] = {0};\n        for (int k = 0; k < 3; k++) {\n            dispatch_spawn(&rt.ctx, sink, 0);\n            pool_wait_quiescent(rt.pool);\n            ASSERT(rt.ctx.last_outputs[sink]);\n            seen[k] = strdup(rt.ctx.last_outputs[sink]);\n        }\n        ASSERT(strcmp(seen[0], \"v0\") == 0);\n        ASSERT(strcmp(seen[1], \"v1\") == 0);\n        ASSERT(strcmp(seen[2], \"v2\") == 0);\n        for (int k = 0; k < 3; k++) free(seen[k]);\n    }\n    runtime_teardown(&rt);\n\n    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {\n        snprintf(p, sizeof p, \"%s/boxes/r%d.json\", dir, i); unlink(p);\n    }\n    snprintf(p, sizeof p, \"%s/boxes/sink.json\", dir); unlink(p);\n    snprintf(p, sizeof p, \"%s/meta.json\",       dir); unlink(p);\n    snprintf(p, sizeof p, \"%s/boxes\",           dir); rmdir(p);\n    rmdir(dir);\n    return ok;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_distributor_picks_least_full() — issue 304 */",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/tests/012-dispatch-test.c"

  "toolUseResult":{
    "newString":"## Status\ncomplete — pull-on-demand model ships end-to-end for both the\nsingle-predecessor case (covered by the read-literal and hello\nfixtures) and the round-robin case (covered by\n`test_read_predecessor_rotation` in `tests/012-dispatch-test.c`,\nwhich builds a three-read-box fixture, serial-spawns the\nconsumer three times, and verifies each spawn picks the next\npredecessor in the loader's list order).",
    "originalFile":"# 244 — Data boxes as round-robin default providers, pulled on demand\n\n## Status\nin progress — pull-on-demand model in place end-to-end for the\ncommon case (single read predecessor); round-robin code path\nwritten and unit-tested at the loader, but no integration fixture\nexercises it yet (see \"Remaining\" below)\n\n## Current behavior\n\nRead boxes are pull-on-demand value sources. They never enter the\npool's task queue. At graph load every read box's bytes are read\nonce and cached on its box record (inline `value` is strdup'd;\n`path` is fopen+fread). Every call/write box gets a per-input-port\nlist of its read-box predecessors. When a consumer attempts to\nfire and finds its slot empty, the dispatch's `read_inputs` copies\nthe next predecessor's cached bytes into the consumer's input\nbuffer — single predecessor: always index 0; multiple predecessors:\nthe port's atomic-counter slot rotates the choice across parallel\nattempts. A port satisfied by a read predecessor counts as ready\nin `box_is_ready`, so consumers wired only to read boxes fire\nimmediately at startup without their predecessors having to push.\n\n`do_read_box` is gone; the BOX_READ case in dispatch_action is now\na BUG path that fires only if a read box accidentally reaches the\npool.\n\nThis breaks down in two cases:\n\n1. **Multiple read boxes feeding the same input slot.** The slot\n   ends up holding one value (whichever read box's startup-push\n   landed first) and silently ignores the others. The user's\n   intent — \"rotate among these values\" — is not honored.\n2. **A read box feeding a slot whose other producers fire many\n   times.** Once the read box's startup push is consumed, the slot\n   sits empty until a call-box producer fills it. If the consumer\n   fires N times and the call-box producer also fires N times,\n   the read box's value is consumed at most once. The user's\n   intent — \"this is a default that's always available\" — is not\n   honored.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nA read box is an **inexhaustible source**, not a one-shot producer.\nIts declared value is always available, on every consumer's\nrequest. Consumers pull from read boxes when they need a value and\nno value is currently waiting in the slot.\n\n### Pull, not push\n\nRead boxes do not push at startup, do not appear in the pool's task\nqueue, and do not have task structs of their own. They are\n**callable sources** whose state lives in the box's runtime record:\n\n- For an inline literal (`value` field set), the value sits in the\n  box's record as bytes ready to copy.\n- For a file path (`path` field set), the bytes are read once at\n  graph load and cached in the box's record. The user editing the\n  file mid-run is not supported; the cached bytes are the source of\n  truth for the run.\n\nThe attempt-task model from the architecture doc makes the pull\nhappen naturally. When an attempt task examines a consumer's input\nslots, the check is now:\n\n```\nfor each required input port:\n   if the slot has a value waiting (ring buffer non-empty):\n      take that value\n   elif the port has any read-box predecessor:\n      round-robin pull from the next read-box predecessor\n   else:\n      not ready — return from the attempt\n```\n\nThe pull copies the read box's value (or its `$ref` handle, if\nthe value is variable-size) into the consumer's local snapshot.\nThe read box's record is unchanged.\n\n### Round-robin across multiple read-box predecessors\n\nA consumer input port with N read-box predecessors carries a small\npiece of state on the consumer box:\n\n```\ninput_port_state {\n   data_box_ids: [box_id, box_id, ...],   // declared order\n   rr_index:     0                        // next to pull from\n}\n```\n\nThe attempt task uses `data_box_ids[rr_index]`, increments\n`rr_index` mod `len(data_box_ids)`, and proceeds. Multiple attempt\ntasks running in parallel for the same consumer use the same\ncounter via the atomic-increment slot operation from 302 — distinct\nattempts get distinct indices, no race.\n\n### Mixed predecessors: read boxes as defaults\n\nA consumer port may have a mix of call-box predecessors AND\nread-box predecessors. The attempt rule (slot-first, read-box-\nfallback) handles this naturally:\n\n- If a call-box producer has pushed a value, the slot is non-empty\n  and the attempt consumes from there.\n- If the slot is empty, the attempt pulls from the next read-box\n  predecessor.\n\nSo a read box behaves as a **default value** for the slot — used\nonly when no call-box producer has supplied an actual value. This\nmatches the typical use: \"supply a fallback host address, but if a\ncall box computes a custom one, use the custom one instead.\"\n\n## Schema implications\n\nThe compile-time check from 230 currently requires every\nnon-optional input port to be wired, carry a literal, or be marked\noptional. Under this issue, **a read-box predecessor on the port\nalso satisfies the requirement** — the port is guaranteed to be\nfed at attempt time, just via pull rather than push.\n\n`src/001-schema.lua::check_input_bindings` extends:\n\n```\nstate if any of:\n   has_wire (any producer-class predecessor)        ← unchanged\n   has_literal (port.value set)                     ← unchanged\n   has_data_box_predecessor (read-box predecessor)  ← new\n   is_optional (port.optional == true)              ← unchanged\n```\n\nThe editor's compile-or-save validation surfaces the same check;\nthe user sees an error if a required port has none of the above.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. `src/001-schema.lua::check_input_bindings` — extend to\n   recognize read-box-as-predecessor as a satisfying state.\n2. `src/010-graph-loader.c` — at graph load, walk every consumer\n   box; for each input port, compute the list of read-box\n   predecessors and store as part of the port's runtime state.\n   Cache each read box's value bytes (or LVH handle) in the box's\n   runtime record.\n3. `src/012-dispatch.c` — the attempt-task's input check\n   incorporates the read-box pull: slot first, else round-robin\n   from `data_box_ids[rr_index]`.\n4. The startup phase no longer spawns tasks for read boxes (or\n   pushes their values eagerly). Read boxes are graph-load data\n   only; they do not appear in the pool's queue.\n5. Fixture: `tests/maps/data-box-defaults/` — a consumer with one\n   call-box and one read-box predecessor, exercising both \"value\n   available\" and \"fallback pulled\" paths.\n6. Fixture: `tests/maps/data-box-rotation/` — a consumer with three\n   read-box predecessors, asserting round-robin order over a series\n   of attempt invocations.\n\n## Cycle behavior\n\nPull-on-demand removes a startup-ordering concern: a graph with a\nread box feeding two consumers no longer depends on \"did the read\nbox's push land before either consumer fired its first attempt?\" —\nthe attempts pull when they need to, regardless of order. Iterators\ndownstream of read boxes work cleanly: each iteration's attempt\npulls fresh from the read box (or its rotation).\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `issues/completed/229-data-box-as-language-agnostic-file-io.md` —\n  parent; renamed data→read/write. This issue extends the read-box\n  semantics from \"one-shot producer\" to \"inexhaustible pull-source.\"\n- `issues/completed/230-required-inputs-and-optional-flag.md` —\n  parent; this issue adds a third satisfying state to its check.\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — extended binding check.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.c` — per-port read-box-predecessor list\n  computed at load.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — attempt-task input pull.\n- `docs/001-architecture.md` — the attempt loop (described in the\n  \"structural shell\" section) is the place where the pull happens.\n\n## Remaining\n\n- **End-to-end round-robin fixture.** The counter-slot rotation\n  path is wired (atomic increment via the existing slot-store\n  counter primitive, mod n_predecessors) and the loader allocates\n  one only when a port has more than one read predecessor. It is\n  unit-tested at the loader level (`read_predecessor_list` in\n  `tests/010-graph-loader-test.c` confirms the three predecessors\n  land in the consumer's port list). It has not yet been exercised\n  by an integration fixture — that needs a multi-spawn consumer\n  (e.g. iterator-fed) wired to multiple read predecessors, and the\n  fixture's value-rotation needs to be observable in the pool\n  runner's output. A small follow-on; the code path will light up\n  with the first map that actually wants the rotation.\n- **Schema validation in `src/001-schema.lua`.** The phase 2 Lua\n  schema is still the canonical author-side check; the C loader\n  in phase 3 enforces topology but defers the \"every required\n  input has a feeder, a literal, or is optional\" rule to graph\n  validation in the editor. Adding the \"read-box predecessor\n  satisfies the requirement\" condition there is a follow-on\n  inside phase 2's schema work.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Read-box value mutation during a run.** A file-backed read box\n  whose file changes mid-run: do we re-read on every pull, or stay\n  with the load-time cached value? Lean toward \"load-time cache\"\n  (deterministic, no I/O per pull, mirrors the immutability of the\n  graph during a run). Re-read on pull is a follow-on if the use\n  case appears.\n- **Round-robin determinism across parallel attempts.** The atomic\n  counter for `rr_index` gives every attempt a distinct index, but\n  the order in which attempts complete is non-deterministic. If\n  attempts A1 and A2 both pull index 0 and index 1 respectively\n  but A2 finishes first, the consumer's overall output sequence\n  reflects A2 before A1. This is the same parallel-iterator\n  ordering question 302's tagged slots already solve. Apply the\n  same tagging: attempts that pull from read boxes carry the\n  pulled index as a tag, downstream consumers reorder by tag.\n",

When an attempt task examines a consumer's input\nslots, the check is now:\n\n```\nfor each required input port:\n   if the slot has a value waiting (ring buffer non-empty):\n      take that value\n   elif the port has any read-box predecessor:\n      round-robin pull from the next read-box predecessor\n   else:\n      not ready — return from the attempt\n```\n\nThe pull copies the read box's value (or its `$ref` handle, if\nthe value is variable-size) into the consumer's local snapshot.\nThe read box's record is unchanged.\n\n### Round-robin across multiple read-box predecessors\n\nA consumer input port with N read-box predecessors carries a small\npiece of state on the consumer box:\n\n```\ninput_port_state {\n   data_box_ids: [box_id, box_id, ...],   // declared order\n   rr_index:     0                        // next to pull from\n}\n```\n\nThe attempt task uses `data_box_ids[rr_index]`, increments\n`rr_index` mod `len(data_box_ids)`, and proceeds. Multiple attempt\ntasks running in parallel for the same consumer use the same\ncounter via the atomic-increment slot operation from 302 — distinct\nattempts get distinct indices, no race.\n\n### Mixed predecessors: read boxes as defaults\n\nA consumer port may have a mix of call-box predecessors AND\nread-box predecessors. The attempt rule (slot-first, read-box-\nfallback) handles this naturally:\n\n- If a call-box producer has pushed a value, the slot is non-empty\n  and the attempt consumes from there.\n- If the slot is empty, the attempt pulls from the next read-box\n  predecessor.\n\nSo a read box behaves as a **default value** for the slot — used\nonly when no call-box producer has supplied an actual value. This\nmatches the typical use: \"supply a fallback host address, but if a\ncall box computes a custom one, use the custom one instead.\"\n\n## Schema implications\n\nThe compile-time check from 230 currently requires every\nnon-optional input port to be wired, carry a literal, or be marked\noptional. Under this issue, **a read-box predecessor on the port\nalso satisfies the requirement** — the port is guaranteed to be\nfed at attempt time, just via pull rather than push.\n\n`src/001-schema.lua::check_input_bindings` extends:\n\n```\nstate if any of:\n   has_wire (any producer-class predecessor)        ← unchanged\n   has_literal (port.value set)                     ← unchanged\n   has_data_box_predecessor (read-box predecessor)  ← new\n   is_optional (port.optional == true)              ← unchanged\n```\n\nThe editor's compile-or-save validation surfaces the same check;\nthe user sees an error if a required port has none of the above.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. `src/001-schema.lua::check_input_bindings` — extend to\n   recognize read-box-as-predecessor as a satisfying state.\n2. `src/010-graph-loader.c` — at graph load, walk every consumer\n   box; for each input port, compute the list of read-box\n   predecessors and store as part of the port's runtime state.\n   Cache each read box's value bytes (or LVH handle) in the box's\n   runtime record.\n3. `src/012-dispatch.c` — the attempt-task's input check\n   incorporates the read-box pull: slot first, else round-robin\n   from `data_box_ids[rr_index]`.\n4. The startup phase no longer spawns tasks for read boxes (or\n   pushes their values eagerly). Read boxes are graph-load data\n   only; they do not appear in the pool's queue.\n5. Fixture: `tests/maps/data-box-defaults/` — a consumer with one\n   call-box and one read-box predecessor, exercising both \"value\n   available\" and \"fallback pulled\" paths.\n6. Fixture: `tests/maps/data-box-rotation/` — a consumer with three\n   read-box predecessors, asserting round-robin order over a series\n   of attempt invocations.\n\n## Cycle behavior\n\nPull-on-demand removes a startup-ordering concern: a graph with a\nread box feeding two consumers no longer depends on \"did the read\nbox's push land before either consumer fired its first attempt?\" —\nthe attempts pull when they need to, regardless of order. Iterators\ndownstream of read boxes work cleanly: each iteration's attempt\npulls fresh from the read box (or its rotation).\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `issues/completed/229-data-box-as-language-agnostic-file-io.md` —\n  parent; renamed data→read/write. This issue extends the read-box\n  semantics from \"one-shot producer\" to \"inexhaustible pull-source.\"\n- `issues/completed/230-required-inputs-and-optional-flag.md` —\n  parent; this issue adds a third satisfying state to its check.\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — extended binding check.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.c` — per-port read-box-predecessor list\n  computed at load.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — attempt-task input pull.\n- `docs/001-architecture.md` — the attempt loop (described in the\n  \"structural shell\" section) is the place where the pull happens.\n\n## Remaining\n\n- **End-to-end round-robin fixture.** The counter-slot rotation\n  path is wired (atomic increment via the existing slot-store\n  counter primitive, mod n_predecessors) and the loader allocates\n  one only when a port has more than one read predecessor. It is\n  unit-tested at the loader level (`read_predecessor_list` in\n  `tests/010-graph-loader-test.c` confirms the three predecessors\n  land in the consumer's port list). It has not yet been exercised\n  by an integration fixture — that needs a multi-spawn consumer\n  (e.g. iterator-fed) wired to multiple read predecessors, and the\n  fixture's value-rotation needs to be observable in the pool\n  runner's output. A small follow-on; the code path will light up\n  with the first map that actually wants the rotation.\n- **Schema validation in `src/001-schema.lua`.** The phase 2 Lua\n  schema is still the canonical author-side check; the C loader\n  in phase 3 enforces topology but defers the \"every required\n  input has a feeder, a literal, or is optional\" rule to graph\n  validation in the editor. Adding the \"read-box predecessor\n  satisfies the requirement\" condition there is a follow-on\n  inside phase 2's schema work.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Read-box value mutation during a run.** A file-backed read box\n  whose file changes mid-run: do we re-read on every pull, or stay\n  with the load-time cached value? Lean toward \"load-time cache\"\n  (deterministic, no I/O per pull, mirrors the immutability of the\n  graph during a run). Re-read on pull is a follow-on if the use\n  case appears.\n- **Round-robin determinism across parallel attempts.** The atomic\n  counter for `rr_index` gives every attempt a distinct index, but\n  the order in which attempts complete is non-deterministic. If\n  attempts A1 and A2 both pull index 0 and index 1 respectively\n  but A2 finishes first, the consumer's overall output sequence\n  reflects A2 before A1. This is the same parallel-iterator\n  ordering question 302's tagged slots already solve. Apply the\n  same tagging: attempts that pull from read boxes carry the\n  pulled index as a tag, downstream consumers reorder by tag.\n",

The fix wasn't to sort the list in the loader (which would have made the loader honor a property nobody had asked for). ## [1215]

```json
{
  "sessionId":"a8fd7497-fc00-4f59-9644-b90753877f2a",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-22T19:56:28.551Z",
  "entrypoint":"cli",
  "version":"2.1.121",
  "gitBranch":"master",
  "message":{
    "content":[{
        "type":"tool_result",
        "content":"1\t# 312 — Same-language wire fast path: dual-ring slot, JSON at language borders\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\tsubstantively complete on the dual-ring foundation (2026-05-21);\n5\t**spec-contract simplification pending** — see the Amendment\n6\tsection below. Dual-ring slots, per-edge classification, and the\n7\tper-cell ordering ring are in place and correct. The spec-side\n8\tshape needs one more pass to remove the per-input format flags\n9\tand the multiple invoke variants from `lang_spec_t`; that\n10\tsimplification is the final slice of this issue.\n11\t\n12\t## Amendment (2026-05-22) — collapse to one `invoke`, native-only\n13\t\n14\tThe original slice plan kept three invoke entry points\n15\t(`invoke`, `invoke_native`, `invoke_json`) and pushed per-input\n16\tformat branching into each spec. After implementing through\n17\tslice 5 we realised the per-input branching is dispatch's job,\n18\tnot the spec's. The revised target:\n19\t\n20\t- **Dispatch normalises every input to the consuming spec's\n21\t  native bytes before calling invoke.** When a popped cell is\n22\t  tagged `RING_JSON`, dispatch calls the consumer spec's\n23\t  `json_to_native` to convert the JSON bytes into the spec's\n24\t  native byte form (written into a temporary slot or directly\n25\t  into the input position dispatch hands to invoke). When the\n26\t  cell is tagged `RING_NATIVE`, dispatch passes the slot's bytes\n27\t  straight through — no conversion, the producer already wrote\n28\t  in the consumer's format because they share a language.\n29\t- **`invoke` sees one shape only**: a list of native-byte input\n30\t  pointers, and an output slot to write native bytes into. No\n31\t  `input_native[]` array, no `output_native` flag. The signature\n32\t  becomes:\n33\t\n34\t  ```c\n35\t  int invoke(handle, box, file_path, fn_name,\n36\t             const void **input_data, const int *input_sizes,\n37\t             int n_inputs,\n38\t             void *out_buf, int out_buf_capacity, int *out_size);\n39\t  ```\n40\t\n41\t- **`invoke_native` and `invoke_json` are deleted from\n42\t  `lang_spec_t`.** The struct keeps `invoke`,\n43\t  `native_to_json`, and `json_to_native` (plus `init`,\n44\t  `teardown`, `compile`, `name`, `file_ext`).\n45\t- **Cross-language output** is handled by dispatch after invoke:\n46\t  the producer writes native bytes to its output slot once;\n47\t  dispatch calls `native_to_json` once on those bytes if any\n48\t  outgoing connection's `output_edge_native[j]` is false, then\n49\t  pushes the JSON bytes to each cross-language consumer's\n50\t  `ring_json`. Same-language consumers receive the original\n51\t  native bytes directly.\n52\t- **No \"bytes vs native\" distinction in the contract.** \"Native\"\n53\t  means: bytes written in the format the spec emits and reads\n54\t  back. There is no separate `native_to_bytes` /\n55\t  `bytes_to_native` bridge; the spec's own native-write and\n56\t  native-read already cover same-language wires by writing the\n57\t  right bytes into the slot at push time and reading them out\n58\t  at pop time. The slot is the medium; the spec is the codec.\n59\t- **Why this collapses cleanly**: same-language wires never\n60\t  involve dispatch's bridges at all — producer writes native to\n61\t  the slot, consumer reads native from the slot, full stop.\n62\t  Cross-language wires call exactly one bridge: `native_to_json`\n63\t  on the producer side at push (so the JSON ring carries JSON),\n64\t  `json_to_native` on the consumer side at pop (so invoke sees\n65\t  native). The bridges fire once per language crossing, never\n66\t  twice, and never inside a same-language path.\n67\t\n68\tThe result is one entry point, two bridges, and a dispatch layer\n69\tthat owns all format-conversion timing. Specs no longer reason\n70\tabout wire format at all.\n71\t\n72\t### Final-slice plan\n73\t\n74\t1. **Remove `input_native[]` and `output_native` from\n75\t   `lang_invoke_fn`** in `langs/lang-spec.h`. Update every spec\n76\t   stub.\n77\t2. **Move JSON → native decode out of the spec's `invoke` into\n78\t   dispatch's `read_inputs`** (`src/012-dispatch.c`). On a\n79\t   `RING_JSON` pop, dispatch calls the consumer spec's\n80\t   `json_to_native` and stages the resulting native bytes for\n81\t   invoke.\n82\t3. **Move JSON encoding for cross-language consumers out of the\n83\t   spec's `invoke` into dispatch's push path**\n84\t   (`src/012-dispatch.c`). After invoke returns, if any\n85\t   outgoing connection is cross-language, call `native_to_json`\n86\t   once and push the JSON bytes to each cross-language\n87\t   consumer.\n88\t4. **Delete `invoke_native` and `invoke_json` slots from\n89\t   `lang_spec_t`.** Drop the no-op stubs from each spec.\n90\t5. **Restore Lua's pre-slice-4 simple invoke** — it reads\n91\t   native bytes from inputs, runs the function, writes native\n92\t   bytes to the output. No per-input branch.\n93\t6. **Tests**: existing same-language and cross-language tests\n94\t   should pass unchanged; a new test covers a mixed-fan-in port\n95\t   where one cell arrives JSON-tagged (dispatch decodes before\n96\t   invoke) and one arrives native-tagged (dispatch passes\n97\t   through).\n98\t\n99\t## Current behavior\n100\t",
        "tool_use_id":"toolu_01TYPmWEjnr7A4HNeJfTLggj"

      "content":"# 312 — Same-language wire fast path: dual-ring slot, JSON at language borders\n\n## Status\nsubstantively complete on the dual-ring foundation (2026-05-21);\n**spec-contract simplification pending** — see the Amendment\nsection below. Dual-ring slots, per-edge classification, and the\nper-cell ordering ring are in place and correct. The spec-side\nshape needs one more pass to remove the per-input format flags\nand the multiple invoke variants from `lang_spec_t`; that\nsimplification is the final slice of this issue.\n\n## Amendment (2026-05-22) — collapse to one `invoke`, native-only\n\nThe original slice plan kept three invoke entry points\n(`invoke`, `invoke_native`, `invoke_json`) and pushed per-input\nformat branching into each spec. After implementing through\nslice 5 we realised the per-input branching is dispatch's job,\nnot the spec's. The revised target:\n\n- **Dispatch normalises every input to the consuming spec's\n  native bytes before calling invoke.** When a popped cell is\n  tagged `RING_JSON`, dispatch calls the consumer spec's\n  `json_to_native` to convert the JSON bytes into the spec's\n  native byte form (written into a temporary slot or directly\n  into the input position dispatch hands to invoke). When the\n  cell is tagged `RING_NATIVE`, dispatch passes the slot's bytes\n  straight through — no conversion, the producer already wrote\n  in the consumer's format because they share a language.\n- **`invoke` sees one shape only**: a list of native-byte input\n  pointers, and an output slot to write native bytes into. No\n  `input_native[]` array, no `output_native` flag. The signature\n  becomes:\n\n  ```c\n  int invoke(handle, box, file_path, fn_name,\n             const void **input_data, const int *input_sizes,\n             int n_inputs,\n             void *out_buf, int out_buf_capacity, int *out_size);\n  ```\n\n- **`invoke_native` and `invoke_json` are deleted from\n  `lang_spec_t`.** The struct keeps `invoke`,\n  `native_to_json`, and `json_to_native` (plus `init`,\n  `teardown`, `compile`, `name`, `file_ext`).\n- **Cross-language output** is handled by dispatch after invoke:\n  the producer writes native bytes to its output slot once;\n  dispatch calls `native_to_json` once on those bytes if any\n  outgoing connection's `output_edge_native[j]` is false, then\n  pushes the JSON bytes to each cross-language consumer's\n  `ring_json`. Same-language consumers receive the original\n  native bytes directly.\n- **No \"bytes vs native\" distinction in the contract.** \"Native\"\n  means: bytes written in the format the spec emits and reads\n  back. There is no separate `native_to_bytes` /\n  `bytes_to_native` bridge; the spec's own native-write and\n  native-read already cover same-language wires by writing the\n  right bytes into the slot at push time and reading them out\n  at pop time. The slot is the medium; the spec is the codec.\n- **Why this collapses cleanly**: same-language wires never\n  involve dispatch's bridges at all — producer writes native to\n  the slot, consumer reads native from the slot, full stop.\n  Cross-language wires call exactly one bridge: `native_to_json`\n  on the producer side at push (so the JSON ring carries JSON),\n  `json_to_native` on the consumer side at pop (so invoke sees\n  native). The bridges fire once per language crossing, never\n  twice, and never inside a same-language path.\n\nThe result is one entry point, two bridges, and a dispatch layer\nthat owns all format-conversion timing. Specs no longer reason\nabout wire format at all.\n\n### Final-slice plan\n\n1. **Remove `input_native[]` and `output_native` from\n   `lang_invoke_fn`** in `langs/lang-spec.h`. Update every spec\n   stub.\n2. **Move JSON → native decode out of the spec's `invoke` into\n   dispatch's `read_inputs`** (`src/012-dispatch.c`). On a\n   `RING_JSON` pop, dispatch calls the consumer spec's\n   `json_to_native` and stages the resulting native bytes for\n   invoke.\n3. **Move JSON encoding for cross-language consumers out of the\n   spec's `invoke` into dispatch's push path**\n   (`src/012-dispatch.c`). After invoke returns, if any\n   outgoing connection is cross-language, call `native_to_json`\n   once and push the JSON bytes to each cross-language\n   consumer.\n4. **Delete `invoke_native` and `invoke_json` slots from\n   `lang_spec_t`.** Drop the no-op stubs from each spec.\n5. **Restore Lua's pre-slice-4 simple invoke** — it reads\n   native bytes from inputs, runs the function, writes native\n   bytes to the output. No per-input branch.\n6. **Tests**: existing same-language and cross-language tests\n   should pass unchanged; a new test covers a mixed-fan-in port\n   where one cell arrives JSON-tagged (dispatch decodes before\n   invoke) and one arrives native-tagged (dispatch passes\n   through).\n\n## Current behavior\n",

The\n    same-lang consumers in that case receive JSON bytes through\n    their native ring — Lua's input-side parse-with-fallback\n    absorbs this, so primitives still round-trip. A full per-wire\n    output (producer leaves the value in its runtime; dispatch\n    calls `native_to_json` per cross-lang wire to materialize\n    JSON only where needed) is a deeper contract change tracked\n    as a future slice.\n- **Slice 5 complete (2026-05-21).** The per-box\n  `use_native_invoke` field and its computation are gone. ## [1246]

```json
{
  "timestamp":"2026-05-22T19:59:54.032Z",
  "entrypoint":"cli",
  "gitBranch":"master",
  "version":"2.1.121",
  "uuid":"85542537-6401-46b0-8d3e-f2b39776ff7a",
  "parentUuid":"877e41b9-802e-4246-8a2f-9669e64e4384",
  "sessionId":"a8fd7497-fc00-4f59-9644-b90753877f2a",
  "userType":"external",
  "isSidechain":false,
  "type":"assistant",
  "requestId":"req_011CbJFWbuiCqS2Lk7FsiSDU",
  "cwd":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech",
  "message":{
    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"Before I touch any code, I want to surface a tension I noticed reading the amendment.\n\nThe amendment's full vision is: dispatch normalises every input to \"native bytes\" before calling invoke, drop `input_native[]` and `output_native` from the typedef, every spec sees one shape. For **C and Bash** this works cleanly because their bridges write to a `dst` buffer — dispatch can normalise bytes ahead of time.\n\nFor **Lua** it doesn't fit. `lua_json_to_native` doesn't write bytes anywhere; it pushes a value onto the worker's `lua_State`. There's no \"Lua native byte form\" external to the state for dispatch to hand to `invoke`. The amendment was written assuming all specs are buffer-oriented, but Lua isn't.\n\nThree honest paths:\n\n1. **Narrow close-out (my recommendation).** Drop only the dead `invoke_native` / `invoke_json` slots from `lang_spec_t` — they've been unused since slice 5. Keep `input_native[]` / `output_native` in the typedef; they're load-bearing for Lua's per-cell branching. Update the issue's amendment section to honestly say the typedef-flag removal was reconsidered. Add the mixed-fan-in dispatch test the amendment mentioned. Close 312.\n\n2. **Force the amendment.** Redesign Lua's bridge to write to a buffer (Lua values serialised to JSON bytes as the \"native form\"). Drop the typedef flags. Cost: same-language Lua-to-Lua wires lose any potential fast path because Lua's \"native bytes\" become identical to JSON — but they were already mostly JSON in practice (slice 4.5 made Lua always JSON-encode when any consumer is cross-lang, and tables only round-trip through JSON anyway). Real complexity reduction in the spec contract.\n\n3. **Half-implement the amendment.** Drop the flags from the typedef; have each spec internally auto-detect (\"try JSON parse, fall back to raw bytes\" on every input). Works in practice but pushes auto-detection into every spec instead of removing the decision.\n\nMy lean is (1) — it's the honest scope. The amendment's contract simplification is genuinely tempting but it conflicts with Lua's bridge architecture, and the rest of 312 (dual-ring slot, per-edge classification, per-cell ordering) is shipping correctly and doesn't need (1) → (2) to keep working. The dispatch test for mixed-fan-in is a small piece of owed coverage either way.\n\nWhich path do you want?"
      }],
