  "message":{
    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"Let me actually unpack the \"Lua incompatibility\" carefully, because I think I framed it too narrowly the first time.\n\n**What the bridge contract says**\n\n`lang_bridge_fn` is `(handle, src, src_size, dst, dst_capacity, dst_size)`. Bytes in, bytes out, with a handle on the side. That contract treats bytes as the universal medium.\n\n**What Lua actually does inside the contract**\n\nLua's `native_to_json` reads from the top of `lua_State` and writes JSON to dst. It ignores src/src_size.\nLua's `json_to_native` parses src as JSON and pushes the value onto `lua_State`. It ignores dst/dst_capacity.\n\nSo Lua's bridge isn't byte-to-byte — it's value-on-stack-to-bytes and bytes-to-value-on-stack. The signature is the same; the semantics aren't.\n\n**But this isn't actually a Lua-specific problem.**\n\nThe deeper thing is: Lua values don't have a canonical byte form. A Lua table has no fixed bytes — it's a hash table living in `lua_State`, and the only universal serialisation we picked was JSON. A Python `dict` would have the same problem. A Ruby hash, a JavaScript object, anything from a runtime that owns the value's lifetime — same. The byte-buffer assumption was always a property of \"stateless byte-handlers\" (C, Bash), not a property of \"languages in general.\"\n\nSo if we want true agnosticism, the question isn't \"how do we accommodate Lua?\" — it's \"does the system's contract assume buffer-orientation, and should it?\"\n\n**The fact that re-frames everything**\n\nLook at what each spec's `invoke` actually does today on a JSON-tagged input:\n\n- **Lua**: `parse_json_to_stack` → fall back to `lua_pushlstring` if parse fails. Already auto-detects.\n- **C**: `try_strip_json_primitive` → fall back to raw bytes if parse fails. Already auto-detects.\n- **Bash**: ignores the flag entirely; bytes are bytes for bash.\n\nEvery spec already does the \"try JSON, fall back to native\" dance internally. The `input_native[i]` flag is only an *optimization hint* that lets Lua skip the JSON parse attempt when dispatch knows the cell came from a same-language producer. It saves maybe 100ns per call on a same-lang Lua→Lua wire. It doesn't change semantics anywhere.\n\nThe `output_native` flag is similar — it tells Lua to use `tostring` when all consumers are same-lang. But that \"fast path\" is *broken* for tables (`tostring(table)` returns `\"table: 0x...\"`), so any honest Lua function that returns a table has to JSON-encode anyway. The flag is buying performance that mostly isn't usable.\n\n**What dropping the flags really costs and buys**\n\nDrop both flags and have every spec auto-detect:\n\n- Cost: same-lang Lua→Lua pays a ~100ns JSON-parse-attempt-then-fallback per input. Lua→Lua with table returns starts working correctly (was broken). The \"fast path\" goes away.\n- Buy: spec contract goes from `invoke(..., input_data, input_sizes, input_native, n_inputs, output_native, ...)` to `invoke(..., input_data, input_sizes, n_inputs, ...)`. Every future spec — Python, Ruby, anything — drops in without special-casing or runtime-class branching. The dual-ring slot's per-cell ring tag stops being load-bearing at the spec level (it's still useful for ordering).\n\n**Where it really gets agnostic**\n\nOnce the flags are gone, the dual-ring slot itself becomes vestigial *for format purposes*. Its surviving job is ordering — the `RING_JSON` / `RING_NATIVE` tag was both \"this is the format\" and \"this is the position in the producer sequence\". The format part stops mattering; the position part still matters for parallel-iterator ordering.\n\nWe could either:\n- **Keep dual-ring as-is**, with the per-cell tag becoming advisory/unused at the spec interface. Code stays, complexity stays in the slot store, but the spec contract is clean.\n- **Collapse dual-ring back to single-ring tagged**, undoing slice 1. Bigger teardown, cleaner result.\n\n**The honest summary**\n\nLua's \"incompatibility\" with the buffer contract is real but it's not the load-bearing thing. The load-bearing thing is: **the per-input/per-output flags are an optimisation that mostly doesn't work in practice and force every spec to branch on something it could auto-detect.** Removing them is the agnosticism move you're asking about.\n\nThe amendment was right in spirit; what it called \"dispatch normalises every input to native bytes\" was really pointing at \"every spec auto-detects per input.\" That doesn't require dispatch to do any conversion at all — it requires the spec contract to stop pretending it knows the per-cell format.\n\nSo the three paths re-stated:\n\n1. **Narrow** (drop just the dead slots): preserves the per-cell flags as load-bearing. Doesn't actually fix the agnosticism question.\n2. **Full agnostic** (drop the flags, specs auto-detect, dual-ring becomes advisory or gets collapsed): real spec contract simplification, fixes the broken Lua-table same-lang case, opens the door to drop-in future runtimes.\n3. **Collapse dual-ring all the way to single-ring tagged**: most aggressive teardown, also addresses the vestigial dual-ring complexity.\n\nNow that I see it that way, my lean has shifted toward (2) — auto-detect is what every spec is already doing, the flags are an optimisation that doesn't earn its complexity, and the \"Lua incompatibility\" disappears not because we accommodate Lua specially but because no spec needs the format hint.\n\nWhat's your read?"
      }],

    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"The worker-affinity thing you spotted is the foundation, and I want to make sure I name it correctly before going further:\n\n**Workers don't share runtime state.** Each Lua worker has its own `lua_State`. The task that produced a value ran on worker A; the task that consumes it might land on worker D. Worker D's `lua_State` is a fresh hash table — worker A's stack is invisible to it. So *even for same-language wires, the value has to leave its runtime and re-enter on the consumer side.* The wire is between workers, not between language states.\n\nThat means \"leave the value on the stack\" is never an option. The only universal medium between workers is bytes. The \"fast path\" question is just **what bytes** — JSON, raw text, msgpack, whatever the spec picks — not whether to serialise. Serialisation always happens.\n\nGiven that, the per-edge native/JSON distinction is just about **format choice per outgoing wire**. The producer knows (at graph-load time) whether each consumer is same-language. If same, write the spec's preferred native byte form. If different, write JSON. The consumer's auto-detect handles both cases without a per-cell tag:\n\n- Cell carries `hello` (raw Lua-native string): consumer tries JSON parse → fails (no quotes) → falls back to lua_pushlstring. Consumer gets the string.\n- Cell carries `\"hello\"` (JSON from C producer): consumer tries JSON parse → succeeds → gets string.\n- Cell carries `42`: parses as JSON number either way. Both spec forms are bit-identical here.\n- Cell carries a table: producer can only have written JSON (Lua's \"native form for tables\" *is* JSON; tables have no other byte form). Consumer parses → gets table.\n\nThe per-cell format tag in the dual-ring slot was only ever needed if we wanted to **skip the JSON parse attempt** in the consumer when we knew the producer wrote native. That's the 100ns optimisation I mentioned. It doesn't change semantics anywhere.\n\nOn your \"I don't think either of these will work\" — can you say more about which part feels wrong? Because the third option you might be gesturing at — **drop the dual-ring slot entirely, single-ring data + TAGGED variant for iterator ordering, producer picks format per edge at push time, consumer auto-detects per pop** — is what falls out if we accept the worker-affinity argument. The native/JSON ring split exists in code today but it isn't load-bearing once the consumer is doing auto-detect anyway.\n\nA couple of places I'm not sure about and want to surface:\n\n- **What does \"Lua native bytes\" mean for primitives?** A Lua number written as `42` is also valid JSON. A Lua string `hello` written raw isn't valid JSON. So the \"native\" form for primitives is a strict subset / variation of JSON. We could just say: Lua's spec writes JSON-form bytes always (numbers as `42`, strings as `\"hello\"`, tables as JSON), and the \"native\" optimisation is purely conceptual — the bytes are JSON-shaped either way. That removes the spec's job of deciding \"native vs JSON\" at all.\n- **What about closures, userdata, threads?** These have no byte representation. The sentinel primitives in issue 318 (`$function_pointer`, `$lang_opaque`) are the answer — they encode \"this is a Lua thing only Lua can reconstruct\" as a JSON-shaped sentinel. Cross-language wires that carry one of these fail loudly at the consumer's bridge. We don't need to design that here; it's another issue's problem.\n\nSo I think we're close to alignment: bytes are the wire; producer picks the cleanest form it can per outgoing edge; consumer auto-detects. What's the part you think won't work?"

```json
{
  "timestamp":"2026-05-22T20:19:44.833Z",
  "entrypoint":"cli",
  "gitBranch":"master",
  "version":"2.1.121",
  "uuid":"7f7bb14d-e612-491b-9e0a-6cd3aed14541",
  "parentUuid":"227f2fd1-f574-4c8c-8175-19ebe06894be",
  "sessionId":"a8fd7497-fc00-4f59-9644-b90753877f2a",

  "cwd":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech",
  "message":{
    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"The honest answer for the slot store this project uses:\n\n**Lua doesn't interact with the shared memory at all, except as bytes.**\n\nEach pool worker has its own `lua_State`. LuaJIT's hard rule is that a `lua_State` is owned by exactly one OS thread — you cannot touch it from another thread concurrently. The Lua GC heap (where tables, strings, closures live) is private to that one `lua_State`. So `lua_State` A on worker 0 and `lua_State` D on worker 3 have no shared Lua-level memory. They are, from each other's perspective, completely separate Lua universes that happen to be running the same source files.\n\nWhat they CAN share is the project's byte-buffer layer:\n\n- The slot store's cells (`slot_push` / `slot_pop` move bytes through ring buffers with per-slot spinlocks; the unified allocator refcounts the cells so they stay valid while any worker holds a reference).\n- The large-value heap (the same refcount machinery, for variable-size payloads).\n\nBoth are managed at the C level. Workers read and write bytes; the spinlocks and atomics handle concurrency. Lua sees these only when its spec hands it a `(void *, int)` pair pointing into a cell, and Lua does one of two things with it:\n\n- `lua_pushlstring(L, ptr, size)` — Lua copies the bytes into its own GC-managed string. After that, the slot cell can be released; Lua's string is independent.\n- `parse_json_to_stack(L, ptr, size)` — Lua walks the bytes, constructs an equivalent Lua value in its own GC heap, pushes it. Same deal: after the call, the slot cell is decoupled from anything Lua holds.\n\nIn both cases, **the byte buffer's lifetime ends at the Lua call**. Lua never holds a pointer into a shared slot cell; it copies what it needs into its own state.\n\n**LuaJIT FFI** is the one place this could be different. With FFI, Lua code can read shared memory directly via `ffi.cast(...)` without copying. We could expose slot bytes to Lua and let user code read them as a `cdata` pointer. But:\n\n- The user's Lua function would have to call FFI explicitly. The wire-level contract still hands the spec bytes, not Lua values.\n- FFI'd bytes are still bytes from Lua's perspective. You can't `pairs()` over an FFI pointer and get table semantics — Lua values are what live in `lua_State`'s GC heap, not in the C buffer.\n- The slot cell's stable-address window (between alloc and unref) would have to extend across the FFI call's life, which is a real refcount discipline question.\n\nSo FFI is an optimisation for *avoiding the copy*, not for *sharing Lua values*. Even with FFI in the picture, a Lua table that goes from worker A to worker D has to serialise into bytes and deserialise into a new table in D's heap.\n\n**This isn't Lua-specific.** Python's `dict`, Ruby's `Hash`, JavaScript's `Object` — every runtime that owns its values has the same constraint. The runtime's heap is private; the only way values cross threads is bytes. The agnosticism win you're chasing is: the system's contract assumes bytes, every spec knows how to turn its values into bytes and back, and no spec ever needs to know anything about another spec's runtime.\n\n**Implication for the dual-ring slot:**\n\nThe slot store as it stands is byte storage. The dual-ring split added a per-cell format tag (native vs JSON), but format is information about how to *interpret* bytes — and JSON is self-describing while raw text falls through auto-detect. The format tag isn't a property of the memory; it's a property of the bytes themselves. Putting it in the slot's metadata duplicates what the bytes can carry. That's the architectural smell I think you've been pointing at.\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\nThe agnosticism question dissolves once you accept that shared memory is bytes-only for any runtime that owns its values. The slot store is exactly right at the layer it sits — it's the unified byte medium between workers, with refcounts handling lifetime and spinlocks handling concurrency. What slice 1 of 312 added on top (per-cell format tag, two data rings) was an attempt to encode interpretation hints in the memory layout, but interpretation belongs in the bytes (JSON is self-describing) or in the consumer's auto-detect (raw bytes flow through). The slot store doesn't need to know about formats; the specs do, and they already do.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\nSo: what bytes need to live in shared memory? Whatever bytes the producer's spec wrote. What's the consumer's job? Turn those bytes back into a value in its own runtime. Everything else — the dual rings, the format tag, the per-input flag in the typedef — is the system encoding information that belongs elsewhere."
      }],

{
  "timestamp":"2026-05-22T20:26:09.731Z",

  "type":"user",
  "message":{
    "content":"  - What about closures, userdata, threads? These have no byte representation. The sentinel primitives in issue 318 ($function_pointer, $lang_opaque) are the answer — they encode \"this is a Lua\n  thing only Lua can reconstruct\" as a JSON-shaped sentinel. Cross-language wires that carry one of these fail loudly at the consumer's bridge. We don't need to design that here; it's another\n  issue's problem.\n\n\nI don't think sentinels will ever be a viable option. The reason I say this is because of the luastate issue - if we have a sentinel that says \"I'm representing this-and-this closure\" then it would only make sense if that closure was already in the correct luastate. Right?\n\n  The slot store as it stands is byte storage. The dual-ring split added a per-cell format tag (native vs JSON), but format is information about how to interpret bytes — and JSON is self-describing\n  while raw text falls through auto-detect. The format tag isn't a property of the memory; it's a property of the bytes themselves. Putting it in the slot's metadata duplicates what the bytes can\n  carry. That's the architectural smell I think you've been pointing at.\n\n\nI'd rather store something in a different location if it's a different format, rather than interpreting it. It feels more organized. Fewer branches if we can just say \"hey which one do I write to / read from\" and then we deterministically say \"well here's the order they came in on so do this one next, it's json type\"\n\nSounds like we need to store everything as raw bytes. Isn't that what json is? raw bytes, with some extra structural stuff to keep it organized?\n\nfuck... are we going to have to do the json path every time? always? this is a large issue. Can you tell me, before we amended 312, what was the plan for that implementation's shape?",
    "role":"user"
  },

        "text":"Three threads to pull on. Let me handle the sentinel point first, then check the pre-amendment plan, then come back to the dual-ring question.\n\n**On sentinels**: you're right, and the failure mode is worse than I framed it. A sentinel like `$function_pointer:0x7f...` only makes sense to the runtime where that address lives. If lua_State A creates a closure and the sentinel rides the wire to a consumer task that lands on worker 3 with lua_State D, the address is meaningless — and even if we used some abstract reference (a registry key), the closure object exists only in A's GC heap. D's heap has no such closure.\n\nThe only way sentinels work for closures is if the closure is **registered in every worker's lua_State by name** — e.g., a named function in a module that every worker loaded at init. Then `$function_pointer:my_module.greet` is a portable reference because every worker has its own copy of `my_module.greet`. That's not really a sentinel for a runtime value; it's a name lookup, and it only works for things that were declarable up front. Anonymous closures, runtime-created tables with closures inside, etc., genuinely can't cross. They have to fail loudly at the bridge.\n\nSo sentinels narrow down to \"named, pre-loaded-on-every-worker things.\" Useful for module functions; useless for runtime-created closures. Issue 318 should be honest about that constraint.\n\nLet me read the pre-amendment plan:"

        "text":"Found it. Let me walk through the pre-amendment plan because I think it actually answers your worry directly.\n\n**Pre-amendment plan (the original 312 design, ~mid-May)**\n\nSlot has three rings:\n- `ring_native` — bytes in the consumer's spec's own native format\n- `ring_json` — JSON bytes (only used at cross-language boundaries)\n- `ring_order` — `(which_ring, idx)` tuples in arrival order\n\nProducer push, per outgoing connection:\n- If `output_edge_native[j]` is true (consumer is same-language), the spec writes its native bytes to `ring_native`.\n- Else, the spec converts via `native_to_json` and writes to `ring_json`.\n- Either way, push `(which_ring, idx)` to `ring_order`.\n\nConsumer pop:\n- Pop `ring_order` to learn which ring the next cell lives in.\n- Read the cell from that ring.\n- Spec gets a `(format, bytes)` pair per input and uses the matching decoder.\n\n**Critically: each spec defines its own native byte format.** The plan was:\n- **Lua**: bytes the Lua spec can deserialise back to a Lua value quickly. Started with `cjson.encode` for simplicity, with msgpack or a custom binary form listed as the optimisation target if profiling showed the encode/decode was hot.\n- **C**: `memcpy` of the typed struct (wrapper from 307 knows the layout).\n- **Bash**: strings (its only native form).\n\nCross-language ring is JSON because JSON is self-describing and every spec implements one pair of bridges. N specs = 2N bridge implementations, not N² pair-wise paths.\n\n**Why this answers your \"do we always have to JSON?\" worry**\n\nNo. JSON is only the **cross-language** wire format. Same-language wires use the spec's own native format, which is whatever bytes that spec can read back fastest. For Lua → Lua, that doesn't have to be JSON — the current `cjson.encode` was a placeholder, not the final answer. msgpack or a custom binary Lua-value codec would be faster.\n\nSo the architecture you're defending — \"different format in different location, deterministic, fewer branches\" — *is* the original plan. The amendment came later and tried to collapse it (move format conversion into dispatch, drop the per-input flag, have specs auto-detect). We established earlier why that doesn't fit Lua's stack-based bridge. **The amendment was the wrong turn.** Walking it back puts us on solid ground.\n\n**On sentinels and closures**\n\nYou're right and I want to be more precise. The pre-amendment plan listed three sentinel kinds:\n\n- `$ref` — pointer + length into the large-value heap. This works because the LVH is shared memory; any worker can deref the pointer. Fine.\n- `$function_pointer` — in-process address. Falls apart for Lua because the address is into one `lua_State`'s GC heap. Only works for things registered by name in every worker's state (module functions). For runtime-created closures, no.\n- `$lang_opaque` — \"these bytes are language-X-internal.\" Only the same-spec consumer can read them. Useful for, say, Lua's own native byte form passing through a wire labelled `$lang_opaque` because it's a black box to anyone else. Not really a closure transport mechanism.\n\nSo sentinels work for `$ref` (shared memory pointers) and `$lang_opaque` (same-spec only). They don't solve closures-across-states. That problem is unsolvable in general because runtime values don't share GC heaps. The honest answer in 318 has to be: closures cross only via named registration, runtime-created closures can't be wired cross-state, the bridge fails loudly.\n\n**Proposed 312 closeout**\n\nGiven all this, the right delivery is:\n\n1. **Revert the amendment in the issue body.** Re-affirm the pre-amendment dual-ring design. The current code already implements it (slices 1–4.5); the amendment was a paper change that the code never followed.\n2. **Drop the dead `invoke_native` / `invoke_json` slots from `lang_spec_t`.** Slice 5 collapsed dispatch's branching to a single `invoke`; the extra slots are vestigial.\n3. **Add the dispatch-level mixed-fan-in test** the original plan called for — one cell arriving JSON-tagged and one arriving native-tagged on the same port, consumer reads them in arrival order, each cell decoded with the right path.\n4. **Document the open optimisation**: Lua's \"native bytes\" is currently `cjson.encode` (JSON-shaped). Replacing with msgpack or a binary Lua-value codec is a future enhancement that would make same-lang Lua-Lua wires faster than they are today. Out of scope for closing 312; tracked as a follow-on.\n\nThis commits to the architecture you've been pointing at, removes the architectural dead-end the amendment created, and the only structural code change is dropping two unused struct slots. Want me to proceed?"

        "input":{
          "old_string":"## Status\nsubstantively complete on the dual-ring foundation (2026-05-21);\n**spec-contract simplification pending** — see the Amendment\nsection below. Dual-ring slots, per-edge classification, and the\nper-cell ordering ring are in place and correct. The spec-side\nshape needs one more pass to remove the per-input format flags\nand the multiple invoke variants from `lang_spec_t`; that\nsimplification is the final slice of this issue.\n\n## Amendment (2026-05-22) — collapse to one `invoke`, native-only\n\nThe original slice plan kept three invoke entry points\n(`invoke`, `invoke_native`, `invoke_json`) and pushed per-input\nformat branching into each spec. After implementing through\nslice 5 we realised the per-input branching is dispatch's job,\nnot the spec's. The revised target:\n\n- **Dispatch normalises every input to the consuming spec's\n  native bytes before calling invoke.** When a popped cell is\n  tagged `RING_JSON`, dispatch calls the consumer spec's\n  `json_to_native` to convert the JSON bytes into the spec's\n  native byte form (written into a temporary slot or directly\n  into the input position dispatch hands to invoke). When the\n  cell is tagged `RING_NATIVE`, dispatch passes the slot's bytes\n  straight through — no conversion, the producer already wrote\n  in the consumer's format because they share a language.\n- **`invoke` sees one shape only**: a list of native-byte input\n  pointers, and an output slot to write native bytes into. No\n  `input_native[]` array, no `output_native` flag. The signature\n  becomes:\n\n  ```c\n  int invoke(handle, box, file_path, fn_name,\n             const void **input_data, const int *input_sizes,\n             int n_inputs,\n             void *out_buf, int out_buf_capacity, int *out_size);\n  ```\n\n- **`invoke_native` and `invoke_json` are deleted from\n  `lang_spec_t`.** The struct keeps `invoke`,\n  `native_to_json`, and `json_to_native` (plus `init`,\n  `teardown`, `compile`, `name`, `file_ext`).\n- **Cross-language output** is handled by dispatch after invoke:\n  the producer writes native bytes to its output slot once;\n  dispatch calls `native_to_json` once on those bytes if any\n  outgoing connection's `output_edge_native[j]` is false, then\n  pushes the JSON bytes to each cross-language consumer's\n  `ring_json`. Same-language consumers receive the original\n  native bytes directly.\n- **No \"bytes vs native\" distinction in the contract.** \"Native\"\n  means: bytes written in the format the spec emits and reads\n  back. There is no separate `native_to_bytes` /\n  `bytes_to_native` bridge; the spec's own native-write and\n  native-read already cover same-language wires by writing the\n  right bytes into the slot at push time and reading them out\n  at pop time. The slot is the medium; the spec is the codec.\n- **Why this collapses cleanly**: same-language wires never\n  involve dispatch's bridges at all — producer writes native to\n  the slot, consumer reads native from the slot, full stop.\n  Cross-language wires call exactly one bridge: `native_to_json`\n  on the producer side at push (so the JSON ring carries JSON),\n  `json_to_native` on the consumer side at pop (so invoke sees\n  native). The bridges fire once per language crossing, never\n  twice, and never inside a same-language path.\n\nThe result is one entry point, two bridges, and a dispatch layer\nthat owns all format-conversion timing. Specs no longer reason\nabout wire format at all.\n\n### Final-slice plan\n\n1. **Remove `input_native[]` and `output_native` from\n   `lang_invoke_fn`** in `langs/lang-spec.h`. Update every spec\n   stub.\n2. **Move JSON → native decode out of the spec's `invoke` into\n   dispatch's `read_inputs`** (`src/012-dispatch.c`). On a\n   `RING_JSON` pop, dispatch calls the consumer spec's\n   `json_to_native` and stages the resulting native bytes for\n   invoke.\n3. **Move JSON encoding for cross-language consumers out of the\n   spec's `invoke` into dispatch's push path**\n   (`src/012-dispatch.c`). For\nLua (and any future stateful runtime — Python, Ruby,\nJavaScript), `json_to_native` doesn't produce bytes; it\npushes a value onto the runtime's own working store\n(`lua_State`'s stack, in Lua's case). The revised target:\n\n- **Dispatch normalises every input to the consuming spec's\n  native bytes before calling invoke.** When a popped cell is\n  tagged `RING_JSON`, dispatch calls the consumer spec's\n  `json_to_native` to convert the JSON bytes into the spec's\n  native byte form (written into a temporary slot or directly\n  into the input position dispatch hands to invoke). When the\n  cell is tagged `RING_NATIVE`, dispatch passes the slot's bytes\n  straight through — no conversion, the producer already wrote\n  in the consumer's format because they share a language.\n- **`invoke` sees one shape only**: a list of native-byte input\n  pointers, and an output slot to write native bytes into. No\n  `input_native[]` array, no `output_native` flag. The signature\n  becomes:\n\n  ```c\n  int invoke(handle, box, file_path, fn_name,\n             const void **input_data, const int *input_sizes,\n             int n_inputs,\n             void *out_buf, int out_buf_capacity, int *out_size);\n  ```\n\n- **`invoke_native` and `invoke_json` are deleted from\n  `lang_spec_t`.** The struct keeps `invoke`,\n  `native_to_json`, and `json_to_native` (plus `init`,\n  `teardown`, `compile`, `name`, `file_ext`).\n- **Cross-language output** is handled by dispatch after invoke:\n  the producer writes native bytes to its output slot once;\n  dispatch calls `native_to_json` once on those bytes if any\n  outgoing connection's `output_edge_native[j]` is false, then\n  pushes the JSON bytes to each cross-language consumer's\n  `ring_json`. Same-language consumers receive the original\n  native bytes directly.\n- **No \"bytes vs native\" distinction in the contract.** \"Native\"\n  means: bytes written in the format the spec emits and reads\n  back. There is no separate `native_to_bytes` /\n  `bytes_to_native` bridge; the spec's own native-write and\n  native-read already cover same-language wires by writing the\n  right bytes into the slot at push time and reading them out\n  at pop time. The slot is the medium; the spec is the codec.\n- **Why this collapses cleanly**: same-language wires never\n  involve dispatch's bridges at all — producer writes native to\n  the slot, consumer reads native from the slot, full stop.\n  Cross-language wires call exactly one bridge: `native_to_json`\n  on the producer side at push (so the JSON ring carries JSON),\n  `json_to_native` on the consumer side at pop (so invoke sees\n  native). The bridges fire once per language crossing, never\n  twice, and never inside a same-language path.\n\nThe result is one entry point, two bridges, and a dispatch layer\nthat owns all format-conversion timing. Specs no longer reason\nabout wire format at all.\n\n### Final-slice plan\n\n1. **Remove `input_native[]` and `output_native` from\n   `lang_invoke_fn`** in `langs/lang-spec.h`. Update every spec\n   stub.\n2. **Move JSON → native decode out of the spec's `invoke` into\n   dispatch's `read_inputs`** (`src/012-dispatch.c`). On a\n   `RING_JSON` pop, dispatch calls the consumer spec's\n   `json_to_native` and stages the resulting native bytes for\n   invoke.\n3. **Move JSON encoding for cross-language consumers out of the\n   spec's `invoke` into dispatch's push path**\n   (`src/012-dispatch.c`). After invoke returns, if any\n   outgoing connection is cross-language, call `native_to_json`\n   once and push the JSON bytes to each cross-language\n   consumer.\n4. **Delete `invoke_native` and `invoke_json` slots from\n   `lang_spec_t`.** Drop the no-op stubs from each spec.\n5. **Restore Lua's pre-slice-4 simple invoke** — it reads\n   native bytes from inputs, runs the function, writes native\n   bytes to the output. No per-input branch.\n6. **Tests**: existing same-language and cross-language tests\n   should pass unchanged; a new test covers a mixed-fan-in port\n   where one cell arrives JSON-tagged (dispatch decodes before\n   invoke) and one arrives native-tagged (dispatch passes\n   through)."
  },

Returns 0 on success, nonzero on\n     * failure. */\n    int   (*compile)(const char *src_path, const char *out_path,\n                     const box_t *box);\n\n    /* invoke: per box call. dual-ring slots are single-cell\n * (slice 1 deferred DUAL_RING + multi-cell combining), so we\n * can't push two cells to the same slot in one run.  */\nstatic int build_describe_fixture(char *dir, size_t cap)\n{\n    char tmpl[] = \"/tmp/soramech-dualring-XXXXXX\";\n    char *got = mkdtemp(tmpl);\n    if (!got) return -1;\n    snprintf(dir, cap, \"%s\", got);\n\n    char abs[4096];\n    if \"%s/boxes/sink.json\", dir);\n    fp = fopen(p, \"w\");\n    fprintf(fp,\n        \"{\\\"id\\\":\\\"sink\\\",\\\"kind\\\":\\\"call\\\",\\\"lang\\\":\\\"lua\\\",\"\n        \"\\\"ref\\\":\\\"%s\\\",\\\"fn\\\":\\\"describe\\\",\"\n        \"\\\"inputs\\\":[{\\\"name\\\":\\\"x\\\",\\\"type\\\":\\\"string\\\"}],\"\n        \"\\\"routing\\\":{\\\"kind\\\":\\\"plain\\\"}}\",\n        abs);\n    fclose(fp);\n    return 0;\n}\n\nstatic void cleanup_describe_fixture(const char *dir)\n{\n    char p[4096];\n    snprintf(p, rmdir(dir);\n}\n\nstatic int test_dual_ring_per_cell_format(void)\n{\n    const char *bytes  = \"{\\\"a\\\":42}\";\n    int         n      = (int)strlen(bytes);\n    int ok = 1;\n\n    /* Half 1: ASSERT(slot_push_native(rt.slots, sb->input_slot_ids[0],\n                                bytes, n, 0) == 0);\n        dispatch_spawn_if_ready(&rt.ctx, sink, 0);\n        pool_wait_quiescent(rt.pool);\n        ASSERT(rt.ctx.last_outputs[sink] != NULL);\n        if (strncmp(rt.ctx.last_outputs[sink], \"string:\", 7) != 0) {\n            fprintf(stderr, \"      native half got: %s\\n\",\n                    rt.ctx.last_outputs[sink]);\n            ok = 0;\n        }\n        runtime_teardown(&rt);\n        cleanup_describe_fixture(dir);\n    }\n\n    /* Half 2: JSON push → Lua parses → \"table:42\" */\n    {\n        char dir[1024];\n        ASSERT(build_describe_fixture(dir, sizeof dir) == 0);\n        runtime_t rt;\n        ASSERT(runtime_setup(&rt, dir, 2, 1) == 0);\n        int sink = graph_box_index(rt.graph, \"sink\");\n        ASSERT(sink >= 0);\n        const box_t *sb = graph_box(rt.graph, sink);\n        ASSERT(slot_push_json(rt.slots, ASSERT(rt.ctx.last_outputs[sink] != NULL);\n        if (strcmp(rt.ctx.last_outputs[sink], \"table:42\") != 0) {\n            fprintf(stderr, \"      json half got: %s\\n\",\n ## [1408]

```json
{
  "sessionId":"a8fd7497-fc00-4f59-9644-b90753877f2a",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-22T20:38:49.153Z",
  "entrypoint":"cli",
  "version":"2.1.121",
  "gitBranch":"master",
  "message":{
    "content":[{
        "type":"tool_result",
        "content":"File created successfully at: /mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/strategems/contracts-must-fit-every-implementer.md",
        "tool_use_id":"toolu_01KSjSe1x6czChtSsbA6Phdq"
      }],
    "role":"user"
  },
  "uuid":"bf5ef312-4372-480f-8bea-6c95056cc2fe",
  "parentUuid":"5312effb-a178-42ef-bae7-8377adafaead",
  "toolUseResult":{
    "content":"# Strategem — a contract must fit every implementer, not just the simplest\n\n## The pattern\n\nWhen designing a contract that several implementers will satisfy\n(spec interfaces, abstract types, system protocols), check whether\nthe contract's assumptions hold for *every* class of implementer,\nnot just the cleanest case in front of you. A contract that works\nfor one class and almost-works for another is a contract that\nforces the awkward class into shims, hacks, or special-cases. The\nright move is to weaken the contract until it fits everyone\nhonestly.\n\nThe trap is subtle: the cleanest implementer often comes to mind\nfirst when you're designing. C and Bash specs in this project both\ntreat values as bytes — their bridges write to and read from `dst`\nbuffers. The proposed amendment to issue 312 designed the\ndispatch-side normalisation around this: \"dispatch calls the\nconsumer spec's `json_to_native` with a buffer, gets native bytes\nback, hands them to invoke.\" Clean, symmetric, byte-oriented.\n\nThe amendment failed when Lua showed up. Lua's `json_to_native`\ndoesn't write to a buffer — it pushes a value onto the worker's\n`lua_State` stack. There is no \"Lua native byte form\" external\nto the state for dispatch to hand to invoke. And Lua isn't an\noutlier: every runtime that owns its values (Python, Ruby,\nJavaScript, anything with a private GC heap) would have the same\nshape. The amendment assumed buffer orientation; half of all\npossible future specs don't have buffer orientation; the contract\nwas wrong.\n\n## How to apply\n\nWhen sketching a new contract:\n\n- List the implementers you can imagine. Not just the ones you\n  have today — the ones a future user might bring.\n- For each, ask: does the contract's central abstraction (bytes,\n  callbacks, state ownership, etc.) actually fit how that\n  implementer naturally works?\n- If even one implementer needs a shim — \"we'll just say its\n  buffer is empty,\" \"it'll ignore that half of the signature,\"\n  \"we'll define a convention where...\" — the contract is doing\n  half the work and the implementer is doing the other half.\n  That asymmetry is a smell.\n- Either weaken the contract so the awkward implementer fits\n  honestly, or accept that the contract is for a narrower\n  category (e.g. \"buffer-oriented specs only\") and design a\n  separate path for the others.\n\nThe litmus test: can the most awkward implementer satisfy the\ncontract *without lying*? If lua_json_to_native has to set\n`*dst_size = 0` and leave dst untouched because Lua doesn't have\nbytes to write, the signature is forcing it to satisfy a shape\nthat doesn't apply. That's the lie. The dispatch can't actually\nuse the (empty, zero-sized) result. The contract has dead\nparameters for half its implementers.\n\n## Adjacent pattern — the \"agnosticism\" question\n\nWhen a user asks \"is this design agnostic to X?\", they're usually\nasking exactly this question. The answer to \"is the system\nagnostic to runtime statefulness?\" is: yes, if and only if the\ncontract doesn't assume statelessness. Buffer-oriented bridges\nassume statelessness. Stack-protocol bridges accommodate\nstatefulness. Neither is wrong; what's wrong is mixing them and\nhoping the awkward case will quietly degrade.\n\n## Why this happens\n\nWhen the contract is being designed, the people in the room are\nusually thinking about the implementers in front of them. Future\nimplementers don't get to participate. So the contract drifts\ntoward what works for the present implementers, and the future\nones inherit the asymmetry. The discipline is to imagine those\nfuture implementers explicitly — to write down their shape and\nask if the contract fits, before shipping.\n\nThis is especially load-bearing for plugin / extension surfaces\n(spec interfaces, hook points, anything with a `register_X` API).\nThe whole point of those surfaces is that new implementers will\nappear. If the contract was built for the first two, the third\nwill not fit.\n",
    "structuredPatch":[],
    "type":"create",
    "userModified":false,
    "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/strategems/contracts-must-fit-every-implementer.md"

        },
        "id":"toolu_01KSjSe1x6czChtSsbA6Phdq",
        "type":"tool_use",
        "input":{
          "content":"# Strategem — a contract must fit every implementer, not just the simplest\n\n## The pattern\n\nWhen designing a contract that several implementers will satisfy\n(spec interfaces, abstract types, system protocols), check whether\nthe contract's assumptions hold for *every* class of implementer,\nnot just the cleanest case in front of you. A contract that works\nfor one class and almost-works for another is a contract that\nforces the awkward class into shims, hacks, or special-cases. The\nright move is to weaken the contract until it fits everyone\nhonestly.\n\nThe trap is subtle: the cleanest implementer often comes to mind\nfirst when you're designing. C and Bash specs in this project both\ntreat values as bytes — their bridges write to and read from `dst`\nbuffers. The proposed amendment to issue 312 designed the\ndispatch-side normalisation around this: \"dispatch calls the\nconsumer spec's `json_to_native` with a buffer, gets native bytes\nback, hands them to invoke.\" Clean, symmetric, byte-oriented.\n\nThe amendment failed when Lua showed up. Lua's `json_to_native`\ndoesn't write to a buffer — it pushes a value onto the worker's\n`lua_State` stack. There is no \"Lua native byte form\" external\nto the state for dispatch to hand to invoke. And Lua isn't an\noutlier: every runtime that owns its values (Python, Ruby,\nJavaScript, anything with a private GC heap) would have the same\nshape. The amendment assumed buffer orientation; half of all\npossible future specs don't have buffer orientation; the contract\nwas wrong.\n\n## How to apply\n\nWhen sketching a new contract:\n\n- List the implementers you can imagine. Not just the ones you\n  have today — the ones a future user might bring.\n- For each, ask: does the contract's central abstraction (bytes,\n  callbacks, state ownership, etc.) actually fit how that\n  implementer naturally works?\n- If even one implementer needs a shim — \"we'll just say its\n  buffer is empty,\" \"it'll ignore that half of the signature,\"\n  \"we'll define a convention where...\" — the contract is doing\n  half the work and the implementer is doing the other half.\n  That asymmetry is a smell.\n- Either weaken the contract so the awkward implementer fits\n  honestly, or accept that the contract is for a narrower\n  category (e.g. \"buffer-oriented specs only\") and design a\n  separate path for the others.\n\nThe litmus test: can the most awkward implementer satisfy the\ncontract *without lying*? If lua_json_to_native has to set\n`*dst_size = 0` and leave dst untouched because Lua doesn't have\nbytes to write, the signature is forcing it to satisfy a shape\nthat doesn't apply. That's the lie. The dispatch can't actually\nuse the (empty, zero-sized) result. The contract has dead\nparameters for half its implementers.\n\n## Adjacent pattern — the \"agnosticism\" question\n\nWhen a user asks \"is this design agnostic to X?\", they're usually\nasking exactly this question. The answer to \"is the system\nagnostic to runtime statefulness?\" is: yes, if and only if the\ncontract doesn't assume statelessness. Buffer-oriented bridges\nassume statelessness. Stack-protocol bridges accommodate\nstatefulness. Neither is wrong; what's wrong is mixing them and\nhoping the awkward case will quietly degrade.\n\n## Why this happens\n\nWhen the contract is being designed, the people in the room are\nusually thinking about the implementers in front of them. Future\nimplementers don't get to participate. So the contract drifts\ntoward what works for the present implementers, and the future\nones inherit the asymmetry. The discipline is to imagine those\nfuture implementers explicitly — to write down their shape and\nask if the contract fits, before shipping.\n\nThis is especially load-bearing for plugin / extension surfaces\n(spec interfaces, hook points, anything with a `register_X` API).\nThe whole point of those surfaces is that new implementers will\nappear. If the contract was built for the first two, the third\nwill not fit.\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/strategems/contracts-must-fit-every-implementer.md"
        }
      }],

        "text":"Let me give you the honest picture. It's medium-sized, well-contained, and the value is structural rather than behavioral.\n\n**What the refactor actually does**\n\nToday's dispatch action is two-phase:\n\n```\nproducer task runs:\n  read inputs from slots\n  invoke spec\n  for each outgoing connection:\n     push output to consumer slot\n     dispatch_spawn_if_ready(consumer)   ← may malloc a new task struct\n                                            and submit it to the pool\n  free this task\n```\n\nThe attempt-task model collapses to one shape:\n\n```\nattempt task runs:\n  if every required input is ready (slot has value, or read predecessor):\n     snapshot inputs\n     invoke spec\n     for each downstream consumer this attempt just wrote to:\n        slab_alloc → new attempt task for that consumer\n        submit to pool\n  return; slab_free this task either way\n```\n\nThe two shapes both work. The differences:\n\n- One task struct shape instead of two roles for the same struct.\n- One allocation path (slab pop from a free list) instead of `malloc` per spawn.\n- The \"is this consumer ready?\" check moves from the producer's epilogue to the consumer attempt's prologue. Same check, different timing.\n- An attempt that finds inputs not ready returns without doing work; the next push to any of that consumer's slots triggers a fresh attempt.\n\n**Code scale**\n\nTouches one file mostly: `src/012-dispatch.c`. Probably 300-500 lines of churn — restructuring the action body, swapping malloc for the existing 302 slab allocator, deleting the inline spawn-if-ready calls. A handful of test references.\n\nThe task struct change is the most visible part:\n\n```c\n// today\ntypedef struct { int box_id; int task_id; void *ctx; } dispatch_task_t;\n\n// after\ntypedef struct {\n    void   *next_free;\n    box_t  *box;\n    uint32_t task_id;\n    uint32_t flags;\n    void   *output_destinations;\n    void   *input_snapshot;\n    uint32_t live_wire_count;\n    uint32_t _pad;\n} attempt_task_t;\n```\n\nThe 64-byte layout is designed to fit one cache line and to use the slab allocator from 302 — which already exists and is in use elsewhere.\n\n**What it buys**\n\n- One allocation path instead of `malloc` per spawn. Real perf win on hot graphs (thousands of tasks per second). Today every spawn does a small `malloc`, every free does a small `free`.\n- The \"task\" abstraction stops carrying two meanings (a check that might run, a worker that will run). Reading the dispatch becomes shorter.\n- The retirement hook (`live_wire_count` — counts how many outgoing wires of a box are still in use, drives box-level cleanup) gets its placeholder in the cell layout, ready for a future slice.\n\n**What it does NOT buy**\n\n- Zero observable behavior change. Every fixture passes today and would pass after.\n- No new routing kinds, no new features for users.\n- No performance win unless the graph is allocation-hot.\n\n**Risk profile**\n\n- Medium. Touches the central dispatch loop, the single most thread-sensitive piece of the system. Any bug here is potentially a race or a leak.\n- Mitigated by: existing test coverage is decent (10 dispatch tests, 11 integration fixtures including the multi-language pipeline). The strategems we've been writing argue against churning code without a concrete trigger. When the trigger arrives — a profile, a feature, a race — that's the right moment to land the attempt-task shape.\n\nWhat's your read?         "type":"text",
        "text":"You're asking exactly the right questions, and they reframe the refactor.\n\n**On malloc and shared memory**\n\n`malloc` returns memory from the process heap. The process heap is shared across all threads in the process — that's a property of Linux's process model, not of malloc specifically. glibc's malloc is thread-safe via internal locking (or per-thread arenas with cross-arena access via locks for cross-thread reads). So a `malloc`'d pointer can be passed from worker A to the pool queue, picked up by worker D, dereferenced safely. That's what `dispatch_spawn` is doing today and it works.\n\nSo the current malloc IS in shared memory. The slab allocator from 302 is *also* in shared memory — it's a global pool with its own locks, just amortised across spawn/free pairs to skip the per-call malloc overhead. Both shapes work; slab is faster on hot graphs because it skips the malloc bookkeeping.\n\nThe \"we need everything accessible from any thread\" check is satisfied either way. Stack memory wouldn't be (it dies with the thread frame). Thread-local storage wouldn't be (per-thread). But process-heap memory — whether from malloc or from a slab allocator that itself sits in the process heap — is fine.\n\n**On the signal question — this is the load-bearing one**\n\nYou're seeing something I glossed over. Let me re-examine.\n\nIn the **current (epilogue) model**:\n- Producer's action runs. Reads inputs, invokes spec, pushes outputs to consumer slots.\n- For each consumer it touched, the producer calls `dispatch_spawn_if_ready(consumer)`:\n  - Checks if the consumer has all its required inputs (via `box_is_ready`).\n  - If yes, `malloc`s a task struct, submits to pool queue.\n  - If no, returns silently. Some *other* producer's later push will trigger another check.\n- The pool worker picks the task up and runs it.\n\nThis is the model in the code today. The signal mechanism is exactly what you described: producer writes inputs, asks \"is the consumer ready?\", submits iff yes.\n\nIn the **proposed attempt-task model**:\n- Producer's action runs. Same as above through the push.\n- For each consumer touched, the producer submits an attempt-task *without checking readiness*.\n- The attempt-task runs. *First thing it does* is check readiness. If not ready, returns without invoking. If ready, snapshots inputs, invokes, etc.\n\nYou're right that the attempt model wastes work on the not-ready case — every producer push to a 3-input consumer with one wire still pending submits an attempt that wakes up, looks around, sees inputs not ready, and quits. The epilogue check skips that whole round-trip.\n\n**So the user's question is correct: why move the check?**\n\nReading the original amendment again with your framing, the conceptual benefit was \"one task shape, one allocation, no separate readiness step.\" But the current model *already has one task shape* (`dispatch_task_t`), *one allocation path* (`malloc` in `dispatch_spawn`), and the readiness check is just a few lines of C in the producer's loop — not a separate task kind.\n\nThe amendment was solving a problem that didn't really exist. The \"check is a separate task\" framing was an artifact of how the design got written down, not a property of the code.\n\n**Re-scoped: what's actually worth doing**\n\nIf we strip the attempt-task rewrite of its conceptual ambition and ask what's left:\n\n1. **Use the slab allocator instead of `malloc` per spawn.** Real perf win on hot graphs; trivial code change (`malloc(sizeof *t)` → `ua_alloc(...)`, paired `free` → `ua_unref`). ~10 lines total. No semantics change.\n\n2. **Maybe expand the task struct to add a `live_wire_count` field.** Placeholder for future box-retirement work. Optional, only if you want it sitting there for the next slice. ~5 lines.\n\n3. **The \"one task shape, no inline check\" rewrite.** Doesn't actually buy what the original framing claimed. Defer indefinitely.\n\n(1) is so small it doesn't need to be its own issue — it's a perf-tweak on an existing path. (2) is design-level; only do it if there's a concrete next slice that needs the field. (3) is the thing I was overselling; skip it.\n\nSo the answer to \"is it a big change or small\": **the actually-useful piece is small.** The big piece I described turns out to be solving a non-problem once you look at what the current code already does.\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\nThe conversation we just had is a small instance of the strategem I wrote earlier — \"describe the runtime, not the paperwork.\" The issue body framed the current model as \"two-phase, check separate from work\" and the refactor as \"unified attempt-task model.\" But the runtime doesn't actually have two phases or a separate check task; it has one task with a few lines of readiness logic inline. The issue's framing exaggerated the structural distance between current and target to justify a refactor that, on inspection, was mostly cosmetic.\n\nYour question — \"what causes the prologue to initiate?\" — cut straight to the runtime. Once we trace the actual signal flow, the answer is \"the producer's epilogue submits, same as today,\" which means the refactor's main feature (move the check) wasn't moving anything load-bearing. The smell I should have caught earlier: any time a refactor description says \"X moves from A to B\" and X is a few lines of code rather than a structural unit, ask whether the \"from A to B\" is real or paper. Here it was paper.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\nWant me to update 304's body to be honest about this, and either close it or scope-tag the remaining items (slab swap + maybe `live_wire_count` placeholder) as the actual deliverables?"
      }],

    "originalFile":"/* src/012-dispatch.h — task dispatch layer, public API.\n *\n * What it is, in a sentence: the C function the thread pool runs\n * per task; reads inputs from the slot store, invokes the box's\n * language spec, pushes outputs to downstream input slots, and\n * spawns consumer tasks on input readiness.\n *\n * Designed in issue 304. As of this iteration: real input\n * reading, real spec invocation via per-worker handles, real\n * output pushing with FIFO + 1-cell peek slots, real\n * spawn-on-input-ready chaining under a single-spawn-per-box\n * rule. Iterator multi-spawn, the routing kinds beyond plain,\n * and the large-value heap path are still ahead.\n *\n * The `dispatch_ctx_t` bundle is the durable runtime state for\n * the whole run: graph, slot store, spec registry, pool, plus\n * a per-box \"ever spawned\" flag array and (optionally) a\n * per-box output-capture table for testing. Tasks carry a\n * pointer to the context so the action has everything it needs\n * without globals.\n */\n\n#ifndef SORAMECH_DISPATCH_H\n#define SORAMECH_DISPATCH_H\n\n#include <stdatomic.h>\n\n#include \"010-graph-loader.h\"\n#include \"011-spec-registry.h\"\n#include \"009-slot-store.h\"\n#include \"014-event-queue.h\"\n#include \"pool.h\"\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\nextern \"C\" {\n#endif\n\n/* {{{ Types */\ntypedef struct dispatch_ctx {\n    const graph_t        *graph;\n    slot_store_t         *slots;\n    spec_registry_t      *specs;\n    pool_t               *pool;\n\n    /* Diagnostic: incremented each time dispatch_action runs. */\n    _Atomic int           tasks_dispatched;\n\n    /* Per-box spawn guard (n_boxes entries). The 1-cell peek model\n     * spawns each box at most once; this flag is the CAS target\n     * that enforces \"only one push wins the spawn.\" */\n    int                   n_boxes;\n    _Atomic int          *box_ever_spawned;\n\n    /* Per-box output capture (opt-in, for tests). When non-NULL,\n     * dispatch_action copies the box's output bytes here on\n     * completion. n_boxes entries. */\n    char                **last_outputs;\n    int                  *last_output_sizes;\n    int                   capture_outputs;\n\n    /* Optional default output buffer size for invoke calls. If 0,\n     * defaults to 4096. */\n    int                   default_out_capacity;\n\n    /* Optional run-log event queue (issue 311). When non-NULL, the\n     * dispatch action emits task_start + task_end events through\n     * it. NULL turns the per-task logging off; the runner emits\n     * run_start / run_end on its own. */\n    event_queue_t        *events;\n\n    /* Verbose-event gate (issue 311 SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES=1). When\n     * 1 and `events` is non-NULL, dispatch_action also emits\n     * task_input / task_output events with the byte payloads\n     * (truncated to 4 KB per the architecture doc). */\n    int                   log_values;\n\n    /* Monotonic task id counter for run-log correlation. */\n    _Atomic int           next_task_id;\n} dispatch_ctx_t;\n\ntypedef struct dispatch_task {\n    int                   box_id;\n    int                   task_id;   /* assigned at dispatch_spawn time */\n    const dispatch_ctx_t *ctx;\n} dispatch_task_t;\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Lifecycle */\n/* Initialize the per-box runtime state owned by the context. The\n * graph + slots + specs + pool fields are caller-owned and just\n * referenced. Call after `graph_attach_runtime` so the per-box\n * runtime data is in place.\n *\n * `enable_output_capture` allocates `last_outputs` and\n * `last_output_sizes` so tests can inspect what each box wrote\n * after `pool_wait_quiescent`. */\nint  dispatch_ctx_init   (dispatch_ctx_t *ctx,\n                          const graph_t *g, slot_store_t *s,\n                          spec_registry_t *r, pool_t *p,\n                          int enable_output_capture, char **err);\n\n/* Free per-box runtime arrays; does not touch the externally-owned\n * graph / slots / specs / pool fields. */\nvoid dispatch_ctx_destroy(dispatch_ctx_t *ctx);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Startup helpers */\n/* Walk every box and push any input-port literal values into the\n * corresponding input slot. After this call, boxes whose inputs\n * are entirely literals are \"ready\" — spawn them with\n * `dispatch_spawn_if_ready` to start the run. */\nint  dispatch_push_literals(dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, char **err);\n\n/* If `box_id` has all required inputs available and hasn't been\n * spawned yet, allocate a task and submit it to the pool. */\nvoid dispatch_spawn_if_ready(dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, int box_id, int priority);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Task submission / action */\n/* Submit a task explicitly, bypassing the spawn-if-ready check.\n * The dispatch_action will still consume inputs from slots and\n * push outputs to downstream slots. */\nvoid dispatch_spawn(const dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, int box_id, int priority);\n\n/* The pool action. Cast `arg` back to `dispatch_task_t *` inside.\n * Frees the task at the end of the action. */\nvoid dispatch_action(void *arg);\n/* }}} */\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\n}\n#endif\n\n#endif /* SORAMECH_DISPATCH_H */\n",

    "originalFile":"/* src/012-dispatch.h — task dispatch layer, public API.\n *\n * What it is, in a sentence: the C function the thread pool runs\n * per task; reads inputs from the slot store, invokes the box's\n * language spec, pushes outputs to downstream input slots, and\n * spawns consumer tasks on input readiness.\n *\n * Designed in issue 304. As of this iteration: real input\n * reading, real spec invocation via per-worker handles, real\n * output pushing with FIFO + 1-cell peek slots, real\n * spawn-on-input-ready chaining under a single-spawn-per-box\n * rule. Iterator multi-spawn, the routing kinds beyond plain,\n * and the large-value heap path are still ahead.\n *\n * The `dispatch_ctx_t` bundle is the durable runtime state for\n * the whole run: graph, slot store, spec registry, pool, plus\n * a per-box \"ever spawned\" flag array and (optionally) a\n * per-box output-capture table for testing. Tasks carry a\n * pointer to the context so the action has everything it needs\n * without globals.\n */\n\n#ifndef SORAMECH_DISPATCH_H\n#define SORAMECH_DISPATCH_H\n\n#include <stdatomic.h>\n\n#include \"010-graph-loader.h\"\n#include \"011-spec-registry.h\"\n#include \"009-slot-store.h\"\n#include \"014-event-queue.h\"\n#include \"pool.h\"\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\nextern \"C\" {\n#endif\n\n/* {{{ Types */\ntypedef struct dispatch_ctx {\n    const graph_t        *graph;\n    slot_store_t         *slots;\n    spec_registry_t      *specs;\n    pool_t               *pool;\n\n    /* Diagnostic: incremented each time dispatch_action runs. */\n    _Atomic int           tasks_dispatched;\n\n    /* Per-box spawn guard (n_boxes entries). The 1-cell peek model\n     * spawns each box at most once; this flag is the CAS target\n     * that enforces \"only one push wins the spawn.\" */\n    int                   n_boxes;\n    _Atomic int          *box_ever_spawned;\n\n    /* Per-box output capture (opt-in, for tests). When non-NULL,\n     * dispatch_action copies the box's output bytes here on\n     * completion. n_boxes entries. */\n    char                **last_outputs;\n    int                  *last_output_sizes;\n    int                   capture_outputs;\n\n    /* Optional default output buffer size for invoke calls. If 0,\n     * defaults to 4096. */\n    int                   default_out_capacity;\n\n    /* Optional run-log event queue (issue 311). When non-NULL, the\n     * dispatch action emits task_start + task_end events through\n     * it. NULL turns the per-task logging off; the runner emits\n     * run_start / run_end on its own. */\n    event_queue_t        *events;\n\n    /* Verbose-event gate (issue 311 SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES=1). When\n     * 1 and `events` is non-NULL, dispatch_action also emits\n     * task_input / task_output events with the byte payloads\n     * (truncated to 4 KB per the architecture doc). */\n    int                   log_values;\n\n    /* Monotonic task id counter for run-log correlation. */\n    _Atomic int           next_task_id;\n} dispatch_ctx_t;\n\n/* Task structs are allocated from the unified allocator's slab\n * pool so spawn/free pairs amortise across the run instead of\n * paying per-call malloc bookkeeping. The chunk back-reference\n * lets dispatch_action release the cell via ua_unref without\n * having to look it up by data pointer. */\nstruct ua_chunk;\n\ntypedef struct dispatch_task {\n    int                   box_id;\n    int                   task_id;   /* assigned at dispatch_spawn time */\n    const dispatch_ctx_t *ctx;\n\n    /* 304 placeholder — live count of outgoing wires that still\n     * carry an unconsumed value pushed by this task. The\n * graph + slots + specs + pool fields are caller-owned and just\n * referenced. Call after `graph_attach_runtime` so the per-box\n * runtime data is in place.\n *\n * `enable_output_capture` allocates `last_outputs` and\n * `last_output_sizes` so tests can inspect what each box wrote\n * after `pool_wait_quiescent`. */\nint  dispatch_ctx_init   (dispatch_ctx_t *ctx,\n                          const graph_t *g, slot_store_t *s,\n                          spec_registry_t *r, pool_t *p,\n                          int enable_output_capture, char **err);\n\n/* Free per-box runtime arrays; does not touch the externally-owned\n * graph / slots / specs / pool fields. */\nvoid dispatch_ctx_destroy(dispatch_ctx_t *ctx);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Startup helpers */\n/* Walk every box and push any input-port literal values into the\n * corresponding input slot. After this call, boxes whose inputs\n * are entirely literals are \"ready\" — spawn them with\n * `dispatch_spawn_if_ready` to start the run. */\nint  dispatch_push_literals(dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, char **err);\n\n/* If `box_id` has all required inputs available and hasn't been\n * spawned yet, allocate a task and submit it to the pool. */\nvoid dispatch_spawn_if_ready(dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, int box_id, int priority);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Task submission / action */\n/* Submit a task explicitly, bypassing the spawn-if-ready check.\n * The dispatch_action will still consume inputs from slots and\n * push outputs to downstream slots. */\nvoid dispatch_spawn(const dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, int box_id, int priority);\n\n/* The pool action.           "new_string":"/* {{{ dispatch_spawn() */\nvoid dispatch_spawn(const dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, int box_id, int priority)\n{\n    if (!ctx || !ctx->pool) return;\n\n    /* Task structs come from the unified allocator's free-list so\n     * hot graphs don't pay per-spawn malloc bookkeeping. The chunk\n     * is stashed on the task itself so dispatch_action can release\n     * it via ua_unref without a lookup. */\n    ua_t *heap = slot_store_allocator(ctx->slots);\n    ua_chunk_t *chunk = ua_alloc(heap, sizeof(dispatch_task_t));\n    if (!chunk) return;\n    dispatch_task_t *t = (dispatch_task_t *)ua_data(chunk);\n    t->chunk = chunk;\n    t->live_wire_count = 0;\n\n    /* Assign task_id at submission so the same id correlates the\n     * task_submit / task_start / task_end events. The next_task_id\n     * counter is atomic so concurrent spawners don't collide. */\n    dispatch_ctx_t *mctx = (dispatch_ctx_t *)ctx;\n    t->task_id = atomic_fetch_add_explicit(&mctx->next_task_id, 1,\n                                           memory_order_relaxed);\n    t->box_id  = box_id;\n    t->ctx     = ctx;\n\n    if (ctx->events) {\n        const box_t *b = graph_box(ctx->graph, box_id);\n        event_queue_task_submit(ctx->events, now_secs(),\n            t->task_id, b ? b->id : \"(unknown)\", -1);\n    }\n    pool_spawn(ctx->pool, dispatch_action, t, priority);\n}",

  "uuid":"ab502f72-ba8d-4401-ac05-e39f057361d7",

  "message":{
    "content":[{
        "name":"Edit",
        "caller":{
          "type":"direct"
        },
        "id":"toolu_01PZinP4vX9i3RSFfhvSSp15",
        "type":"tool_use",
        "input":{
          "old_string":"## Attempt-task refactor (future)\n\nThe design rewrite below replaces the current two-phase\n(\"producer inlines spawn-if-ready check per consumer\") shape with\na single attempt-task shape — one allocation per invocation, one\nloop body. It is a structural refactor; observable behavior\nacross every fixture stays the same.\n\nIt does not block any phase-3 feature: every routing kind ships,\nread boxes pull on demand, multi-spawn iteration works, cross-\nlanguage wires work. The refactor's value is in code clarity and\nallocation count, not user-visible features. Tracked here so the\nshape doesn't get lost; will move to its own issue when picked\nup.",
          "replace_all":false,
          "new_string":"## Attempt-task rewrite — reconsidered\n\nThe \"attempt-task model\" rewrite (originally drafted 2026-05-20,\npreserved in the historical log below) framed itself as\n\"replacing the two-phase dispatch with a unified attempt-task\nshape — one allocation per invocation, one loop body, no\nseparate readiness check.\" On inspection the current code\nalready has one task shape (`dispatch_task_t`), one allocation\npath, and the readiness check is just a few lines of C in the\nproducer's epilogue — not a separate task kind. The rewrite\nwas framing a few lines of inline logic as a structural unit\nand proposing to \"move\" them; the \"from A to B\" wasn't real.\n\nThe two pieces of the rewrite that *were* useful, restated and\nshipped:\n\n1. **Slab allocation of task structs.** `dispatch_spawn` now\n   pulls task cells from the unified allocator (`ua_alloc`)\n   instead of `malloc`-ing per spawn. `dispatch_action` releases\n   via `ua_unref` paired with a `chunk` back-reference on the\n   task itself. Hot graphs no longer pay per-call malloc\n   bookkeeping; the free-list amortises spawn/free pairs across\n   the run. ~10 lines of code; no semantic change.\n\n2. **`live_wire_count` field placeholder** on `dispatch_task_t`,\n   initialised to 0 by `dispatch_spawn` and otherwise unread for\n   now. The box-retirement consumer that *does* something with\n   the count is the lifetime-tracking slice — it lands when a\n   future feature needs it (run statistics, GC of unused\n   producer outputs, etc.). The field is in the layout so a\n   future slice can wire up the read without changing the\n   struct shape callers depend on.\n\nWhat was *not* shipped — and would be a mistake to ship without\na concrete trigger:\n\n- Moving the readiness check from the producer's epilogue to a\n  consumer-side attempt prologue. The epilogue check is the\n  honest signal mechanism: producer writes inputs, checks\n  \"consumer ready?\", submits iff yes. The attempt-side check\n  would submit attempts that find inputs not ready and return —\n  strictly more work for the same outcome.\n- Restructuring `dispatch_action` into a single attempt-loop\n  body. The action already has one loop body; the \"two-phase\"\n  framing was paper.\n\nIf the same architectural pressure surfaces again — usually\nphrased as \"tasks have two meanings\" or \"we should unify the\nshape\" — the answer is to trace the runtime, not the issue\nbody. Two meanings on paper, one shape in code, is fine.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md"
        }
      }],
    "role":"assistant",
    "id":"msg_01Vq1F1qMYCojjXQjozQrY5p",

The box-retirement consumer that *does* something with\n   the count is the lifetime-tracking slice — it lands when a\n   future feature needs it (run statistics, GC of unused\n   producer outputs, etc.). The field is in the layout so a\n   future slice can wire up the read without changing the\n   struct shape callers depend on.\n\nWhat was *not* shipped — and would be a mistake to ship without\na concrete trigger:\n\n- Moving the readiness check from the producer's epilogue to a\n  consumer-side attempt prologue. The epilogue check is the\n  honest signal mechanism: producer writes inputs, checks\n  \"consumer ready?\", submits iff yes. The attempt-side check\n  would submit attempts that find inputs not ready and return —\n  strictly more work for the same outcome.\n- Restructuring `dispatch_action` into a single attempt-loop\n  body. The action already has one loop body; the \"two-phase\"\n  framing was paper.\n\nIf the same architectural pressure surfaces again — usually\nphrased as \"tasks have two meanings\" or \"we should unify the\nshape\" — the answer is to trace the runtime, not the issue\nbody. Two meanings on paper, one shape in code, is fine.",

          "command":"git commit -m \"$(cat <<'EOF'\n304 — closeout: slab-allocate task structs, retire the attempt-task rewrite\n\nThe \"attempt-task model rewrite\" tracked here was reconsidered\nafter walking through it carefully. The dispatch action already\nhas one task shape and one loop body; the readiness check is a\nfew lines of C in the producer's epilogue, not a separate task\nkind. The proposed rewrite framed inline logic as a structural\nunit and proposed \"moving\" it — but the \"from A to B\" wasn't a\nreal architectural move, and shifting the check from producer's\nepilogue to consumer-side attempt prologue would have *added*\nwork (submitting attempts that find inputs not ready and return)\nwithout buying anything observable.\n\nThe two pieces of the rewrite that turned out to be genuinely\nuseful, restated and shipped without restructuring the dispatch:\n\n- Task structs come from the unified allocator's slab pool\n  (ua_alloc) instead of being malloc'd per spawn. The chunk\n  back-reference is stashed on the task itself so\n  dispatch_action releases via ua_unref without a lookup. Hot\n  graphs amortise spawn/free bookkeeping across the run.\n- The live_wire_count field is added to dispatch_task_t,\n  initialised to 0 on every spawn and otherwise unread. The\n  box-retirement consumer that reads it is the lifetime-\n  tracking slice; the field is in the layout so a future slice\n  can wire up the read without changing the struct shape\n  callers depend on.\n\nThe issue body is updated to be honest about what shipped and\nwhy the larger rewrite was the wrong move. Full suite green:\n22 / 19 / 5 / 10 / 3 / 4 / 8 / 13 / 11 / 2 / 9 / 13 / 5 / 22 /\n5 / 12 / 11.\n\nCo-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>\nEOF\n)\"",

    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"312 closed earlier this session — moved to `issues/completed/`. Here's where it landed:\n\n**Status (closed)**\n\n- Dual-ring slot foundation: shipped (slice 1, 2026-05-21). Three rings per slot — `ring_native`, `ring_json`, and an ordering ring that sequences cells across mixed fan-in. `slot_push_native`, `slot_push_json`, `slot_pop_ordered` API.\n- Per-edge classification: shipped. The graph loader computes `input_edge_native[]` per input port and `output_edge_native[]` per outgoing connection. Producer picks ring at push time; consumer reads ring at pop time from the ordering tag.\n- Per-cell ordering tag: shipped. Iterator-fed wires propagate the iterator counter as a tag so parallel iterator workers' pushes land in invocation order at the consumer.\n- Spec contract: single `invoke` entry point with per-input / per-output flags, plus `native_to_json` / `json_to_native` bridges. The dead `invoke_native` / `invoke_json` function-pointer slots in `lang_spec_t` are gone.\n\n**What the closeout commit did this session**\n\nThe big move was **walking back the 2026-05-22 amendment**. That amendment had proposed dispatch normalising every input to native bytes before invoke, dropping the per-input flag, having every spec see one buffer shape. We figured out it assumed buffer-oriented bridges — works for C and Bash, doesn't work for Lua (whose `json_to_native` pushes onto `lua_State` rather than writing to a buffer) or for any future stateful runtime. The amendment forced stateful runtimes into a contract that didn't fit. We reverted it.\n\nThe architectural lesson — \"a contract must fit every implementer, not just the simplest\" — got its own strategem: `strategems/contracts-must-fit-every-implementer.md`.\n\n**Code change in the closeout commit**\n\nSmall. Two dead struct slots removed from `lang_spec_t` (`invoke_native`, `invoke_json` had been unused since slice 5 collapsed dispatch's branching). One new dispatch test (`dual_ring_per_cell_format`) that proves the per-cell ring tag flows from producer push through `read_inputs` to the consumer spec's `input_native[i]` flag — push the same bytes via `slot_push_native` and `slot_push_json` in two halves, observe a Lua consumer's `M.describe` returning `\"string:...\"` vs `\"table:42\"`.\n\n**One future enhancement, noted out-of-scope**\n\nLua's \"native bytes\" today is JSON-shaped (via the same encoder as `native_to_json`). The pre-amendment design said the spec could pick any native byte format it can read back fast — msgpack, `lua_dump`, custom binary. Replacing today's JSON-shaped output with one of those would make same-language Lua-to-Lua wires cheaper. Contract supports the swap; no fixture exercises it today; left for a profile-driven slice later.\n\n**Suite at closeout**\n\n17 test groups green including the new dual-ring dispatch test, all bridge tests, the integration pipeline that exercises Lua → C → Bash with real JSON crossing language boundaries.\n\nAnything specific about 312 you wanted to look at — the slot store internals, the per-edge classification rules, the bridge contract, the strategem? Or were you scoping for the next move?"

Does the\n   incremental-compile model (issue 309's mtime check) still apply,\n   or do edits require a full rebuild of the merged region?\n3. **Debug story**: a stack trace inside the merged region needs to\n   point back to a specific box. Either source-map-style mapping or\n   per-function preserved names — both have costs.\n\nThe right way to answer these is to prototype: take a small all-Lua\ngraph (like the hello map) and see what a merged version looks\nlike, both for runtime cost and for build-system complexity. The\nprototype should be able to fall back to the per-box path if the\nmerge fails for any reason.\n\n## Why blocked until rest of phase 3 completes\n\nThe merge optimization piggybacks on the per-box model — same\nspecs, same compile callback, same dispatch layer for cross-language\nwires. Building it before the per-box model is settled risks\ndesigning against a target that's still moving. After phase 3 ships\nand the per-box path is stable, the merge becomes a clean\n\"everything except spec invocation gets shorter for this region.\"\n\nIt's also genuinely lower priority than getting the runtime working\nat all. The same-language fast path (issue 312) captures the\n~2x JSON-skip win without any of this complexity. The merge wins a\nfurther factor only if profile data shows function-call overhead\nmatters at all after 312 ships.\n\n## Scope of the research output\n\nThe deliverable is a written design (not code) with:\n- Concrete answers to the three questions above.\n- A worked example: the merged C generated from a 5-box C-only\n  graph, showing what the build artifact looks like.\n- Estimated runtime cost of the per-box path vs the merged path\n  on that example.\n- A recommendation: ship as a feature, ship as an opt-in flag, or\n  shelve indefinitely.\n\nAfter the design is reviewed, a separate implementation issue\nopens (or doesn't, depending on the recommendation).\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — the immediate JSON-\n  skip win this builds on\n- `issues/307-c-language-spec.md` — `compile` callback that would\n  grow whole-program-aware semantics\n- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md` — Lua-side bytecode pre-compile\n- `issues/309-build-system.md` — how the merge integrates with the\n  compile/package step\n\n## Implementation log\n\n### Lua slice — 2026-05-21\n\n`scripts/soramech-compile.sh` grows a `merge_lua_sources` step\nbetween source-copy and per-spec packaging. For every `.lua` file\nin the map's `src/`, the merger wraps the file's body in a closure\nand binds the closure's return value to `merged[basename]` of a\nsingle output table. The result lands at `compiled/src/__merged__.lua`\nalongside the original files (which stay untouched, so any caller\nthat hasn't been told about the merge still works).\n\n`langs/lua/spec.c` grows `load_via_merged()`, called on the\ncache-miss path of `lua_invoke`. The helper derives a candidate\n`__merged__.lua` path next to the requested source file; if the\nfile exists, it loads the merged module once per worker (cached\nunder `LUA_MERGED_CACHE_KEY` in the Lua registry), then indexes\nthe returned table by the source file's basename to recover the\nper-file module. Lookup misses (no merged file, or no matching\nbasename inside it) fall back to per-file lazy load — the\nexisting path stays as the safety net. The dispatch never knows\nabout the merge; the spec redirects transparently.\n\nA unit test in `tests/306-lua-spec-test.c` exercises the merged\npath on a synthetic temp directory: it writes a `__merged__.lua`\nthat exports a sub-module under basename `calc` and invokes a\nphantom `calc.lua` file (no such file on disk). The invoke\nsucceeds, proving the merged path is reached. The existing\n\"compile pipeline (portable run)\" integration test verifies the\nend-to-end flow: `soramech-compile.sh` produces the merged file\nwhen packaging the `pipeline` fixture, the compiled artifact\nruns from `/tmp`, and the output matches what the source-tree\nrunner produces — the merge is transparent.\n\nDeferred to follow-on slices:\n\n- **C merge.** Concatenating C source needs care with static\n  vs. non-static functions, file-scoped declarations, and header\n  inclusion. Plausible approach: wrap each box's source in an\n  anonymous namespace-equivalent (C doesn't have namespaces, but\n  static-by-default at file scope + unique mangled exposure of\n  the box's entry function would do it). Real work; not done.\n- **Bash merge.** Bash already runs one persistent subprocess\n  per worker (issue 308's UDS-server model); the \"merge\" would\n  source every box's `.sh` file into the same subprocess\n  environment at server startup. Smaller surface than C; sized\n  somewhere in between.\n- **Inline-into-dispatch optimization.** This slice loads the\n  merged module per worker but still goes through the spec's\n  `lua_pcall` for every box invocation. The big optimization the\n  issue body talks about — turning box-to-box transitions into\n  direct function calls inside the merged module — needs\n  dispatch-layer work that hasn't started. The current slice is\n  the foundation: load-once-per-worker. The direct-call\n  optimization rides on top.\n\n## Open questions (for the research, not for now)\n\n- Cross-language wires inside the merged region: the merged region\n  still has cross-language outputs that exit to other regions. The\n  spec interface still applies at those boundaries, so the merge is\n  region-internal optimization, not a global rearchitecture.\n- C ABI for inlined wrappers: with whole-program optimization the\n  wrapper-per-box generation might collapse to nothing. If the\n  optimizer can prove a wire endpoint is always called from the\n  merged region with known types, it can skip the wrapper.\n- Iterators-with-side-effects: an iterator self-rescheduling its\n  own task is normally dispatch-layer machinery. Inside a merged\n  region, it could become a `while` loop. Whether that's safe\n  depends on whether other tasks are blocked on the iterator's\n  output slots — which they shouldn't be in a same-language region,\n  but the analysis has to confirm.\n",
      "totalLines":198,
