        "text":"313's status, honestly read:\n\n**Stated scope** — it's labelled `research / blocked` in phase progress and says \"the deliverable is a written design (not code) with: concrete answers to three open questions, a worked example, runtime-cost estimate, and a recommendation: ship / flag / shelve.\"\n\n**What actually shipped** — May 21, the Lua slice went well beyond research:\n\n- `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` grew a `merge_lua_sources` step that wraps every map `.lua` file into closures inside one `compiled/src/__merged__.lua`.\n- `langs/lua/spec.c` got `load_via_merged()` on the cache-miss path — derives the merged file's location, loads it once per worker, indexes by basename. Misses fall back to per-file lazy load (safety net).\n- `tests/306-lua-spec-test.c::test_invoke_via_merged_module` proves the merged path is reached.\n- The compile-pipeline integration test verifies the merged file is produced when packaging the `pipeline` fixture and the compiled artifact still runs.\n\n**What didn't ship**\n\n- **C merge** — concatenating C source files with name-mangling, static-scope handling, and header dedup. Real work.\n- **Bash merge** — but the persistent-subprocess server from 308 effectively already does this. Every worker's bash process loads all scripts at server startup. The \"merge\" is functionally redundant for Bash.\n- **The inline-into-dispatch optimisation** — the *big* win the body describes: turning box-to-box transitions into direct function calls inside the merged region, bypassing spec invocation per call. Hasn't started.\n\n**Reading what the body claims the merge buys**\n\nStep 3 of the issue's \"what a merged box invocation looks like\" loop is \"Dispatch jumps to the merged function directly (this is what 313 wins).\" Steps 2 and 5 — input read / output push — are unchanged from 312. So the merge's gain is just the spec-invocation indirection (dlsym + bridge + lua_pcall through the spec interface). That's a few hundred nanoseconds per call at most. The body acknowledges this directly: *\"boxes still run as separate thread-pool tasks. ... The merge wins on the per-call indirection cost, not on the wire format.\"*\n\nThat's a smaller win than \"merge everything\" first reads as.\n\n**My honest read**\n\nThe Lua slice that shipped is the practical part — keeping the lua_State warm with all box modules loaded, skipping the per-file `luaL_loadfile + pcall` on cache miss. That's real, real-world useful, and it's done.\n\nThe three open research questions:\n1. *Iterator boundaries* — only matters if we do inline-into-dispatch. Without that, iterators stay dispatch-layer routing, no change.\n2. *Compile-time cost* — for Lua, none (concatenation only, no optimisation). For C if we ever do it, real cost. For Bash, nothing.\n3. *Debug story* — Lua's slice keeps per-file basenames in the merged module's table keys, so traces still attribute correctly. Solved for Lua.\n\nThe genuinely open question is whether inline-into-dispatch is worth pursuing. Reading the body's own analysis — pool parallelism depends on tasks being scheduled independently across workers, and collapsing wire transitions to synchronous function calls would defeat the pool — the answer points at *no*. The merge can't actually skip the slot machinery without breaking parallelism, so the win is bounded to the spec-invocation indirection, which is small.\n\n**Three honest paths**\n\n1. **Close 313 now**: write the research recommendation directly into the issue body — \"Lua module merging shipped; C merge deferred until profiling shows need; Bash merge is functionally done via 308's persistent server; inline-into-dispatch shelved because it conflicts with the parallelism model\" — and move to completed.\n\n2. **Trim 313 to just the Lua slice**: split the C / inline-into-dispatch piece off as a separate future issue. Close 313 with what shipped.\n\n3. **Keep 313 open** as ongoing research, no action needed.\n\nMy lean is **(1) — close it with the recommendation written in.** Phase 3 is essentially done, the Lua practical part shipped, and the bigger merge optimisation has a real architectural conflict (parallelism vs synchronous calls) that the body itself surfaces. Writing that conflict down as the recommendation is honest research output.\n\nWhat's your read?"

## [1562]

```json
{
  "sessionId":"a8fd7497-fc00-4f59-9644-b90753877f2a",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-22T21:05:49.930Z",
  "entrypoint":"cli",
  "version":"2.1.121",
  "gitBranch":"master",
  "message":{
    "content":[{
        "type":"tool_result",
        "content":"210\t## Runtime model — two paths, needs a decision\n211\t\n212\tTwo implementation paths exist. The encapsulating box being a\n213\tnormal `call` box from the editor's perspective doesn't pick\n214\tbetween them; the choice lives in what the map-language spec\n215\tdoes behind the scenes and what (if anything) the compile\n216\tpipeline does at build time.\n217\t\n218\t### Path A — Compile-time inlining\n219\t\n220\tThe compile pipeline (issue 309) recognizes encapsulating call\n221\tboxes and **expands them into their sub-graphs at build time**.\n222\tSteps the compile step takes per encapsulating box:\n223\t\n224\t1. Load the sub-map's graph from `ref`.\n225\t2. Rename every internal box with a parent-namespaced id:\n226\t   `stats_pipeline__compute`, `stats_pipeline__filter`, etc.\n227\t3. Copy every internal wire across, with the renamed ids.\n228\t4. For each marked data box inside the sub-map: replace it with\n229\t   a wire that brings the encapsulating box's matching input\n230\t   value directly to wherever the data box's output was wired.\n231\t5. For each write box inside the sub-map: route its emitted\n232\t   value into the packed-blob writer that produces the\n233\t   encapsulating box's output (or, alternatively, expose each\n234\t   write box's value as a separate output wire that downstream\n235\t   consumers can wire to individually — see \"Output unpacking\n236\t   under inlining\" below).\n237\t6. Remove the encapsulating call box from the parent's graph.\n238\t\n239\tAfter expansion, the compiled artifact is **one flat graph**.\n240\tThe runtime never sees `lang: \"map\"`. The map-language spec\n241\texists only for the editor's sake (validating refs, listing\n242\tthe sub-map's inputs/outputs for the inspector).\n243\t\n244\t**Pros:**\n245\t\n246\t- No new runtime machinery. The dispatch, slot store, and spec\n247\t  registry all operate on flat graphs as today.\n248\t- Best per-call performance — no sub-graph startup cost, no\n249\t  nested dispatch.\n250\t- **Composes cleanly with issue 313** (whole-program same-\n251\t  language merge). The inlined sub-graph's same-language regions\n252\t  merge into the parent's merge as if they were always one map.\n253\t- Debugging stack traces inside the inlined region point to\n254\t  flat box ids — readable once you know the naming convention.\n255\t\n256\t**Cons:**\n257\t\n258\t- The sub-map gets baked into every parent that uses it. Edit\n259\t  the sub-map → every parent must recompile.\n260\t- No hot-reload of sub-maps. The editor would have to\n261\t  re-expand on every parent map edit, or accept that the\n262\t  parent's last-compiled artifact lags the sub-map source.\n263\t- Compile time grows with sub-map size × number of\n264\t  encapsulations.\n265\t- Deep recursion (sub-maps inside sub-maps inside sub-maps)\n266\t  inflates the parent's compiled output proportionally.\n267\t- Output unpacking under inlining is awkward: the packed-blob\n268\t  output format makes sense at a boundary; with no boundary,\n269\t  downstream consumers either wire to individual sub-write-box\n270\t  outputs (more efficient but a different mental model) or get\n271\t  the packer's blob baked in too (the packer is just another\n272\t  inlined function call).\n273\t\n274\t### Path B — Runtime sub-graph dispatch\n275\t\n276\tThe encapsulating box stays as one box in the parent's flat\n277\tgraph. The map-language spec's `invoke` runs the sub-graph at\n278\tcall time:\n279\t\n280\t1. **`map_init(worker_idx)`** — load every sub-map referenced\n281\t   by the running program (or lazily on first invoke). Each\n282\t   worker gets its own copy of the sub-graph state (slot store,\n283\t   dispatch context).\n284\t2. **`map_invoke(handle, sub_map_dir, ..., inputs, ..., out_buf, ...)`** —\n285\t   for each input, write the bytes into the shared-memory chunk\n286\t   that the matching marked data box reads from. Then drive the\n287\t   sub-graph to quiescence using the existing pool's dispatch\n288\t   loop (the sub-graph's tasks are normal pool tasks distinguished\n289\t   by a nested namespace). When quiescent, walk the write boxes,\n290\t   read their emitted values, pack them into the size-index +\n291\t   data-section blob, write the blob to `out_buf`.\n292\t\n293\tThe sub-graph's parallelism uses the same thread pool as the\n294\tparent's. A sub-graph's tasks compete for workers alongside the\n295\tparent's tasks. From the pool's perspective, the difference is\n296\tjust box-id prefix.\n297\t\n298\t**Pros:**\n299\t\n300\t- Sub-map loaded once per worker, reused across many parent\n301\t  invocations and across many parent maps.\n302\t- Hot-reload friendly: change the sub-map, parent picks up the\n303\t  new version on next run (no parent recompile).\n304\t- The packed-blob output format is the natural shape — the\n305\t  boundary exists, the spec packs at the boundary, downstream\n306\t  consumers unpack with the helper library.\n307\t- Debugging stack traces preserve the sub-map identity (the\n308\t  task's namespace says \"this came from `stats-pipeline`\").\n309\t- Recursion is natural — the spec's invoke can nest-invoke its\n310\t  own spec for a sub-sub-map.\n311\t\n312\t**Cons:**\n313\t\n314\t- New runtime machinery: the map spec's `invoke` runs a nested\n315\t  dispatch loop. Either the dispatch layer grows a re-entrancy\n316\t  contract, or the map spec replicates enough of the dispatch\n317\t  machinery to drive the sub-graph itself.\n318\t- Each encapsulating-box call pays sub-graph startup cost —\n319\t  seeding inputs, possibly resetting slot state from a previous\n320\t  invocation, collecting outputs at the end. Small but real.\n321\t- Does NOT compose with issue 313's same-language merge — the\n322\t  sub-map's source can't merge with the parent's, because at\n323\t  build time they're separate compilation units. (313 could be\n324\t  extended to merge across encapsulation boundaries, but that's\n325\t  a separate design.)\n326\t- Re-using the sub-graph across invocations requires reset\n327\t  semantics. Either the sub-graph's slots and counters get\n328\t  reset between invocations (cost), or each invocation gets a\n329\t  fresh sub-graph instance (allocation cost).\n330\t\n331\t### What to weigh\n332\t\n333\tThe choice turns on whether encapsulation is **a build-time\n334\tabstraction (like a C macro or a Lua-function-inlined-by-LuaJIT)**\n335\tor **a runtime composition (like calling a function in a shared\n336\tlibrary)**.\n337\t\n338\tPath A treats it as a build-time abstraction. Encapsulation is\n339\thow the user organizes source; the compiled artifact is one\n340\tflat program. Best for raw performance and integration with\n341\tthe existing machinery. Cost: rebuild propagation.\n342\t\n343\tPath B treats it as a runtime composition. Encapsulation is a\n344\treal boundary at execution time, with the packed-blob output\n345\tas the wire format across the boundary. Best for modularity,\n346\thot-reload, and clear semantics. Cost: per-call overhead and\n347\tloss of cross-boundary optimization.\n348\t\n349\tA third option exists — **support both, picked per encapsulating\n350\tbox** via a small flag in the box JSON (`encap_mode: \"inline\" |\n351\t\"runtime\"`). The compile pipeline expands inline-mode boxes;\n352\truntime-mode boxes stay encapsulated. Each user picks per\n353\tencapsulation based on their needs. Higher implementation cost\n354\tbut maximally flexible. Probably not in the first slice; flag it\n355\tfor later if either A or B alone proves too narrow.\n356\t\n357\tRecursion (a sub-map encapsulates another sub-map) works under\n358\teither path. Cycles between maps are a compile-time (or\n359\tload-time, under B) error.\n360\t\n361\t## Relationship to existing issues\n362\t\n363\t- **Issue 207 (source-file-browser)** — the file browser is the\n364\t  entry point for the \"encapsulate\" action.",
        "tool_use_id":"toolu_01SqrmXKowx8DhzTzqNo3ZrL"
      }],
    "role":"user"
  },
  "uuid":"abf4aa78-ef07-4140-b425-873d045cae3e",
  "parentUuid":"1319c817-e072-4d3e-b70b-1afa83f89bb7",
  "toolUseResult":{
    "type":"text",
    "file":{
      "content":"## Runtime model — two paths, needs a decision\n\nTwo implementation paths exist. The encapsulating box being a\nnormal `call` box from the editor's perspective doesn't pick\nbetween them; the choice lives in what the map-language spec\ndoes behind the scenes and what (if anything) the compile\npipeline does at build time.\n\n### Path A — Compile-time inlining\n\nThe compile pipeline (issue 309) recognizes encapsulating call\nboxes and **expands them into their sub-graphs at build time**.\nSteps the compile step takes per encapsulating box:\n\n1. Load the sub-map's graph from `ref`.\n2. Rename every internal box with a parent-namespaced id:\n   `stats_pipeline__compute`, `stats_pipeline__filter`, etc.\n3. Copy every internal wire across, with the renamed ids.\n4. For each marked data box inside the sub-map: replace it with\n   a wire that brings the encapsulating box's matching input\n   value directly to wherever the data box's output was wired.\n5. For each write box inside the sub-map: route its emitted\n   value into the packed-blob writer that produces the\n   encapsulating box's output (or, alternatively, expose each\n   write box's value as a separate output wire that downstream\n   consumers can wire to individually — see \"Output unpacking\n   under inlining\" below).\n6. Remove the encapsulating call box from the parent's graph.\n\nAfter expansion, the compiled artifact is **one flat graph**.\nThe runtime never sees `lang: \"map\"`. The map-language spec\nexists only for the editor's sake (validating refs, listing\nthe sub-map's inputs/outputs for the inspector).\n\n**Pros:**\n\n- No new runtime machinery. The dispatch, slot store, and spec\n  registry all operate on flat graphs as today.\n- Best per-call performance — no sub-graph startup cost, no\n  nested dispatch.\n- **Composes cleanly with issue 313** (whole-program same-\n  language merge). The inlined sub-graph's same-language regions\n  merge into the parent's merge as if they were always one map.\n- Debugging stack traces inside the inlined region point to\n  flat box ids — readable once you know the naming convention.\n\n**Cons:**\n\n- The sub-map gets baked into every parent that uses it. Edit\n  the sub-map → every parent must recompile.\n- No hot-reload of sub-maps. The editor would have to\n  re-expand on every parent map edit, or accept that the\n  parent's last-compiled artifact lags the sub-map source.\n- Compile time grows with sub-map size × number of\n  encapsulations.\n- Deep recursion (sub-maps inside sub-maps inside sub-maps)\n  inflates the parent's compiled output proportionally.\n- Output unpacking under inlining is awkward: the packed-blob\n  output format makes sense at a boundary; with no boundary,\n  downstream consumers either wire to individual sub-write-box\n  outputs (more efficient but a different mental model) or get\n  the packer's blob baked in too (the packer is just another\n  inlined function call).\n\n### Path B — Runtime sub-graph dispatch\n\nThe encapsulating box stays as one box in the parent's flat\ngraph. The map-language spec's `invoke` runs the sub-graph at\ncall time:\n\n1. **`map_init(worker_idx)`** — load every sub-map referenced\n   by the running program (or lazily on first invoke). Each\n   worker gets its own copy of the sub-graph state (slot store,\n   dispatch context).\n2. **`map_invoke(handle, sub_map_dir, ..., inputs, ..., out_buf, ...)`** —\n   for each input, write the bytes into the shared-memory chunk\n   that the matching marked data box reads from. Then drive the\n   sub-graph to quiescence using the existing pool's dispatch\n   loop (the sub-graph's tasks are normal pool tasks distinguished\n   by a nested namespace). When quiescent, walk the write boxes,\n   read their emitted values, pack them into the size-index +\n   data-section blob, write the blob to `out_buf`.\n\nThe sub-graph's parallelism uses the same thread pool as the\nparent's. A sub-graph's tasks compete for workers alongside the\nparent's tasks. From the pool's perspective, the difference is\njust box-id prefix.\n\n**Pros:**\n\n- Sub-map loaded once per worker, reused across many parent\n  invocations and across many parent maps.\n- Hot-reload friendly: change the sub-map, parent picks up the\n  new version on next run (no parent recompile).\n- The packed-blob output format is the natural shape — the\n  boundary exists, the spec packs at the boundary, downstream\n  consumers unpack with the helper library.\n- Debugging stack traces preserve the sub-map identity (the\n  task's namespace says \"this came from `stats-pipeline`\").\n- Recursion is natural — the spec's invoke can nest-invoke its\n  own spec for a sub-sub-map.\n\n**Cons:**\n\n- New runtime machinery: the map spec's `invoke` runs a nested\n  dispatch loop. Either the dispatch layer grows a re-entrancy\n  contract, or the map spec replicates enough of the dispatch\n  machinery to drive the sub-graph itself.\n- Each encapsulating-box call pays sub-graph startup cost —\n  seeding inputs, possibly resetting slot state from a previous\n  invocation, collecting outputs at the end. Small but real.\n- Does NOT compose with issue 313's same-language merge — the\n  sub-map's source can't merge with the parent's, because at\n  build time they're separate compilation units. (313 could be\n  extended to merge across encapsulation boundaries, but that's\n  a separate design.)\n- Re-using the sub-graph across invocations requires reset\n  semantics. Either the sub-graph's slots and counters get\n  reset between invocations (cost), or each invocation gets a\n  fresh sub-graph instance (allocation cost).\n\n### What to weigh\n\nThe choice turns on whether encapsulation is **a build-time\nabstraction (like a C macro or a Lua-function-inlined-by-LuaJIT)**\nor **a runtime composition (like calling a function in a shared\nlibrary)**.\n\nPath A treats it as a build-time abstraction. Encapsulation is\nhow the user organizes source; the compiled artifact is one\nflat program. Best for raw performance and integration with\nthe existing machinery. Cost: rebuild propagation.\n\nPath B treats it as a runtime composition. Encapsulation is a\nreal boundary at execution time, with the packed-blob output\nas the wire format across the boundary. Best for modularity,\nhot-reload, and clear semantics. Cost: per-call overhead and\nloss of cross-boundary optimization.\n\nA third option exists — **support both, picked per encapsulating\nbox** via a small flag in the box JSON (`encap_mode: \"inline\" |\n\"runtime\"`). The compile pipeline expands inline-mode boxes;\nruntime-mode boxes stay encapsulated. Each user picks per\nencapsulation based on their needs. Higher implementation cost\nbut maximally flexible. Probably not in the first slice; flag it\nfor later if either A or B alone proves too narrow.\n\nRecursion (a sub-map encapsulates another sub-map) works under\neither path. Cycles between maps are a compile-time (or\nload-time, under B) error.\n\n## Relationship to existing issues\n\n- **Issue 207 (source-file-browser)** — the file browser is the\n  entry point for the \"encapsulate\" action.",
      "totalLines":466,
      "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/248-encapsulated-map-as-box.md",
      "numLines":155,

    }

        "text":"248's relationship to 313 is direct and is actually called out in 248's body. Here's the short version:\n\n**248 in one line**: a sub-map becomes a single box on a parent map's canvas, exposing marked-as-external `read` boxes as inputs and `write` boxes as packed outputs. Sub-graphs become reusable, composable units.\n\n**Two implementation paths in 248, and they differ exactly on 313**\n\n**Path A — Compile-time inlining.** The compile pipeline expands the encapsulating box into its sub-graph at build time: rename internal boxes with a parent namespace, copy every internal wire, replace marked external-reads with direct wires from the parent's matching inputs, replace write boxes with the packed-output writer. Encapsulating box vanishes. Result: one flat graph at runtime. The runtime never sees `lang: \"map\"`.\n\nThis **composes cleanly with 313** — and the body says so directly: *\"The inlined sub-graph's same-language regions merge into the parent's merge as if they were always one map.\"* Because once the sub-graph is inlined into the parent, its Lua boxes and the parent's Lua boxes look indistinguishable to 313's merger; they go into the same `__merged__.lua`. The encapsulation boundary disappears at compile time, so the language-merge boundary also disappears.\n\n**Path B — Runtime sub-graph dispatch.** The encapsulating box stays one box. The map-language spec's `invoke` runs the sub-graph at call time, via a nested dispatch loop. Sub-map loaded once per worker; sub-graph's tasks compete for workers alongside the parent's tasks; outputs collected and packed at quiescence.\n\nThis **does NOT compose with 313** — body again: *\"The sub-map's source can't merge with the parent's, because at build time they're separate compilation units.\"* The sub-map keeps its own compiled artifact (its own `__merged__.lua`); 313's merge stops at the encapsulation boundary.\n\n**The relationship summarised**\n\n- Path A treats encapsulation as a build-time abstraction. 313's same-language merger then operates across the (now flat) parent + inlined sub-graphs, getting more value because there's more same-language code to merge.\n- Path B treats encapsulation as a runtime composition. 313's merger stops at every encapsulation boundary; each sub-map has its own merge.\n\nThe body even floats a Path C: a per-box `encap_mode: \"inline\" | \"runtime\"` flag so each encapsulation picks. That gives 313 the benefit on inline-mode boxes and isolates runtime-mode ones.\n\n**One other thing worth flagging while we're here**\n\n248 still uses `kind: \"data\"` in its body (the old terminology). Issue 229 renamed `data` → `read`/`write` long ago, and 244 made read boxes pull-on-demand. The body's \"marked data boxes\" should be \"marked read boxes,\" and the description of how external inputs flow into them — *\"a small shared-memory chunk seeded by the encapsulating call's invoke; the marked data box reads from that chunk on each fire\"* — is essentially 244's read-box `cached_value`, just seeded by the parent at invoke time instead of by graph load. The terminology drift would be worth fixing if/when 248 moves forward.\n\n**Where you are with 248**\n\nIt's open. No implementation. The path decision (A vs B vs both) is the load-bearing question; everything else (UI, file layout, output packing) waits on that. Scoping it would mean either picking a path or building Path C's flag-based \"support both.\"\n\nWhat angle are you on it from — picking the path, scoping the work, or just mapping how the issues connect?"

```json
{
  "timestamp":"2026-05-22T21:12:21.541Z",

    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"Yes, this works cleanly — and your framing of the two use cases is exactly the lens for picking per-encapsulation. Let me sketch what \"both\" actually looks like.\n\n**The flag and the two use cases**\n\nThe encapsulating box's JSON carries an `encap_mode` field:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"stats\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"lang\": \"map\",\n  \"ref\": \"maps/stats-pipeline\",\n  \"encap_mode\": \"inline\",          // or \"runtime\"\n  \"inputs\":  [...],\n  \"outputs\": [...]\n}\n```\n\n- `\"inline\"` → \"I know this sub-map at compile time, I want it folded into the parent, and I want 313 to merge across the boundary.\"\n- `\"runtime\"` → \"I'm picking this sub-map by name at run time, or I want it hot-reloadable, or I want it isolated.\"\n\nA user's typical run-time case maps to this: a `read` box feeds a name string into the encapsulating box; the spec resolves \"load `maps/<that-name>`\" lazily. The parent can't know the name at compile time, so `inline` isn't an option — `runtime` is forced.\n\nA user's typical compile-time case: the user dragged a known sub-map from the file browser onto the canvas. The reference is static; `inline` is the natural default; the compiled artifact stays one piece.\n\n**What the compile pipeline does for each**\n\n`scripts/soramech-compile.sh` grows a graph-rewrite pass *before* the existing source-merge and per-spec packaging. For every encapsulating box in the parent:\n\n- If `encap_mode == \"inline\"`:\n  1. Load the sub-map's graph.\n  2. Namespace every internal box id (`stats__filter`, `stats__compute`).\n  3. Copy every wire across with the renamed ids.\n  4. For each marked external-input `read` box in the sub-map, replace it with a direct wire from the parent's matching input on the encapsulating box.\n  5. For each `write` box in the sub-map, either pack into a blob (preserving the boundary's output shape) or expose individually as separate outputs from the encapsulating-box site.\n  6. Delete the encapsulating box from the parent's box list.\n  7. Recurse: if the sub-map itself contains inline encapsulations, expand those too.\n\nAfter this pass, the parent's flat graph is what the rest of the pipeline (and 313's merge step) sees. 313's `merge_lua_sources` then groups same-language boxes — including the ones that came from the inlined sub-map — into one module.\n\n- If `encap_mode == \"runtime\"`:\n  1. Leave the encapsulating box alone.\n  2. Also compile the sub-map's own artifacts (its own `__merged__.lua`, its own C `.so`s) into a side directory the parent's runtime can find.\n  3. The encapsulating box stays a `lang: \"map\"` call box in the parent's flat graph.\n\nA single parent can have both. The pipeline iterates every box, decides per-box, runs the right transform.\n\n**What the runtime does for each**\n\nFor `inline` boxes: nothing special. They're already flat in the compiled artifact; the dispatch sees ordinary boxes.\n\nFor `runtime` boxes: the map-language spec — `langs/map/spec.so` — implements the standard `lang_spec_t`:\n\n- `map_init(worker_idx)`: empty cache of loaded sub-graphs.\n- `map_invoke(handle, box, sub_map_path, fn_name, inputs, ..., out_buf, ...)`:\n  1. Resolve the sub-map (cache key = path or runtime-supplied name). On miss, `graph_load(path)`, `graph_attach_runtime(...)` against a *fresh* per-worker slot store dedicated to this sub-graph instance.\n  2. For each input, seed the matching marked external-`read` box's `cached_value` with the bytes the parent supplied.\n  3. Drive the sub-graph to quiescence on the *same pool* — its tasks share workers with the parent. Per-task box ids get a nested-namespace prefix so traces stay distinguishable.\n  4. Walk the `write` boxes, collect their captured outputs, pack into the size-indexed blob format, write to `out_buf`.\n  5. Optionally reset slot state for re-invocation (cheaper than re-loading the whole sub-graph).\n\nThis is exactly Path B from 248's body, modular and self-contained.\n\n**Where 313 sits in the picture**\n\n- Inline-mode boxes contribute their source files to the parent's `__merged__.lua`. 313's existing merger handles them uniformly — it doesn't even need to know about encapsulation; it just sees more boxes after the inline pass ran.\n- Runtime-mode boxes get their own `__merged__.lua` in their own compiled directory. 313 merges within each sub-map's region but doesn't cross the boundary.\n\n**The schema constraint, which \"both\" doesn't escape**\n\nEven in runtime mode, the parent needs to wire the encapsulating box's input ports and output channels at compile time. So the encapsulating box's JSON must declare the schema: input port names, output channel names, output blob layout. Sub-maps loaded at runtime have to *match* that schema (the spec checks at load time; mismatch is a fatal error).\n\nThis is like a function-pointer typedef in C — you can swap which function the pointer holds at run time, but the signature is fixed in source. For maps, the analogue is: the encapsulating box says \"this sub-map will have inputs A/B/C and outputs X/Y,\" and any sub-map referenced by name at runtime has to satisfy that contract.\n\n**Cost summary, honest**\n\n- The map-language spec is built either way (it's the foundation for runtime mode and the dynamic-load case is your stated motivating use).\n- Inline-mode is a graph-rewrite step in the compile pipeline. Probably 100–200 lines of clean code: load the sub-map, namespace, splice, recurse. Lives in `soramech-compile.sh` or a sibling.\n- The encap_mode flag is one field in the box JSON, one branch in the rewrite pass, one branch in the dispatch's \"is this a real call or a runtime sub-graph?\" decision (and the latter is just \"what spec answers this `lang`\").\n- Output packing/unpacking is the same helper library either way (used at the boundary in runtime mode, used at the inlined `write`-replacement in inline mode if the user wants the blob format).\n\nSo \"both\" is roughly **Path B's work plus a graph-rewrite pass for Path A's transform**. It's bigger than either path alone, but the *runtime* surface area is just Path B's spec; everything Path A adds happens at compile time and disappears before the runtime sees the graph. That separation keeps \"both\" from compounding complexity at the hot path — the dispatch loop never branches on `encap_mode`.\n\n**One last thing worth surfacing**\n\nIf `encap_mode` is a per-box choice, the user can mix freely in one parent. Stats-pipeline as inline (perf-critical, known at compile time); user-template-loader as runtime (dynamic, hot-reloadable). The semantics are the same from the parent's perspective — both look like a call box with declared inputs and outputs. The difference is invisible to the parent's other boxes; it only shows up in build output (one is gone, one stays) and in the runtime profile (one calls inline, one calls through the map spec).\n\nThat clean separation — \"both modes look the same to the rest of the parent\" — is what makes \"both\" cheaper than it sounds. The encapsulating box's *contract* is the same; only the implementation behind it varies.\n\nWhat's your read — is the schema-at-compile-time constraint OK for the runtime use case you have in mind?"
      }],

For Lua, it's a\n231\tfew lines that decode via the existing JSON / native helpers\n232\tbased on `input_native`.\n233\t\n234\tThe user can run the shim without edits and behaviour matches the\n235\tno-shim default. Edits typically replace one branch (the\n236\tspecific weird case) and leave the rest alone.         "type":"text",
        "text":"**246 in short**\n\nA per-input-port shim the user writes — runs before the consumer's `invoke` sees the value, intercepts raw bytes plus the `which_ring` tag, and produces translated native bytes the spec then receives as if the default decode had produced them.\n\nTwo distinct motivating cases — and you can see why they share the same mechanism:\n\n- **Cross-language ambiguity**: a C++ class arriving at a C box, a `void *` carrying a libcurl handle, a tagged union whose discriminator is on a separate port. JSON's structure can't carry these losslessly; the user has knowledge the spec can't ever infer. Per-port shim is where that knowledge lives.\n- **Same-language user transformation**: a C box emits a float; the next C box wants it truncated-then-rounded. Or degrees → radians on one port. Or clamp-to-range. No language boundary, just user semantics that don't belong in the box's main function.\n\n**The principled choices behind the design**\n\n- **Per-port, not per-box.** Each port carries one kind of value; only the weird ports get shims. A box with three string inputs and one C++ class input writes one shim, not four.\n- **Input-side only.** A producer's spec always knows how to serialise its own language's values — full reflective access to its own type system. Reading is the asymmetric direction: the receiver can't infer what the sender meant by an opaque pointer. So shims live where the ambiguity is.\n- **Shim's output is always treated as native by `invoke`.** The shim does the decode; the consumer's main function sees native bytes, same as if a same-language producer had pushed them.\n\n**Where it sits architecturally**\n\nSlots into the existing dual-ring shape from 312. The shim sees both the raw bytes AND the per-cell `which_ring` tag, so it can branch on \"this is JSON from cross-lang\" vs \"this is native from same-lang\" inside the shim. The default decode runs when no shim is attached — nothing about the existing fast path changes.\n\nComposes with 313's merge: translation files are just another function in the same-language merged module.\n\nComposes with 245's wire-colouring (the goldenrod-cheddar colour activates automatically once a port has a custom translation attached — visual marker that this wire is non-default).\n\n**Status, honestly**\n\nOpen. No implementation. Nothing blocks it:\n\n- 312's dual-ring is in place (shim's `which_ring` argument has its source).\n- The dispatch's per-port read loop exists (the branch hook lives in `read_inputs`).\n- The compile pipeline (309) already walks per-box source; extending the walk to per-port translation files is the same pattern.\n- The editor side has the inspector infrastructure for input-port rows.\n\n**Implementation shape, ~6 slices in order of dependency**\n\nThe body lays out a sensible sequence:\n1. Box JSON schema gains optional per-input `custom_translation` path field. Loader reads it onto `box_t->inputs[i]`. Pure data plumbing.\n2. HTTP backend CRUD for translation files (editor-side).\n3. Editor inspector New / View / Delete buttons.\n4. Box-delete confirmation when ports have attached translations.\n5. Dispatch input-read branch: if `custom_translation` set, route through the shim before default decode.\n6. Compile pipeline packages translation files into `compiled/translations/` and per-language source bundle.\n\nSlices 1, 5, 6 are the C runtime work — that's the path that makes the feature *usable* from hand-edited box JSON without any editor UI. Slices 2, 3, 4 are the editor side that makes it ergonomic. The minimum-viable feature could ship as just 1 + 5 + 6.\n\n**One thing the body acknowledges as a hard limit**\n\nA shim only sees its own port's bytes. Cross-port logic (a union with a discriminator on a sibling port) doesn't fit the per-port isolation. The body's stance: that case falls back to plain decode-then-validate inside the box's main function. Honest — per-port is the principled abstraction, and cross-port logic is what the main function already exists for.\n\n**Where you might be in deciding about it**\n\n- Schema-and-runtime slice (1 + 5 + 6) is small and clean — maybe a few hundred lines of C across loader, dispatch, and the compile script. Solid foundation.\n- Editor slice (2 + 3 + 4) is JavaScript work; separately scoped.\n- The whole thing is opt-in per port; existing maps don't change.\n\nWhat's your angle on it — scoping the runtime slice, or just mapping the design?"
      }],
